````
sections.Purpose: Write release notes from your commit history. Commits that follow the conventional format (`feat: ...`, `fix(scope): ...`, `feat!: ...`) are grouped into Features, Bug fixes, Documentation and so on, with breaking changes called out first.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+, and `git` on your PATH for real repositories.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python changelog_generator.py [--repo PATH] [--since TAG_OR_DATE] [--version 1.2.0]
                              [--date YYYY-MM-DD] [-o CHANGELOG.md --apply]
python changelog_generator.py --log git-log.txt
```
By default it reads `git log` from the repository; `--since v1.1.0` limits it to commits after that tag. The section is printed; with `-o` and `--apply` it is added under the `# Changelog` title, above older releases. To use a saved history instead (for example on the website), create one with:
```bash
git log --date=short --pretty=format:'@@%H%x1f%an%x1f%ae%x1f%ad%x1f%s' > git-log.txt
```
sections.Example:
```bash
python changelog_generator.py --log git-log.txt --version 1.2.0 --date 2026-01-14
```
```
sections.[1.2.0] - 2026-01-14:
### BREAKING CHANGES

- drop support for Node 16 (d0e1f2a)

### Features

- add password reset flow (a1b2c3d)
- **ui:** add dark mode toggle (f6a7b8c)
- export orders as CSV (c9d0e1f)
- add a very long subject line that goes well beyond the recommended seventy two character limit (e1f2a3b)
- initial project setup (f2a3b4c)

### Bug fixes

- handle empty cart in checkout (b2c3d4e)
- drop support for Node 16 (d0e1f2a)

### Refactoring

- split the router into modules (e5f6a7b)

### Documentation

- update install guide (c3d4e5f)

### Chores

- bump dependencies (b8c9d0e)
```
sections.Notes:
- Commits without a recognised `type:` prefix are counted and left out rather than guessed at.
- Each entry ends with the short commit hash so you can trace it.
- Review the result: a changelog is for people, so reword anything unclear.

tools.name: branch-lister
tools.summary: List local git branches with how long ago each was last committed to.

schema.description: List branches by last activity.

arguments.help: read a saved for-each-ref file instead of git
treat this date as today, YYYY-MM-DD (for testing)

sections.Purpose: See which branches are alive and which have been forgotten. Every local branch is listed newest first with its last commit date, a friendly age (`4d ago`, `3mo ago`), the author and the last commit message, and branches that haven't moved in a while are marked `STALE`.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+, and `git` on your PATH for real repositories.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python branch_lister.py [--repo PATH] [--stale-days N]
python branch_lister.py --refs branches.txt [--today YYYY-MM-DD]
```
By default it asks git for the local branches. To use a saved list instead (for example on the website), create one with:
```bash
git for-each-ref --format='%(refname:short)%1f%(committerdate:short)%1f%(authorname)%1f%(subject)' refs/heads > branches.txt
```
`--stale-days` sets how many days of silence count as stale (default 90).
sections.Example:
```bash
python branch_lister.py --refs branches.txt --today 2026-01-13
```
```
main               2026-01-13     today  Ada Lovelace  feat: add password reset flow
feature/dark-mode  2026-01-09    4d ago  Lin Chen      feat(ui): add dark mode toggle
release/1.0        2025-12-15    4w ago  Ada Lovelace  chore: prepare release 1.0
fix/cart-bug       2025-11-20    7w ago  Lin Chen      fix: cart total rounding
old/experiment     2025-06-02   7mo ago  Max Weber     try a new layout  STALE
5 branch(es), 1 older than 90 days.
```
sections.Notes:
- Read-only: it never deletes or changes a branch. When you are ready to clean up, check `git branch --merged` first.
- `--today` pins the date, which makes the output repeatable.
- Ages are measured from each branch's last commit date.

tools.name: repo-size-reporter
tools.summary: Report how big a repository is and which files and file types take the most space.

schema.description: Report repository size.

arguments.help: how many big files to list (5)
also count node_modules and virtual environments

sections.Purpose: Find out why a repository is heavy. It reports the size of the working tree and of the `.git` history separately, lists the biggest files, and breaks the total down by file type, so an accidentally committed video or data dump stands out.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python repo_size_reporter.py [FOLDER] [-n TOP] [--include-deps]
```
`node_modules` and virtual environments are skipped unless you pass `--include-deps`. If the folder contains a `.git` directory its size is shown on its own line.
sections.Example:
```bash
python repo_size_reporter.py demo-project
```
```
Working tree: 723 B in 5 file(s)

Largest 5 file(s):
      254 B  src/app.js
      206 B  package.json
      128 B  src/utils.js
       93 B  tests/app.test.js
       42 B  LICENSE

By file type:
  .js         3 file(s)      475 B   66%
  .json       1 file(s)      206 B   28%
  (none)      1 file(s)       42 B    6%
```
sections.Notes:
- Read-only.
- A very large `.git` size usually means big files were committed at some point, even if they were deleted later; they remain in the history.
- Sizes are the files' byte sizes, not disk blocks, so they can differ slightly from your file manager.

tools.name: pdf-merger
tools.summary: Merge several PDF files into one, in the order you give them.

schema.description: Merge PDF files into one.

arguments.help: PDF files, in the order to merge
add a bookmark for each source file
really write the merged file (default is a dry run)

sections.Purpose: Combine several PDFs into one document, in exactly the order you list them. Handy for bundling scans, chapters or receipts into a single file. Optional bookmarks make it easy to jump between the original parts.
sections.Install:
Needs `pypdf`:
```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```
sections.Usage:
```bash
python pdf_merger.py FILE.pdf FILE.pdf [...] [-o merged.pdf] [--bookmarks] [--apply]
```
Dry run by default: it shows each file's page count and what the result would hold. Pass `--apply` to write the merged file. An existing output file is never overwritten.
sections.Example:
```bash
python pdf_merger.py report.pdf handbook.pdf -o combined.pdf --bookmarks
```
```
report.pdf: 3 page(s)
handbook.pdf: 5 page(s)
Dry run: would write combined.pdf with 8 page(s). Use --apply to do it.
```
sections.Notes:
- The source files are never changed.
- A file that isn't a readable PDF (or is password protected) stops the run with a message naming it.
- To split a PDF again, see `pdf-splitter`.

tools.name: pdf-splitter
tools.summary: Split a PDF by page ranges, or into fixed-size parts (one page each by default).

schema.description: Split a PDF into parts.

arguments.help: pages to extract into ONE file, e.g. 1-3,5,8-
one file per N pages (1 = one per page)
really write the files (default is a dry run)

sections.Purpose: Pull pages out of a PDF. Either extract a selection (such as pages 1 to 3 and 5) into one new file, or break the whole document into parts of a fixed size, down to one file per page.
sections.Install:
Needs `pypdf`:
```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```
sections.Usage:
```bash
python pdf_splitter.py FILE.pdf --pages 1-3,5,8- [-o OUTDIR] [--apply]
python pdf_splitter.py FILE.pdf --every N [-o OUTDIR] [--apply]
```
Use exactly one of `--pages` or `--every`. Page numbers start at 1, and `8-` means page 8 to the end. Dry run by default: it lists the files it would create. Pass `--apply` to write them next to the original (or into `-o`).
sections.Example:
```bash
python pdf_splitter.py handbook.pdf --every 2
```
```
handbook_part001.pdf  (pages 1-2 of 5)
handbook_part002.pdf  (pages 3-4 of 5)
handbook_part003.pdf  (page 5 of 5)
Would write 3 file(s). Use --apply to do it.
```
sections.Notes:
- The original PDF is never changed.
- Output names are `<name>_pages_<ranges>.pdf` or `<name>_part001.pdf`, `<name>_part002.pdf` and so on.
- A page number outside the document stops the run with a clear message.

tools.name: pdf-page-counter
tools.summary: Count the pages in PDF files and folders of PDFs.

schema.description: Count pages across PDFs.

sections.Purpose: Find out how many pages a stack of PDFs adds up to, for example before printing, estimating translation work or checking an upload limit. It lists each file with its page count and size, then the grand total.
sections.Install:
Needs `pypdf`:
```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```
sections.Usage:
```bash
python pdf_page_counter.py PATH [PATH ...] [-r]
```
`PATH` can be PDF files or folders. Folders are searched for `.pdf` files, including subfolders when you pass `-r`. The exit code is 1 if any file had to be skipped.
sections.Example:
```bash
python pdf_page_counter.py report.pdf handbook.pdf scan_0001.pdf
```
```
report.pdf         3 page(s)     1.4 KB
handbook.pdf       5 page(s)     2.0 KB
scan_0001.pdf      1 page(s)      679 B
3 PDF(s), 9 page(s) in total.
```
sections.Notes:
- Password-protected and damaged files are reported as skipped instead of stopping the run.
- Sizes are the files' sizes on disk.
- Read-only.

tools.name: pdf-text-extractor
tools.summary: Extract the text from PDF files, to the screen or into .txt files.

schema.description: Extract text from PDFs.

arguments.help: characters of each file to show (0 = all; default 600)
really write the .txt files (default only prints a preview)

sections.Purpose: Get the text out of PDFs so you can search it, quote it or feed it to other tools. By default it prints a short preview of each file; with `--apply` it saves each PDF's full text as a `.txt` file.
sections.Install:
Needs `pypdf`:
```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```
sections.Usage:
```bash
python pdf_text_extractor.py FILE.pdf [FILE.pdf ...] [--markers] [--preview N] [-o OUTDIR --apply]
```
`--markers` adds a `--- page N ---` line before each page. `--preview 0` shows the whole text. Without `--apply` nothing is written. With it, `report.pdf` becomes `report.txt` next to the PDF (or in `-o`).
sections.Example:
```bash
python pdf_text_extractor.py report.pdf --markers
```
```
== report.pdf: 3 page(s), 42 word(s)
--- page 1 ---
Quarterly report
Page one: summary of results.
Revenue grew 12 percent.

--- page 2 ---
Page two: details
Costs were flat compared with last quarter.

--- page 3 ---
Page three: outlook
We expect steady growth next quarter.

Preview only. Use --apply to save .txt files.
```
sections.Notes:
- This reads the text layer of the PDF. A scan made of pictures has no text layer, and the tool says so instead of printing nothing.
- Password-protected or damaged files are reported and skipped; the exit code is then 1.
- Layout (columns, tables) is flattened to plain text, so check anything that depends on position.

tools.name: pdf-rotator
tools.summary: Rotate all or some pages of a PDF, writing the result to a new file.

schema.description: Rotate pages of a PDF.

arguments.help: pages to rotate, e.g. 1-3,5 (default: all pages)
really write the file (default is a dry run)

sections.Purpose: Fix sideways scans. Turn every page of a PDF, or just the ones you choose, by 90, 180 or 270 degrees clockwise. The result is saved as a new file and the original stays untouched.
sections.Install:
Needs `pypdf`:
```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```
sections.Usage:
```bash
python pdf_rotator.py FILE.pdf --angle 90|180|270 [--pages 1-3,5] [-o OUTPUT] [--apply]
```
Without `--pages` every page is rotated. Dry run by default: it tells you what would happen. Pass `--apply` to write `<name>_rotated.pdf` (or the file you name with `-o`). An existing output file is never overwritten.
sections.Example:
```bash
python pdf_rotator.py handbook.pdf --angle 90 --pages 2-3
```
```
handbook.pdf: rotate 2 of 5 page(s) by 90 degrees
Dry run: would write handbook_rotated.pdf. Use --apply to do it.
```
sections.Notes:
- Rotation is clockwise and adds to any rotation a page already has.
- Page numbers start at 1; `3-` means page 3 to the end.
- The page content is not re-rendered, so there is no loss of quality.

tools.name: markdown-to-pdf
tools.summary: Turn a markdown file into a clean, readable PDF.

schema.description: Convert markdown to PDF.

arguments.help: really write the PDF (default is a dry run)

sections.Purpose: Turn notes, READMEs and reports written in markdown into a tidy A4 PDF you can print or share. It handles headings, paragraphs, bullet and numbered lists, code blocks and horizontal rules, and tidies links, bold and italics into plain text.
sections.Install:
Needs `fpdf2`:
```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```
sections.Usage:
```bash
python markdown_to_pdf.py FILE.md [-o OUTPUT.pdf] [--apply]
```
Dry run by default: it renders in memory and reports how many pages the PDF would have. Pass `--apply` to write `<name>.pdf` (or the file you name with `-o`). An existing file is never overwritten.
sections.Example:
```bash
python markdown_to_pdf.py README.md
```
```
README.md: 9 block(s) -> 1 page(s), 1237 bytes
Dry run: would write README.pdf. Use --apply to do it.
```
sections.Notes:
- It uses the PDF standard fonts, which only cover Western European characters; anything else is replaced with `?`. Curly quotes and dashes are converted to plain ones.
- Tables and images in the markdown are not rendered, only their text.
- For heavily styled documents, a browser's "print to PDF" on rendered HTML will look richer.

tools.name: invoice-renamer
tools.summary: Rename invoice PDFs to 'date_vendor_number.pdf' using the text inside them.

schema.description: Rename invoice PDFs from their contents.

arguments.help: really rename the files (default is a dry run)

sections.Purpose: Turn a folder of anonymous scans such as `scan_0001.pdf` into files you can find again: `2026-01-15_ACME-Supplies-Ltd_INV-1042.pdf`. It reads the text on the first pages, finds the invoice date, the vendor (the first line) and the invoice number, and builds the name from them.
sections.Install:
Needs `pypdf`:
```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```
sections.Usage:
```bash
python invoice_renamer.py FOLDER [--pattern "{date}_{vendor}_{number}"] [--monthfirst] [--apply]
```
Dry run by default: it shows each rename. Pass `--apply` to rename the files. Dates like `12/02/2026` are read day first (12 February); add `--monthfirst` for US style. The pattern can use any of `{date}`, `{vendor}` and `{number}`.
sections.Example:
```bash
python invoice_renamer.py .
```
```
skip handbook.pdf: couldn't find everything the pattern needs (found vendor=Handbook chapter 1)
skip report.pdf: couldn't find everything the pattern needs (found vendor=Quarterly report)
scan_0001.pdf -> 2026-01-15_ACME-Supplies-Ltd_INV-1042.pdf
scan_0002.pdf -> 2026-02-12_Blue-Sky-Hosting_BS-7781.pdf
Would rename 2 invoice(s), skipped 2. Use --apply to do it.
```
sections.Notes:
- Invoices where a needed part can't be found are skipped and left alone, with a note of what was found.
- It never overwrites an existing file, and two invoices that would get the same name are not both renamed.
- Scanned images with no text layer can't be read (they need OCR first).

tools.name: pdf-metadata-viewer
tools.summary: Show a PDF's title, author, dates, page count and page size.

schema.description: Show PDF metadata.

sections.Purpose: Look inside a PDF without opening it: title, author, creating program, dates, page count, page size (recognised as A4, Letter and so on) and whether it is password protected. Useful for checking documents before you send them, since metadata often reveals more than you intended.
sections.Install:
Needs `pypdf`:
```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```
sections.Usage:
```bash
python pdf_metadata_viewer.py FILE.pdf [FILE.pdf ...] [--json]
```
sections.Example:
```bash
python pdf_metadata_viewer.py report.pdf handbook.pdf
```
```
report.pdf
  bytes      1462
  encrypted  False
  pages      3
  title      Quarterly Report
  author     Ada Lovelace
  creator    Demo Writer
  page size  210 x 297 mm (A4)
handbook.pdf
  bytes      2028
  encrypted  False
  pages      5
  title      Team Handbook
  author     People Team
  page size  210 x 297 mm (A4)
```
sections.Notes:
- Only fields that are present are shown. Many PDFs have no title or author.
- Encrypted files show just their size and encryption status, since the rest can't be read without the password.
- Read-only. To remove or edit metadata you need a PDF editor.

tools.name: docx-text-extractor
tools.summary: Pull plain text (or simple markdown) out of Word .docx files without Word.

schema.description: Extract text from .docx files.

arguments.help: keep headings, bullets and tables as markdown
really write the files (default only prints the text)

sections.Purpose: Read Word documents without Word. It pulls out the text in order, including bullet points and tables, and can keep headings, bullets and tables as markdown so the result drops straight into notes, a wiki or a search index.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python docx_text_extractor.py FILE.docx [FILE.docx ...] [--markdown] [-o OUTDIR --apply]
```
The text is printed; with `--apply` each document is saved as `<name>.txt` (or `<name>.md` with `--markdown`) next to it or in `-o`.
sections.Example:
```bash
python docx_text_extractor.py contract.docx --markdown
```
```
== contract.docx: 44 word(s)
# Service Agreement

This agreement is made between Demo Corp and the client.

Payment is due within 30 days of the invoice date.

- Confidentiality applies to both parties.

| Item | Price |
| --- | --- |
| Consulting | $1,200 |

Preview only. Use --apply to save the text to files.
```
sections.Notes:
- Only the modern `.docx` format is supported, not the old `.doc`.
- Headers, footers, footnotes and text boxes are not included, only the main body.
- It never opens the file in Word, so macros cannot run. Very large documents are refused.

tools.name: images-to-pdf
tools.summary: Combine images into a single PDF, one image per page.

schema.description: Combine images into one PDF.

arguments.help: a4 pages with the image centred, or pages sized to each image
really write the PDF (default is a dry run)

sections.Purpose: Turn photos, scans or screenshots into one PDF, one image per page, in the order you give. Choose neat A4 pages with the picture centred, or pages that match each image's own size.
sections.Install:
Needs Pillow (and `pypdf` only for the tests):
```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```
sections.Usage:
```bash
python images_to_pdf.py IMAGE_OR_FOLDER [...] [--size a4|fit] [-o images.pdf] [--apply]
```
A folder contributes its images sorted by name; individual files keep the order you list them. Dry run by default: it lists the pages. Pass `--apply` to write the PDF. An existing output file is never overwritten.
sections.Example:
```bash
python images_to_pdf.py "Holiday Photo 01.JPG" "Holiday Photo 02.JPG" logo.png -o album.pdf
```
```
Holiday Photo 01.JPG: 320x200
Holiday Photo 02.JPG: 300x200
logo.png: 240x120
3 page(s), a4 size
Dry run: would write album.pdf. Use --apply to do it.
```
sections.Notes:
- Transparent images are flattened onto white, and photos are turned upright using their EXIF orientation.
- On A4 pages, wide images get landscape pages and tall ones portrait pages, with a small margin.
- Unreadable files are skipped with a message.

tools.name: bulk-url-checker
tools.summary: Check the HTTP status of many URLs at once: working, redirecting or broken.

schema.description: Check the status of many URLs.

arguments.help: URLs, or text files with one URL per line
only list what would be checked (no requests are made)

sections.Purpose: Find out which links in a list still work. Every URL gets its HTTP status, response time and the final address after redirects, and the run exits with 1 if anything is broken, so it works in scheduled checks and CI.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python bulk_url_checker.py URL_OR_FILE [URL_OR_FILE ...] [--plan] [--timeout SEC] [--workers N]
```
Pass URLs directly or text files with one URL per line (`#` starts a comment). Duplicates are removed (`https://Example.com` and `https://example.com/` count as one). `--plan` only lists what would be checked and sends nothing. Requests run several at a time, politely, with a `HEAD` request first and `GET` only if the server refuses `HEAD`.
sections.Example:
```bash
python bulk_url_checker.py urls.txt --plan
```
```
SKIP  not an http(s) URL: not a url
WOULD CHECK  https://example.com/
WOULD CHECK  https://www.python.org/
WOULD CHECK  http://example.org/page?utm_source=news&id=7
Would check 3 URL(s); 1 invalid, 2 duplicate(s) removed.
```
sections.Notes:
- Checking URLs needs network access, so the website demo can only run the `--plan` mode; run the real check on your own computer.
- Only check sites you are allowed to; keep `--workers` low for small servers.
- A timeout or connection failure is reported as `FAIL` with the reason.

tools.name: link-extractor
tools.summary: List the links on a web page (a URL or a saved .html file), sorted into internal and external.

schema.description: Extract the links from a web page.

arguments.help: a page URL, or a saved .html file
page address, to resolve links in a saved file

sections.Purpose: See every link on a page at a glance. It lists each unique link with its visible text, tells internal links from external ones, and marks links with `rel="nofollow"`. Useful for audits, migrations and finding what a page points to.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python link_extractor.py URL_OR_FILE [--base PAGE_URL] [--only internal|external]
```
Give a page address to download it, or a saved `.html` file (add `--base` so relative links such as `/products` can be turned into full addresses and classified). Links like `mailto:`, `tel:`, `javascript:` and `#anchors` are skipped, and repeated links appear once.
sections.Example:
```bash
python link_extractor.py page.html --base https://example.com/
```
```
internal  https://example.com/products  'Products'
internal  https://example.com/about.html  'About us'
internal  https://example.com/docs  'Docs'
external  https://partner.test/page  'partner' [nofollow]
4 unique link(s): 3 internal, 1 external.
```
sections.Notes:
- Downloading a page needs network access. The website demo works from the sample saved page; with a real URL, run it on your own computer.
- Pages are read up to 2 MB. Links added later by JavaScript are not seen, because the page is not run.
- Read-only.

tools.name: robots-checker
tools.summary: Check whether a URL or path is allowed by a site's robots.txt, for a given crawler name.

schema.description: Check URLs against robots.txt.

arguments.help: a saved robots.txt to check against

sections.Purpose: Before scraping or crawling a site, find out what its `robots.txt` allows. Give it URLs and it tells you which are allowed or blocked for your crawler name, which rule decided it, the requested crawl delay and any sitemaps listed.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python robots_checker.py URL [URL ...] [--agent NAME]
python robots_checker.py PATH [PATH ...] --robots robots.txt [--agent NAME]
```
With full URLs it downloads each site's `robots.txt` once. With `--robots` it uses a saved file instead and you can give plain paths such as `/private/page`. The exit code is 1 if anything is blocked.
sections.Example:
```bash
python robots_checker.py /private/public/page /private/secret /admin/panel /products --robots robots.txt
```
```
ALLOWED /private/public/page  (rule: Allow /private/public/)
BLOCKED /private/secret  (rule: Disallow /private)
BLOCKED /admin/panel  (rule: Disallow /admin/)
ALLOWED /products
Crawl-delay for *: 5 seconds between requests.
Sitemaps: https://example.com/sitemap.xml
```
sections.Notes:
- It follows the standard rules: the most specific (longest) matching rule wins, `*` and a trailing `$` are supported, and a crawler-specific group beats the `*` group.
- A missing `robots.txt` (404) means everything is allowed.
- Fetching a real `robots.txt` needs network access; the website demo uses the sample file.
- This is a courtesy check, not permission: sites can also have terms of use.

tools.name: rss-digest
tools.summary: Turn RSS and Atom feeds into a short markdown digest of the newest items.

schema.description: Make a markdown digest from feeds.

arguments.help: feed URLs or saved feed files
only items on or after this date, YYYY-MM-DD
save the digest to this file
really write --output (default only prints the digest)

sections.Purpose: Skim your feeds without opening a reader. It reads RSS and Atom feeds, picks the newest items from each, tidies the summaries (no HTML) and writes a short markdown digest you can read, paste into notes or email to yourself.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python rss_digest.py FEED [FEED ...] [--since YYYY-MM-DD] [--limit N] [-o digest.md --apply]
```
`FEED` is a feed URL or a saved feed file. By default it shows the 5 newest items per feed. The digest is printed; to save it pass `-o` with `--apply` (an existing file is never overwritten).
sections.Example:
```bash
python rss_digest.py feed.xml --since 2026-01-01 --limit 3
```
```
# Feed digest (3 item(s) from 1 feed(s))
sections.ACME Blog:
- **Launching widgets 2.0** (2026-01-13) - Faster, lighter and cheaper than ever. [read](https://example.com/blog/widgets-2)
- **How we test our widgets** (2026-01-12) - A look inside the lab. [read](https://example.com/blog/testing)
- **Holiday opening hours** (2026-01-02) - We are closed on public holidays. [read](https://example.com/blog/holidays)
```
sections.Notes:
- Downloading a feed needs network access; the website demo uses a sample feed file.
- Feeds that contain a DOCTYPE or entity definitions are refused, which protects against malicious XML.
- Items with no date are listed after dated ones and are left out when you use `--since`.

tools.name: header-inspector
tools.summary: Show the HTTP response headers for a URL (or a saved header dump) with plain-English notes.

schema.description: Inspect HTTP response headers.

arguments.help: a URL, or a saved header dump (e.g. from curl -I)

sections.Purpose: See what a web server says about itself. It prints a URL's HTTP response headers in a tidy table and adds plain-English notes: the content type and size, how long browsers may cache it, where it redirects, what software it announces, how many cookies it sets and whether HSTS (forced HTTPS) is on.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python header_inspector.py URL [--follow]
python header_inspector.py saved-headers.txt
```
For a URL it sends one `HEAD` request and shows the first response, so a redirect shows its `Location` instead of being followed (add `--follow` to follow it). You can also read a saved dump, for example one made with `curl -I https://example.com > saved-headers.txt`.
sections.Example:
```bash
python header_inspector.py headers.txt
```
```
HTTP/2 200
  content-type               text/html; charset=utf-8
  server                     nginx/1.24
  cache-control              max-age=3600
  content-length             18211
  strict-transport-security  max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains
  x-powered-by               Express
  set-cookie                 session=abc123; HttpOnly
  set-cookie                 theme=dark; Path=/
  x-content-type-options     nosniff

Notes:
  - Content: text/html (17.8 KB)
  - Caching: reusable for 1 hour
  - Server software announced: nginx/1.24
  - Technology revealed by X-Powered-By: Express
  - Sets 2 cookies
  - HSTS is on
```
sections.Notes:
- Requesting a URL needs network access; the website demo reads the sample file.
- Repeated headers such as `set-cookie` are all shown.
- Read-only. Only inspect sites you are allowed to; for a full security review see the security tools later in this challenge.

tools.name: page-title-fetcher
tools.summary: Get the title (and description) of web pages or saved .html files.

schema.description: Fetch page titles.

sections.Purpose: Turn a list of links into readable ones. For each page it reads the `<title>` (and optionally the meta description), so you can label bookmarks, build a link list for a document or spot pages with a missing title.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python page_title_fetcher.py SOURCE [SOURCE ...] [--description] [--csv]
```
A `SOURCE` is a page URL or a saved `.html` file. Pages are fetched several at a time, and only the first 256 KB of each is read. `--csv` prints a table you can open in a spreadsheet. The exit code is 1 if any page couldn't be read.
sections.Example:
```bash
python page_title_fetcher.py page.html page-two.html --description
```
```
ACME Widgets - Home  <-  page.html
    Quality widgets since 1999
Contact ACME  <-  page-two.html
2 of 2 page(s) read.
```
sections.Notes:
- Fetching URLs needs network access; the website demo reads the sample pages.
- Whitespace and line breaks inside titles are collapsed into single spaces.
- Titles set by JavaScript after the page loads are not seen.

tools.name: broken-link-finder
tools.summary: Find broken links on a web page: it reads the page, then checks every link on it.

schema.description: Find broken links on a page.

arguments.help: page URL, or a saved .html file (use --base with a file)
the page's address, to resolve relative links
only list the links that would be checked (no requests)
seconds to wait between requests, to be gentle on small sites

sections.Purpose: Catch dead links before your visitors do. It reads one page, collects every link on it and checks each one, listing the ones that return an error or don't answer at all. Handy for a website you maintain or documentation you publish.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python broken_link_finder.py PAGE_URL [--only internal|external] [--max N] [--delay SEC] [--plan]
python broken_link_finder.py saved.html --base https://example.com/ --plan
```
A saved `.html` file needs `--base` so relative links can be resolved. `--plan` lists the links that would be checked without sending any request. `--delay` waits between requests (and checks one at a time), which is kinder to small servers. The exit code is 1 when any link is broken.
sections.Example:
```bash
python broken_link_finder.py page.html --base https://example.com/ --plan
```
```
WOULD CHECK  https://example.com/products
WOULD CHECK  https://example.com/about.html
WOULD CHECK  https://example.com/docs
WOULD CHECK  https://partner.test/page
Would check 4 link(s) found on page.html.
```
sections.Notes:
- Checking links needs network access, so the website demo can only run `--plan`. Run the real check on your own computer.
- It checks the links on a single page, not a whole site, and stops at 100 links unless you raise `--max`.
- Only check sites you own or have permission to test. Some sites block automated checks and may report a working link as broken.

tools.name: sitemap-lister
tools.summary: List every URL in a sitemap.xml (a URL or a saved file), with last-modified dates.

schema.description: List the URLs in a sitemap.

arguments.help: only entries modified on or after YYYY-MM-DD
show at most this many (0 = all)

sections.Purpose: Get a clean list of every page a site publishes. It reads a `sitemap.xml` (or the sitemap index that points to several), shows each URL with its last-modified date and lets you filter by text or by date. A good starting point for audits, redirects and crawl planning.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python sitemap_lister.py SITEMAP [--contains TEXT] [--newer-than YYYY-MM-DD] [--limit N] [--csv]
```
`SITEMAP` is a sitemap URL or a saved `.xml` file. A sitemap index lists its child sitemaps; run the tool on each child to see the pages. `--csv` prints a table for a spreadsheet.
sections.Example:
```bash
python sitemap_lister.py sitemap.xml --newer-than 2025-12-01
```
```
2026-01-10  https://example.com/
2026-01-08  https://example.com/products
2025-12-20  https://example.com/products/widget-a
3 of 5 URL(s).
```
sections.Notes:
- Downloading a sitemap needs network access; the website demo reads the sample file.
- Dates are taken from the `lastmod` field, which not every site fills in; undated entries are hidden when you filter by date.
- Sitemaps containing a DOCTYPE or entity definitions are refused, which protects against malicious XML.

tools.name: url-expander
tools.summary: Follow redirects to see where a short link really goes, and strip tracking junk from URLs.

schema.description: Expand short links and clean tracking junk.

arguments.help: don't contact the server; only clean the URL

sections.Purpose: See where a link really goes before you click it. It follows the redirects of short links (bit.ly style) and tracking links one hop at a time, reports the final address and can strip tracking parameters such as `utm_source` and `fbclid` to give you a clean URL.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python url_expander.py URL [URL ...] [--clean] [--chain] [--max-hops N] [--no-follow]
```
By default each URL is followed through its redirects. `--chain` lists every hop with its HTTP status, `--clean` removes tracking parameters from the final address, and `--no-follow` skips the network entirely and only cleans the URL you gave. Redirect loops and over-long chains are detected and reported.
sections.Example:
```bash
python url_expander.py "http://Example.org/page?utm_source=news&id=7&fbclid=abc" --clean --no-follow
```
```
http://Example.org/page?utm_source=news&id=7&fbclid=abc
  -> http://example.org/page?id=7
```
sections.Notes:
- Following links needs network access, so the website demo runs the `--no-follow` cleaning mode. Following redirects works on your own computer.
- The tool only asks the server for headers and never downloads the page.
- Only the tracking parameters it knows are removed; the rest of the query string is kept as it was.

tools.name: ping-checker
tools.summary: Ping hosts and log the response times, or analyse saved ping output.

schema.description: Ping hosts and log response times.

arguments.help: host names or IP addresses to ping
analyse a saved ping output file instead
append each result to this CSV file

sections.Purpose: Keep an eye on your connection. It pings one or more hosts, summarises replies, packet loss and response times (min, average, max) and can log every check to a CSV so you can see when things got slow. It also reads saved ping output from Linux, macOS or Windows.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. It uses your system's `ping` command.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python ping_checker.py HOST [HOST ...] [-c COUNT] [--log pings.csv]
python ping_checker.py --parse ping-output.txt
```
Run it on a schedule (cron or Windows Task Scheduler) with `--log` to build up a history. The exit code is 1 if any host sent no replies at all. Host names are validated before anything is run, and nothing goes through a shell.
sections.Example:
```bash
python ping_checker.py --parse ping.txt
```
```
example.com              4/5 replies, 20% loss, min 11.9 / avg 21.1 / max 48.2 ms
```
sections.Notes:
- Pinging needs a real network and the `ping` program, so the website demo can only analyse saved output with `--parse`.
- Some networks block ping; "no replies" doesn't always mean the host is down.
- The CSV has the columns `timestamp, host, sent, received, loss_percent, min_ms, avg_ms, max_ms`.

tools.name: web-scraper
tools.summary: Scrape text or attributes from a page using CSS selectors, honoring robots.txt.

schema.description: Scrape a page with CSS selectors.

arguments.help: a page URL, or a saved .html file
what to scrape; repeat for several, e.g. title=h1 or 'a.buy'
read this attribute (href, src...) instead of the text
page address, to resolve relative links
robots.txt to check a URL against

sections.Purpose: Pull exactly the bits you want out of a web page. Give it one or more CSS selectors and it prints the text (or an attribute such as `href`) of every match, as plain text, JSON or CSV. When you point it at a live URL it reads the site's `robots.txt` first and politely refuses to fetch pages the site has asked bots to stay away from.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python web_scraper.py SOURCE -s "[NAME=]CSS" [-s ...] [--attr href] [--format text|json|csv]
                      [--limit N] [--base URL] [--robots-file robots.txt]
```
`SOURCE` is a URL or a saved `.html` file. Selectors support tags, `.class`, `#id`, `[attr]`, `[attr=value]` (also `^=`, `$=`, `*=`), the descendant and `>` combinators, and comma lists. Give a selector a name with `price=li b` and the CSV gets a column for it. The exit code is 2 when `robots.txt` disallows the page and 1 when nothing matched.
sections.Example:
```bash
python web_scraper.py page.html -s "link=a" -s "internal=nav a" --attr href --base https://example.com/
```
```
[link] https://example.com/products
[link] https://example.com/about.html
[link] https://example.com/docs
[link] https://example.com/#top
[link] mailto:hello@example.com
[link] https://example.com/docs
[link] https://partner.test/page
[link] javascript:void(0)
[internal] https://example.com/products
[internal] https://example.com/about.html
[internal] https://example.com/docs
[internal] https://example.com/#top
```
sections.Notes:
- Only one page is fetched per run, with an honest `User-Agent`. Scraping is polite, not stealthy: if a site forbids it, the tool stops.
- Selectors with spaces inside attribute values (`[title="a b"]`) are not supported.
- Pages that build their content with JavaScript aren't rendered; you only get the HTML the server sends.
- On the website demo only saved files can be scraped; fetching URLs works on your own computer.

tools.name: price-tracker
tools.summary: Read a product price from a page, keep a history in a CSV and flag price drops.

schema.description: Track a product price over time.

arguments.help: a product page URL, or a saved .html file
CSV file that keeps the price history
compare only, don't add a row
tell me when the price is at or below this
pattern with one group that captures the price

sections.Purpose: Know when something gets cheaper. It reads the price of a product page, compares it with the readings you saved before, and tells you whether it dropped, rose or stayed the same, and whether it's the lowest price yet. Every run can add a row to a CSV, so a daily schedule builds a price history you can chart.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python price_tracker.py SOURCE [--history prices.csv] [--no-record] [--target 50] [--regex PATTERN]
```
`SOURCE` is a product URL or a saved `.html` file. The price is looked up in the page's structured data first, then meta tags and `itemprop="price"`, then your `--regex` (one capture group), and finally the first price with a currency symbol. Without `--history` it just prints the price.
sections.Example:
```bash
python price_tracker.py product.html --history prices.csv --no-record --target 80
```
```
Price now: 79.99 USD
PRICE DROP: 10.00 less than 89.99 on 2026-10-15 (11.1%)
Lowest price seen so far!
At or below your target of 80.00.
(read from structured data)
```
sections.Notes:
- The history CSV has the columns `timestamp, url, price, currency`; each page is tracked by the exact source you gave.
- `--no-record` compares without adding a row, handy for trying a new page.
- Run it from cron or Task Scheduler for a real tracker. Pick a sensible interval, such as once a day.
- Shops that load prices with JavaScript may not show one in the raw HTML; use `--regex` or a saved copy of the rendered page.
- On the website demo only saved files can be read; fetching a URL works on your own computer.

tools.name: html-table-extractor
tools.summary: Export the tables on a web page (or saved .html file) to CSV files. Dry run by default.

schema.description: Export HTML tables to CSV.

arguments.help: a page URL, or a saved .html file
only this table (1 = first); repeat for several

sections.Purpose: Turn the tables on a web page into spreadsheets. It finds every `<table>` in a page or saved HTML file, shows you a preview of each, and (when you ask) writes them out as CSV files that open straight in Excel or Google Sheets. Header cells, captions and `colspan` are handled for you.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python html_table_extractor.py SOURCE [--table N ...] [--out-dir DIR] [--preview ROWS] [--apply]
```
By default it only shows what it would write. Add `--apply` to create `<name>-table-<N>.csv` files in the output folder. Existing files are never overwritten.
sections.Example:
```bash
python html_table_extractor.py tables.html --preview 2
```
```
Table 1 (Sales by region): 4 row(s) x 3 column(s)
   Region | Q1 | Q2
   North | 1,200 | 1,450
   would write tables-table-1.csv
Table 2 (untitled): 3 row(s) x 2 column(s)
   Name | Role
   Asha & Co | Lead
   would write tables-table-2.csv
Dry run - nothing written. Add --apply to create the CSV files.
```
sections.Notes:
- Tables nested inside other tables are exported as their own tables; their text is not repeated in the outer cell.
- A cell that spans several columns is padded with empty cells so every row has the same width.
- Pages that fill their tables with JavaScript won't show them here; save the page after it has loaded and use that file instead.
- On the website demo only saved files can be read, and the CSV files are written into your browser's temporary folder.

tools.name: page-change-detector
tools.summary: Check whether a page's visible content has changed since the last time you looked.

schema.description: Detect when a page's content changes.

arguments.help: a page URL, or a saved .html file
JSON file that remembers the last version
compare with this earlier saved page instead
regex for text to ignore, e.g. dates or visitor counts

sections.Purpose: Find out when a web page changes without staring at it. The tool reduces a page to its visible text, remembers the last version, and tells you which lines were added or removed the next time you run it. The exit code is 1 when something changed, so it slots straight into cron, Task Scheduler or a shell `if`.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python page_change_detector.py SOURCE --state last-seen.json [--ignore REGEX] [--no-update]
python page_change_detector.py SOURCE --previous old-copy.html
```
With `--state` the first run saves a baseline and later runs compare against it, then store the new version. `--no-update` keeps the old baseline so you're told about the change every time until you accept it. `--previous` compares with a saved page and writes nothing. Use `--ignore` for text that always changes, such as `Visitors: \d+`.
sections.Example:
```bash
python page_change_detector.py jobs.html --previous jobs-old.html
```
```
CHANGED: 2 line(s) added, 1 removed.
  - Summer Intern - London
  + Product Designer - Berlin
  + Data Analyst - London
```
sections.Notes:
- Only visible text is compared. Changes to scripts, styles and markup don't count.
- Exit codes: 0 means no change (or a new baseline), 1 means the page changed or couldn't be checked.
- Be kind to the sites you watch: check every few hours, not every few seconds.
- On the website demo only saved files can be compared; watching a URL works on your own computer.

tools.name: meta-tag-auditor
tools.summary: Audit a page's title, description, Open Graph and other SEO tags.

schema.description: Audit title, description and Open Graph tags.

sections.Purpose: Check the small things search engines and social networks read before they show your page. The tool audits the title and description length, canonical link, viewport, language, heading structure, `noindex` flags and the Open Graph and Twitter card tags, then lists what's fine and what needs fixing.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python meta_tag_auditor.py SOURCE [SOURCE ...] [--problems-only] [--strict]
```
Each `SOURCE` is a URL or a saved `.html` file. A missing title or description counts as a failure and makes the exit code 1; other issues are warnings (exit 0) unless you add `--strict`. Use `--problems-only` for a short to-do list.
sections.Example:
```bash
python meta_tag_auditor.py seo-page.html --problems-only
```
```
seo-page.html: 1/12 checks passed
  [WARN] title: only 4 characters (aim for 30-60)
  [FAIL] meta description: missing
  [WARN] canonical link: missing
  [WARN] viewport: missing (not mobile friendly)
  [WARN] html lang: missing
  [WARN] h1: found 2, expected exactly one
  [WARN] robots: page tells search engines not to index it
  [WARN] og:description: missing
  [WARN] og:image: missing
  [WARN] og:url: missing
  [WARN] twitter:card: missing
```
sections.Notes:
- Recommended lengths are 30-60 characters for the title and 70-160 for the description. They are rules of thumb, not hard limits.
- Only the first `<meta>` tag with a given name is used, as most crawlers do.
- The audit reads the HTML the server sends. Tags added later by JavaScript are not seen.
- On the website demo only saved files can be audited; URLs work on your own computer.

tools.name: image-downloader
tools.summary: List the images on a page and download them to a folder. Dry run by default.

schema.description: Download all the images from a page.

arguments.help: a page URL, or a saved .html file
page address, to resolve links in a saved file
only these types, e.g. --ext jpg --ext png

sections.Purpose: Grab every picture from a page in one go. The tool finds the images on a web page (normal `` tags, lazy-loaded images, responsive `srcset` lists and the social preview image), works out the full web address of each, and downloads them into a folder. Without `--apply` it only lists what it would fetch.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python image_downloader.py SOURCE [--out images] [--ext jpg --ext png] [--limit 100] [--base URL] [--apply]
```
`SOURCE` is a page URL or a saved `.html` file (add `--base` so relative links can be resolved). From a `srcset` it picks the largest version. Tiny inline `data:` images are ignored. Files that already exist are never overwritten: a copy gets a number (`photo-2.jpg`).
sections.Example:
```bash
python image_downloader.py gallery.html --base https://example.com/shop/ --ext jpg --ext webp
```
```
1. would download https://cdn.example.com/cover.jpg
2. would download https://example.com/img/a.jpg
3. would download https://example.com/img/lazy.webp
4. would download https://example.com/img/large.jpg
4 image(s) found. Dry run - add --apply to download them to images.
```
sections.Notes:
- Each image is limited to 20 MB, and a run stops at `--limit` images (100 by default).
- Responses that aren't images, such as an HTML error page, are reported and skipped.
- Check that you're allowed to reuse the pictures. Downloading is easy; copyright still applies.
- The website demo can only list images from saved files; downloading works on your own computer.

tools.name: headline-collector
tools.summary: Collect the headlines from news pages and (optionally) keep a running list in a CSV file.

schema.description: Collect headlines from news pages.

arguments.help: heading levels to take, e.g. 2-3 (default) or 1-6
address to resolve links in saved files
CSV file to add new headlines to

sections.Purpose: Skim the news without opening ten tabs. Point the tool at one or more news pages and it lists their headlines with links, skipping menu labels and duplicates. Give it a CSV file and it keeps a running archive, adding only headlines it hasn't saved before, so a daily run builds a searchable log.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python headline_collector.py SOURCE [SOURCE ...] [--levels 2-3] [--min-words 3] [--base URL] [--out headlines.csv]
```
By default it reads `<h2>` and `<h3>` headings with at least three words (the page's own title in `<h1>` and short labels like "Menu" are left out). Use `--levels 1-6` to take everything. With `--out`, new headlines are marked `*` and appended as `date, source, headline, url`.
sections.Example:
```bash
python headline_collector.py news.html --base https://dailyexample.test/
```
```
news.html: 3 headline(s)
  - Council approves new city budget  <https://dailyexample.test/news/budget>
  - Bridge reopens after six months of repairs  <https://dailyexample.test/news/bridge>
  - Schools add coding to the curriculum  <https://dailyexample.test/news/schools>
```
sections.Notes:
- Headlines are matched case-insensitively, so a re-capitalised repeat isn't saved twice.
- It only reads the page the server sends, so sites that load stories with JavaScript need a saved copy.
- Read the site's terms and keep to a gentle schedule. An RSS feed, if the site has one, is often the friendlier source (see `rss-digest`).
- The website demo only reads saved files; URLs work on your own computer.

tools.name: wayback-checker
tools.summary: Look up Wayback Machine snapshots for URLs, or read saved lookup responses.

schema.description: Find Wayback Machine snapshots for URLs.

arguments.help: text file with one URL per line
find the snapshot closest to this date (YYYYMMDD)
read saved availability responses (JSON) instead of asking

sections.Purpose: Check whether the Internet Archive has a copy of a page. Give it URLs (or a text file full of them) and it asks the Wayback Machine's public availability API for the closest saved snapshot, printing the date and a link you can open. It's handy for rescuing dead links, citing sources and checking what a page used to say.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python wayback_checker.py URL [URL ...] [--file urls.txt] [--timestamp 20200101] [--delay 1]
python wayback_checker.py --response saved-lookups.json
```
`--timestamp` asks for the snapshot closest to a date. Lookups are spaced `--delay` seconds apart to be kind to the free service. `--response` reads availability responses you saved earlier (one JSON object, or a list of them) without touching the network. The exit code is 1 if any URL has no snapshot.
sections.Example:
```bash
python wayback_checker.py --response wayback.json
```
```
example.com: 2024-01-15 08:30 UTC  https://web.archive.org/web/20240115083000/http://example.com/
gone.example.net: no snapshot saved
1 of 2 URL(s) have a snapshot.
```
sections.Notes:
- The tool only reads from the public API; it doesn't ask the Archive to save anything.
- A snapshot may be days or years from the date you asked for. Check the date in the output.
- The website demo only reads saved responses; live lookups work on your own computer.

tools.name: page-text-extractor
tools.summary: Pull the readable article text out of a web page, without menus, ads and scripts.

schema.description: Extract the readable text from a page.

arguments.help: a page URL, or a saved .html file
save the text to this new file

sections.Purpose: Read an article without the clutter. The tool finds the main content of a web page (the `<article>` or `<main>` part when there is one), drops menus, footers, sidebars, forms, scripts and styles, and prints clean, wrapped text with headings and bullet points kept in a Markdown-like layout. It also tells you the word count and a rough reading time.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python page_text_extractor.py SOURCE [--width 80] [--out article.txt]
```
`SOURCE` is a URL or a saved `.html` file. With `--out` the text is saved to a new file (an existing file is never overwritten).
sections.Example:
```bash
python page_text_extractor.py article.html --width 70
```
```
Why small scripts win - Example Blog
(71 words, about 1 min read)

# Why small scripts win

By Sam Writer

Small scripts are easy to read, easy to test and easy to throw away
when they stop being useful. A script that does one thing well can be
understood in a single sitting.
sections.Three habits:
- Name things plainly
- Print what you did
- Keep a dry-run mode

Start with the smallest version that solves your problem and grow from
there.
```
sections.Notes:
- If the page has no `<article>` or `<main>` element the whole page is used, minus the obvious clutter, so results on unusual layouts may include extra lines.
- Reading time assumes about 220 words per minute.
- Pages that need JavaScript to show their content come out empty; save the page from your browser after it loads and use that file.
- Respect copyright: keep saved text for your own reading unless the licence says otherwise.
- The website demo only reads saved files; URLs work on your own computer.

tools.name: job-listing-watcher
tools.summary: Watch a careers page and report new and closed job postings.

schema.description: Watch a careers page for new postings.

arguments.help: a careers page URL, or a saved .html file
JSON file that remembers the postings seen
compare with this earlier saved page instead
only postings whose title matches, e.g. 'engineer|data'
regex a link address must match to count as a posting
page address, to resolve links in saved files

sections.Purpose: Be first to know about a new opening. The tool reads a company's careers page, picks out the links that look like job postings, remembers them, and on every later run tells you which postings are new and which have closed. Use `--match` to care only about the roles you want. The exit code is 1 when something new appeared, so cron or Task Scheduler can notify you.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python job_listing_watcher.py SOURCE --state seen-jobs.json [--match "engineer|data"] [--base URL]
python job_listing_watcher.py SOURCE --previous earlier-copy.html
```
A link counts as a posting when its address contains words like `job`, `career`, `position` or `opening`; change that with `--link-pattern`. With `--state` the first run saves a baseline. `--previous` compares against a saved page and writes nothing.
sections.Example:
```bash
python job_listing_watcher.py jobs.html --previous jobs-old.html --base https://acme.test/
```
```
  NEW     Product Designer  <https://acme.test/jobs/102-designer>
  NEW     Data Analyst  <https://acme.test/jobs/103-data-analyst>
  CLOSED  Summer Intern
2 new, 1 closed, 1 unchanged.
```
sections.Notes:
- Links are matched on their address and need some visible text; image-only links are skipped.
- Careers pages built with JavaScript often don't list jobs in the raw HTML. Save the rendered page, or look for the company's job-board address and watch that instead.
- Check a few times a day at most; there is no rush that justifies hammering a website.
- The website demo only compares saved files; watching a URL works on your own computer.

tools.name: email-digest
tools.summary: Summarize recent unread mail over IMAP (read-only) or from a saved mbox file.

schema.description: Summarize unread mail, read-only.

arguments.help: read a saved mbox file instead of IMAP

sections.Purpose: Get a quick summary of what's waiting in your inbox without opening a mail app. The tool lists your newest unread messages with sender, subject, size and a short preview. It is strictly read-only: the folder is opened in read-only mode and messages are fetched with `BODY.PEEK`, so nothing is marked as read, moved or deleted.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
export IMAP_HOST=imap.example.com IMAP_USER=you@example.com IMAP_PASSWORD='app-password'
python email_digest.py [--folder INBOX] [--limit 20] [--all] [--snippet 100]
python email_digest.py --mbox saved-mail.mbox
```
On Windows PowerShell set the variables with `$env:IMAP_HOST = "imap.example.com"` and so on. `IMAP_PORT` defaults to 993 (SSL). Use an app password where your provider offers one; the password is only read from the environment and is never printed or stored. `--mbox` reads a mail export instead of connecting.
sections.Example:
```bash
python email_digest.py --mbox inbox.mbox --limit 3
```
```
5 unread message(s) in inbox.mbox, showing the newest 3:

2026-11-01 07:30  Daily Brief <news@brief.example>
    Your daily brief  (314 B)
    Top stories for today. Schools add coding lessons.

2026-10-20 12:00  Shop Deals <deals@shop.example>
    50% off this weekend  (411 B)
    Big sale! Everything must go.

2026-10-12 09:12  Alice Chen <alice@acme.test>
    Re: Invoice September  (20.6 KB)
    Sending the spreadsheet and a photo of the receipt as well.
```
sections.Notes:
- Only the first 20 KB of each message is downloaded, which is plenty for headers and a preview.
- "Unread" comes from the server's `UNSEEN` flag (or the `Status` header in an mbox file).
- Some providers need IMAP switched on in their settings before they accept the connection.
- The website demo can only read the sample mailbox; connecting to a real account works on your own computer.

tools.name: unsubscribe-finder
tools.summary: Find newsletters and mailing lists that offer a List-Unsubscribe header. Read-only.

schema.description: Find mail that offers an unsubscribe link.

arguments.help: read a saved mbox file instead of IMAP

sections.Purpose: Clear out the newsletters you never read. The tool scans your recent mail for the standard `List-Unsubscribe` header that legitimate mailing lists include, groups the messages by sender, and shows how many each one sent along with the official unsubscribe links. It only reads headers (read-only, `BODY.PEEK`) and never unsubscribes for you, so you stay in control of what you click.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
export IMAP_HOST=imap.example.com IMAP_USER=you@example.com IMAP_PASSWORD='app-password'
python unsubscribe_finder.py [--folder INBOX] [--limit 200]
python unsubscribe_finder.py --mbox saved-mail.mbox
```
Credentials come from environment variables and are never printed. Senders are listed busiest first, with web links and `mailto:` addresses. A `[one-click supported]` note means the sender allows unsubscribing with a single request.
sections.Example:
```bash
python unsubscribe_finder.py --mbox inbox.mbox
```
```
2 sender(s) offer an unsubscribe link (7 message(s) checked).

news@brief.example (Daily Brief) - 2 messages, latest: 'Your daily brief'
    web:  https://brief.example/unsub?u=1
    mail: unsubscribe@brief.example

deals@shop.example (Shop Deals) - 1 message, latest: '50% off this weekend'
    mail: stop@shop.example?subject=unsubscribe

Nothing was changed. Open a link yourself to unsubscribe.
```
sections.Notes:
- Only the headers of the newest `--limit` messages are downloaded, so it stays fast on big mailboxes.
- Mail without a `List-Unsubscribe` header (including much spam) won't appear. Be wary of "unsubscribe" links in messages from senders you don't know.
- The website demo can only read the sample mailbox; connecting to a real account works on your own computer.

tools.name: attachment-lister
tools.summary: List the messages that have attachments, with file names and sizes. Read-only.

schema.description: List messages that have attachments.

arguments.help: read a saved mbox file instead of IMAP
hide attachments smaller than this many KB

sections.Purpose: Find out where your mailbox space went. The tool lists the messages that carry attachments, with each file's name, type and real (decoded) size, and totals them up. It only reads mail: the folder is opened read-only and messages are fetched with `BODY.PEEK`, so nothing is flagged as read, downloaded to disk or deleted.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
export IMAP_HOST=imap.example.com IMAP_USER=you@example.com IMAP_PASSWORD='app-password'
python attachment_lister.py [--folder INBOX] [--limit 50] [--min-kb 100]
python attachment_lister.py --mbox saved-mail.mbox
```
Credentials come from environment variables and are never printed. Use `--min-kb` to focus on the big files.
sections.Example:
```bash
python attachment_lister.py --mbox inbox.mbox --min-kb 3
```
```
2026-10-12  Alice Chen <alice@acme.test>
    Re: Invoice September
    - report.xlsx  (5.9 KB, application/vnd.ms-excel)
    - photo.jpg  (8.8 KB, image/jpeg)

1 of 7 message(s) have attachments: 2 file(s), 14.7 KB in total.
```
sections.Notes:
- To measure attachments the tool has to download whole messages, so the default is the newest 50. Raise `--limit` when you're on a fast connection.
- Sizes are the files' real sizes, not the larger encoded size inside the email.
- Inline images in HTML mail can show up as attachments too.
- The website demo can only read the sample mailbox; connecting to a real account works on your own computer.

tools.name: sender-stats
tools.summary: Rank the senders (or domains) that fill your inbox, by message count and size. Read-only.

schema.description: Rank the senders filling your inbox.

arguments.help: read a saved mbox file instead of IMAP
group by full address or just the domain

sections.Purpose: See who is really filling your inbox. The tool counts the messages from each sender (or each domain) and ranks them by volume, with their share of your mail and the space they take. It is read-only: it opens the folder in read-only mode and asks the server for just the `From` line and size of each message, so it is quick even on big mailboxes.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
export IMAP_HOST=imap.example.com IMAP_USER=you@example.com IMAP_PASSWORD='app-password'
python sender_stats.py [--folder INBOX] [--limit 1000] [--top 10] [--by address|domain]
python sender_stats.py --mbox saved-mail.mbox
```
Credentials come from environment variables and are never printed. `--by domain` merges everything from one company, which is handy for spotting noisy services.
sections.Example:
```bash
python sender_stats.py --mbox inbox.mbox --by domain
```
```
7 message(s) from 4 domain(es):

brief.example      3   42.9%     1.1 KB
acme.test          2   28.6%    24.5 KB
shop.example       1   14.3%      411 B
home.test          1   14.3%      313 B
```
sections.Notes:
- Sizes are the full size of each message including attachments.
- Addresses are compared in lower case, so `Ann@Acme.test` and `ann@acme.test` count together.
- Only the newest `--limit` messages are counted.
- The website demo can only read the sample mailbox; connecting to a real account works on your own computer.

tools.name: subject-search
tools.summary: Search message subjects across IMAP folders (or saved mbox files). Read-only.

schema.description: Search subjects across folders, read-only.

arguments.help: words that must all appear in the subject
IMAP folder to search; repeat for several (default: all folders)

sections.Purpose: Find that one email without a mail app. Give it a few words and it searches the subject lines of every folder on your account (or just the folders you name) and lists the matches with date, subject and sender. The search is done by the mail server and is read-only: folders are opened read-only and only headers are fetched with `BODY.PEEK`.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
export IMAP_HOST=imap.example.com IMAP_USER=you@example.com IMAP_PASSWORD='app-password'
python subject_search.py WORD [WORD ...] [--folder INBOX --folder Archive] [--limit 50]
python subject_search.py WORD --mbox saved-mail.mbox [--mbox other.mbox]
```
Every word has to appear in the subject, in any order and any case. Without `--folder` every selectable folder is searched. The exit code is 1 when nothing matched.
sections.Example:
```bash
python subject_search.py invoice --mbox inbox.mbox
```
```
2 match(es) for 'invoice' in 1 place(s):

inbox.mbox
  2026-10-12  Re: Invoice September  <- Alice Chen <alice@acme.test>
  2026-09-15  Invoice September  <- Alice Chen <alice@acme.test>
```
sections.Notes:
- Searches with non-English characters use the server's UTF-8 search; very old servers may not support it.
- Only subjects are searched, not message bodies.
- Credentials come from environment variables and are never printed.
- The website demo can only search the sample mailbox; connecting to a real account works on your own computer.

tools.name: mailbox-size-reporter
tools.summary: Report how many messages and how much space each mail folder uses. Read-only.

schema.description: Report message counts and size per folder.

arguments.help: report on a saved mbox file; repeat for several
only this IMAP folder; repeat for more

sections.Purpose: Find out which folder is eating your mail quota. The tool lists every folder with its message count and total size, biggest first, plus a grand total. It is read-only: folders are opened read-only and only message sizes are requested (no message content is downloaded).
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
export IMAP_HOST=imap.example.com IMAP_USER=you@example.com IMAP_PASSWORD='app-password'
python mailbox_size_reporter.py [--folder INBOX --folder Archive] [--sort size|count|name]
python mailbox_size_reporter.py --mbox inbox.mbox --mbox archive.mbox
```
Credentials come from environment variables and are never printed. Without `--folder` every selectable folder is included. With `--mbox` each file is treated as one folder.
sections.Example:
```bash
python mailbox_size_reporter.py --mbox inbox.mbox
```
```
Folder      Messages        Size
inbox.mbox         7     26.3 KB
Total              7     26.3 KB
```
sections.Notes:
- Sizes are what the server reports for each message, including attachments.
- Some providers count labels as folders, so the same message can appear in more than one row and the total can exceed your real usage.
- Very large mailboxes may take a little while, since the server has to report a size for every message.
- The website demo can only read the sample mailbox; connecting to a real account works on your own computer.

tools.name: eml-to-text
tools.summary: Convert .eml email files to plain text (printed, or saved with --apply).

schema.description: Convert .eml files to plain text.

arguments.help: wrap the body at this width

sections.Purpose: Read saved emails without a mail program. The tool converts `.eml` files (the format you get from "save as" or "download message") into plain text: the main header lines, the readable body (plain text when there is one, otherwise the HTML turned into text with links kept), and a list of attachment names. It works on single files or whole folders.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python eml_to_text.py PATH [PATH ...] [--width 80] [--out-dir DIR] [--apply]
```
By default the text is printed. With `--out-dir` it shows which `.txt` files it would write; add `--apply` to create them. Existing files are never overwritten: a copy gets a number (`message-2.txt`).
sections.Example:
```bash
python eml_to_text.py message.eml --width 60
```
```
From: Daily Brief <news@brief.example>
To: Sam Reader <sam@example.org>
Date: Mon, 02 Nov 2026 07:29:00 +0000
Subject: Your Monday brief

Good morning!

Here is your Monday brief.

- Council approves budget
- Bridge reopens

Unsubscribe: https://brief.example/unsub?u=1
```
sections.Notes:
- Attachments aren't extracted, only listed by name.
- Remote images and tracking pixels in HTML mail are ignored, and nothing is fetched from the network.
- Messages with several languages or odd encodings are decoded using the charset they declare; broken ones may show replacement characters.
- On the website demo, saved files are written to your browser's temporary folder.

tools.name: email-validator
tools.summary: Check email addresses for valid syntax and (optionally) a working mail server (MX record).

schema.description: Validate email addresses.

arguments.help: text file with one address per line
check syntax only, no DNS lookups

sections.Purpose: Weed out bad addresses before you send. The tool checks each address for valid syntax (name part, dots, domain labels, international domains) and, unless you turn it off, asks DNS whether the domain really accepts mail by looking up its MX record. It reports every address as ok, warn or BAD with a plain-English reason.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python email_validator.py ADDRESS [ADDRESS ...] [--file addresses.txt] [--no-mx]
```
Lines starting with `#` in the `--file` are ignored. The exit code is 1 if any address is bad or can't be checked. MX lookups use Cloudflare's public DNS-over-HTTPS service (`cloudflare-dns.com`), so only the domain part of each address is sent, once per domain.
sections.Example:
```bash
python email_validator.py --file emails.txt --no-mx
```
```
ok    alice@acme.test  (syntax only)
ok    bob.smith+news@example.com  (syntax only)
BAD   not-an-email  (missing @)
BAD   sam@@example.org  (needs exactly one @)
BAD   .dot@example.com  (dots in the wrong place in the name part)
ok    name@sub-domain.example.co.uk  (syntax only)
BAD   user@-bad-.com  (domain has invalid characters, hyphens or lengths)
BAD   trailing.dot.@example.com  (dots in the wrong place in the name part)
BAD   ünïcode@example.com  (non-ASCII characters in the name part)
3 of 9 address(es) look fine.
```
sections.Notes:
- A valid-looking address with a mail server can still be a mailbox that doesn't exist. Only sending a message proves that.
- Addresses with non-ASCII characters before the `@` are reported as BAD because many mail systems can't deliver to them.
- A domain with no MX record but an address record is marked `warn`, since mail servers will still try delivering there.
- A "null MX" record (a domain saying it never receives mail) counts as BAD.
- The website demo checks syntax only (`--no-mx`); MX lookups work on your own computer.

tools.name: header-analyzer
tools.summary: Trace the route an email took, and check its SPF, DKIM and DMARC results, from its headers.

schema.description: Trace the hops in an email's headers.

arguments.help: an .eml file, or a text file of headers

sections.Purpose: See where an email really came from. The tool reads a saved message (an `.eml` file, or just its headers pasted into a text file) and lays out the route it took, one hop per `Received` line from the sender's server to yours, with the time each hop took. It also reports the SPF, DKIM and DMARC verdicts your mail provider recorded and flags things that deserve a second look.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python header_analyzer.py message.eml
```
In most mail apps you can save the original message with "Download message", "Show original" or "View source". Warnings cover failed SPF/DKIM/DMARC checks, a Return-Path or Reply-To on a different domain from the sender, missing authentication results, and slow or out-of-order hops. The exit code is 1 when there is at least one warning.
sections.Example:
```bash
python header_analyzer.py message.eml
```
```
From:       Daily Brief <news@brief.example>
To:         Sam Reader <sam@example.org>
Subject:    Your Monday brief
Date:       Mon, 02 Nov 2026 07:29:00 +0000
Message-ID: <brief-1102@brief.example>

Route (3 hop(s), oldest first):
  1. app01.brief.example -> relay.brief.example   2026-11-02 07:29:02 +0000
  2. relay.brief.example -> mx1.example.org   2026-11-02 07:30:05 +0000  (+63s)
  3. mx1.example.org -> inbox.example.org   2026-11-02 07:30:09 +0000  (+4s)
  total transit: 67 seconds

Authentication:
  SPF   pass
  DKIM  pass
  DMARC fail
  signed by brief.example

Warnings:
  ! DMARC result is 'fail'
```
sections.Notes:
- Everything is read from the file; nothing is sent over the network.
- Headers can be forged by the original sender. Only the topmost `Received` lines, added by servers you trust, are reliable.
- Newsletters often send from a sub-domain (such as `mailer.brand.example`); that counts as aligned and isn't flagged.
- If your provider doesn't record `Authentication-Results`, the tool falls back to the `Received-SPF` header.

tools.name: mbox-splitter
tools.summary: Split an mbox mail export into one file per month. Dry run by default.

schema.description: Split an mbox file by month.

arguments.help: where to write the pieces (default: next to the source)
text to put before each file name

sections.Purpose: Cut a huge mail export into manageable pieces. Many mail programs export a whole mailbox as one `.mbox` file. This tool sorts the messages by the month they were sent and writes one file per month (`2026-09.mbox`, `2026-10.mbox`, ...), which are easier to archive, search and import. The original file is only read, never changed.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python mbox_splitter.py all-mail.mbox [--out-dir pieces] [--prefix mail-] [--apply]
```
By default it only shows which files it would create and how many messages go in each. Add `--apply` to write them. Without `--out-dir` the pieces go next to the source file. A file that already exists is skipped, never overwritten.
sections.Example:
```bash
python mbox_splitter.py inbox.mbox --out-dir pieces
```
```
2026-09.mbox: 2 message(s), 4.2 KB - would write
2026-10.mbox: 4 message(s), 21.8 KB - would write
2026-11.mbox: 1 message(s), 314 B - would write
7 message(s) would go into 3 file(s). Dry run - add --apply to write them.
```
sections.Notes:
- The month comes from each message's `Date` header, or from the mbox `From ` line when the header is missing. Messages with no usable date go to `unknown-date.mbox`.
- Messages are copied as they are, including attachments.
- Keep the original export until you've checked the pieces.
- On the website demo the pieces are written to your browser's temporary folder.

tools.name: github-stats-reporter
tools.summary: Report stars, forks and recent activity for a GitHub user or repository.

schema.description: Report stars, forks and activity on GitHub.

arguments.help: read a saved API response instead
treat this date as today, YYYY-MM-DD (for testing)

sections.Purpose: Get the numbers behind a GitHub profile or project at a glance. Give it a repository (`owner/repo`) to see its stars, forks, open issues, language, licence and when it was last pushed, or give it a user name for a roll-up of all their public repositories: total stars and forks, the most-used languages, how many were active this month, and the top repositories by stars.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python github_stats_reporter.py octocat/Hello-World
python github_stats_reporter.py octocat [--include-forks]
python github_stats_reporter.py --from-file saved-response.json

The token is only sent to the GitHub API and is never printed. `--from-file` reads a response you saved earlier (`curl https://api.github.com/users/octocat/repos > repos.json`).

```bash
python github_stats_reporter.py --from-file gh-repos.json --today 2026-11-09
```

  Languages: Python (2), TypeScript (1), Shell (1), Go (1)

Top 5 by stars:
````
