```
sections.Notes:
- Forks are left out of the totals unless you pass `--include-forks`.
- Only the first 500 repositories of a user are read.
- Set `GITHUB_API_URL` to use a GitHub Enterprise server.
- The website demo reads the sample file; live lookups work on your own computer.

tools.name: stale-branch-cleaner
tools.summary: Find merged branches nobody has touched for a while, and delete them only with --apply.

schema.description: Find and optionally delete stale merged branches.

arguments.help: branch the others must be merged into
saved for-each-ref output instead of git
saved list of merged branch names
treat this date as today, YYYY-MM-DD (for testing)

sections.Purpose: Tidy up branches that are finished. The tool lists branches that are already merged into your main branch and haven't had a commit for a while (90 days by default), oldest first. Nothing is deleted unless you add `--apply`, and even then only those branches are removed. Unmerged work, the base branch, protected names (`main`, `master`, `develop`, `dev`, `trunk`) and the branch you're on are always left alone.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+, and `git` on your PATH for real repositories.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python stale_branch_cleaner.py [--repo PATH] [--base main] [--days 90] [--apply]
python stale_branch_cleaner.py --remote [--apply]
python stale_branch_cleaner.py --refs branches.txt --merged merged.txt
```
Local branches are deleted with `git branch -d`, which refuses to remove anything unmerged. With `--remote` it works on `origin`'s branches and `--apply` runs `git push origin --delete` for each one, so run the dry run first and read the list. `--refs` and `--merged` read saved output instead of git (dry run only); create them with:
```bash
git for-each-ref --format='%(refname:short)%1f%(committerdate:short)%1f%(authorname)%1f%(subject)' refs/heads > branches.txt
git branch --merged main > merged.txt
```
sections.Example:
```bash
python stale_branch_cleaner.py --refs branches.txt --merged merged.txt --today 2026-01-13
```
```
1 stale merged local branch(es) (merged into main, idle 90+ days) out of 5:
  old/experiment                225 days  Max Weber

Dry run - nothing deleted. Add --apply to delete the branches listed above.
```
sections.Notes:
- "Merged" is judged by git from the branch history, so squash-merged branches may not be recognised.
- A deleted local branch can be restored from `git reflog` for a while; a deleted remote branch is harder to bring back.
- Add a `--base` other than `main` if your default branch has a different name.

tools.name: issue-exporter
tools.summary: Export the issues of a GitHub repository to CSV.

schema.description: Export a repository's issues to CSV.

arguments.help: read a saved API response instead
write to this new CSV file instead of printing

sections.Purpose: Take your issues out of GitHub and into a spreadsheet. The tool downloads the issues of a repository and turns them into CSV with one row per issue: number, title, state, author, assignees, labels, comment count, dates and link. Pull requests (which GitHub also lists as issues) are left out unless you ask for them. The CSV opens in Excel and Google Sheets, or feeds other scripts.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python issue_exporter.py owner/repo [--state open|closed|all] [--label bug --label docs] [--include-prs] [--out issues.csv]
python issue_exporter.py --from-file saved-issues.json
```
Several `--label` options mean the issue must have all of them. Without `--out` the CSV is printed; with it, a new file is written (an existing file is never overwritten). Public repositories work without a login; for private ones set `GITHUB_TOKEN` (`export GITHUB_TOKEN=ghp_...` or `$env:GITHUB_TOKEN = "ghp_..."` in PowerShell). The token is only sent to the GitHub API and never printed.
sections.Example:
```bash
python issue_exporter.py --from-file gh-issues.json --state open
```
```
number,title,state,author,assignees,labels,comments,created,updated,closed,url
41,Login fails on Safari,open,mira,sam,bug;priority: high,4,2026-10-30,2026-10-30,,https://github.com/octo-demo/api-server/issues/41
40,"Add dark mode, please",open,tom,,enhancement,2,2026-10-25,2026-10-25,,https://github.com/octo-demo/api-server/issues/40
37,Support Python 3.14,open,sam,,enhancement;good first issue,1,2026-09-14,2026-09-14,,https://github.com/octo-demo/api-server/issues/37
```
sections.Notes:
- Up to 1,000 issues are read by default (`--max-pages` changes that).
- Labels and assignees are joined with `;` inside their cell.
- `--from-file` takes a response saved with `curl https://api.github.com/repos/owner/repo/issues > issues.json`.
- The website demo reads the sample file; live exports work on your own computer.

tools.name: pr-review-queue
tools.summary: List the open pull requests that are waiting for your review.

schema.description: List PRs waiting for your review.

arguments.help: only repositories of this organisation or user
read a saved search response instead
treat this date as today, YYYY-MM-DD (for testing)

sections.Purpose: Never lose track of a review you owe. The tool asks GitHub for every open pull request where your review has been requested, then lists them with the longest-waiting first, showing how many days each has been open, who wrote it, how many comments it has and a direct link. Drafts are hidden by default, and slow ones are flagged.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
export GITHUB_TOKEN=ghp_...    # PowerShell: $env:GITHUB_TOKEN = "ghp_..."
python pr_review_queue.py [--org my-org] [--include-drafts] [--warn-days 7]
python pr_review_queue.py --user octocat
python pr_review_queue.py --from-file saved-search.json
```
`@me` (the default) needs a token so GitHub knows who you are; a token with read access to the repositories is enough. With `--user NAME` the search works without a token for public repositories. The token is only sent to the GitHub API and is never printed. `--from-file` reads a saved response, for example from `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $GITHUB_TOKEN" "https://api.github.com/search/issues?q=is:pr+is:open+review-requested:@me"`.

python pr_review_queue.py --from-file gh-review-prs.json --today 2026-11-09
```

```

- At most 100 pull requests are listed.

tools.name: star-tracker
tools.summary: Log the star counts of a user's repositories over time and show what changed.

schema.description: Track repository stars over time.

arguments.help: read a saved repos response instead
CSV file that keeps the history
treat this date as today, YYYY-MM-DD (for testing)

sections.Purpose: Watch your projects grow. Each time you run it, the tool reads the star count (and forks) of every one of your public repositories, compares them with the readings saved last time and shows how many stars each gained or lost, then appends today's numbers to a CSV history file. Run it daily or weekly from cron or Task Scheduler and you get a record you can chart in any spreadsheet.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python star_tracker.py USER --log stars.csv [--no-record] [--include-forks]
python star_tracker.py --from-file saved-repos.json --log stars.csv
```
The log has the columns `date, repo, stars, forks`. A repository is recorded at most once per day, so re-running the same day is safe. Forks are skipped unless you pass `--include-forks`. Without a token GitHub allows 60 requests an hour, which is plenty; to raise that, set `GITHUB_TOKEN` (`export GITHUB_TOKEN=ghp_...`). It is only sent to the GitHub API and never printed.
sections.Example:
```bash
python star_tracker.py --from-file gh-repos.json --log stars.csv --no-record --today 2026-11-09
```
```
octo-demo/api-server    1,240  +140 since 2026-10-01
octo-demo/web-app         860  +40 since 2026-10-01
octo-demo/data-tools      310  +0 since 2026-10-01
octo-demo/old-lib         120  first reading
octo-demo/dotfiles         45  -5 since 2026-10-01
Total                   2,575  +175 across repos with history
```
sections.Notes:
- `--no-record` shows the comparison without adding a row, handy for a quick look.
- A repository seen for the first time says "first reading"; its change appears on the next run.
- Stars can also fall when people un-star, so negative numbers are normal.
- The website demo reads the sample files; live lookups work on your own computer.

tools.name: language-breakdown
tools.summary: Show which languages your GitHub repositories are written in.

schema.description: Language share across your repositories.

arguments.help: read a saved repos response instead
count repos (default), or weight by stars or repository size
use real code bytes per language (online, one request per repo)

sections.Purpose: Find out what you actually write. The tool looks at all of a user's public repositories and shows the share of each language as a text bar chart. By default it counts repositories by their main language; you can weight the share by stars or repository size instead, or ask GitHub for real code bytes per language for the most accurate picture.

sections.Usage:
```bash
python language_breakdown.py USER [--weight count|stars|size] [--skip-archived] [--include-forks]
python language_breakdown.py USER --bytes [--max-repos 30]
python language_breakdown.py --from-file saved-repos.json
```
`--weight size` uses the repository size GitHub reports, which is a quick stand-in for "how much code". `--bytes` makes one extra request per repository for exact language bytes (limited by `--max-repos`; forks are skipped). Without a token GitHub allows 60 requests an hour; set `GITHUB_TOKEN` (`export GITHUB_TOKEN=ghp_...`) for more. It is only sent to the GitHub API and never printed.
sections.Example:
```bash
python language_breakdown.py --from-file gh-repos.json --weight size
```
```
Languages by size:

TypeScript      60.5%  ##################             12,800 KB
Python          28.8%  #########                      6,100 KB
Go               9.9%  ###                            2,100 KB
Shell            0.7%  #                              150 KB
```
sections.Notes:
- Repositories with no detected language are ignored.
- Forks are left out unless you pass `--include-forks`.
- A repository's "main language" is GitHub's best guess; it can differ from the code bytes view.
- The website demo reads the sample file; live lookups work on your own computer.

tools.name: release-notifier
tools.summary: Check GitHub repositories for releases published since the last time you looked.

schema.description: Check repos for new releases.

arguments.help: text file with one owner/name per line
JSON file that remembers the last tag seen
read saved releases ({repo: release}) instead of asking GitHub
treat repos seen for the first time as new too

sections.Purpose: Hear about new versions of the tools you depend on without watching every repository. Give the tool a list of repositories and it looks up each one's latest release, compares it with the tag it remembered last time, and prints what's new with the release title, date, the first lines of the notes and a link. The exit code is 1 when there is something new, so cron, Task Scheduler or a shell `if` can send you an alert.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python release_notifier.py owner/repo [owner/repo ...] --state releases.json
python release_notifier.py --file watched.txt --state releases.json [--include-prereleases]
python release_notifier.py --releases saved-releases.json --state releases.json
```
The first time a repository is seen its current tag is only remembered (a "baseline"); add `--report-all` to report it as new. After that, a changed tag is reported as new and saved, unless you add `--no-update`. Pre-releases and drafts are ignored by default. Without a token GitHub allows 60 requests an hour, enough for dozens of repositories checked a few times a day; `export GITHUB_TOKEN=ghp_...` raises the limit and is never printed.
sections.Example:
```bash
python release_notifier.py --releases gh-releases.json --state release-state.json --no-update
```
```
*  octo-demo/api-server: NEW v2.4.0
     Pagination and speedups, published 2026-11-03
       Adds pagination.
       faster queries
       fixes #41
     https://github.com/octo-demo/x/releases/tag/v2.4.0
   octo-demo/web-app: v1.9.0 (nothing new)
   octo-demo/data-tools: v0.5.0-rc1 is a pre-release, ignored
   octo-demo/dotfiles: no releases yet

1 new release(s) across 4 repositories.
```
sections.Notes:
- State is a small JSON file mapping each repository to the last tag seen.
- A repository with no releases is reported as such; it isn't an error.
- If a lookup fails (network or rate limit) that repository is skipped for this run and the exit code is 1.
- The website demo reads saved releases; live checks work on your own computer.

tools.name: contributor-leaderboard
tools.summary: Rank the contributors of a GitHub repository by number of commits.

schema.description: Rank a repository's contributors.

arguments.help: read a saved API response instead

sections.Purpose: See who really builds a project. The tool fetches a repository's contributors and ranks them by commits, showing each person's count, share of all commits and a small bar, plus how much of the work the top few did. Bots such as Dependabot can be filtered out so the ranking reflects people.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python contributor_leaderboard.py owner/repo [--top 10] [--exclude-bots]
python contributor_leaderboard.py --from-file saved-contributors.json
```
Public repositories work without a login (60 requests an hour). For private ones, or a higher limit, set `GITHUB_TOKEN` (`export GITHUB_TOKEN=ghp_...`, or `$env:GITHUB_TOKEN = "ghp_..."` in PowerShell). It is only sent to the GitHub API and never printed. `--from-file` reads a response saved with `curl https://api.github.com/repos/owner/repo/contributors > contributors.json`.
sections.Example:
```bash
python contributor_leaderboard.py --from-file gh-contributors.json --top 5 --exclude-bots
```
```
  1. sam      412   50.2%  ########################
  2. mira     268   32.6%  ################
  3. tom       97   11.8%  ######
  4. lee       41    5.0%  ##
  5. ana        3    0.4%  #

5 contributor(s), 821 commits. The top 5 wrote 100%.
```
sections.Notes:
- Counts are commits to the default branch as GitHub reports them; one person using several email addresses can appear more than once.
- Anonymous contributors (commits not linked to an account) are listed by their commit name.
- For very large repositories GitHub refuses to compute this list and answers 403.
- The website demo reads the sample file; live lookups work on your own computer.

tools.name: rate-limit-checker
tools.summary: Show how much of your GitHub API rate limit is left and when it resets.

schema.description: Show your GitHub API rate limit status.

arguments.help: exit 1 when any limit has less than this percent left (10)
treat this UTC time as now, e.g. 2026-11-09T11:30 (testing)

sections.Purpose: Know how close you are to GitHub's API limits before a script of yours starts failing. The tool asks GitHub's rate-limit endpoint (which doesn't use up any quota itself) and shows each limit - core, search, GraphQL and others - with how many requests are left, how many you've used and when the counter resets. The exit code is 1 when any limit is nearly used up, so it works as a guard at the start of a cron job.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python rate_limit_checker.py [--warn-below 10]
python rate_limit_checker.py --from-file saved-rate-limit.json
```
With no token set, GitHub counts you as anonymous: 60 requests an hour. With a token (`export GITHUB_TOKEN=ghp_...`, or `$env:GITHUB_TOKEN = "ghp_..."` in PowerShell) the core limit is 5,000 an hour. The tool says which one it used; the token is only sent to the GitHub API and never printed. `--warn-below` is the percentage left that triggers the warning and exit code 1 (default 10).
sections.Example:
```bash
python rate_limit_checker.py --from-file gh-rate-limit.json --now 2026-11-09T11:18:30
```
```
core          179 of 5,000  left (  3.6%)  used 4,821  resets 12:00 UTC in 41m 30s  <-- LOW
graphql     5,000 of 5,000  left (100.0%)  used 0  resets 12:50 UTC in 1h 31m
search         26 of 30     left ( 86.7%)  used 4  resets 11:10 UTC already reset
```
sections.Notes:
- Times are shown in UTC.
- Limits that GitHub reports as zero (not available to you) are left out.
- `--now` only exists so examples and tests give the same answer every time.
- The website demo reads a saved response; a live check works on your own computer.

tools.name: label-auditor
tools.summary: Compare issue labels across GitHub repositories and report the differences.

schema.description: Compare issue labels across repositories.

arguments.help: read saved labels ({repo: [labels]}) instead of asking GitHub

sections.Purpose: Keep your issue labels consistent across projects. The tool fetches the labels of two or more repositories and shows where they disagree: labels that exist in some repositories but not others, the same label spelled with different capitalisation, and labels that have a different colour or description. It's the quick check to run before you standardise your triage setup.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python label_auditor.py owner/repo-one owner/repo-two [owner/repo-three ...]
python label_auditor.py --from-file saved-labels.json
```
The exit code is 1 when any difference is found and 0 when the labels all match. Public repositories need no login (60 requests an hour is plenty here); for private ones set `GITHUB_TOKEN` (`export GITHUB_TOKEN=ghp_...`, or `$env:GITHUB_TOKEN = "ghp_..."` in PowerShell). It is only sent to the GitHub API and never printed. The tool only reads labels; it never changes them. `--from-file` takes a JSON object mapping each repository to the list of labels GitHub returns.
sections.Example:
```bash
python label_auditor.py --from-file gh-labels.json
```
```
Compared 3 repositories and 5 distinct label(s).

Missing from some repositories (3):
  'docs': missing in octo-demo/web-app
  'documentation': missing in octo-demo/api-server, octo-demo/data-tools
  'good first issue': missing in octo-demo/web-app, octo-demo/data-tools

Different colours (1):
  'bug': api-server=d73a4a; web-app=ee0701; data-tools=d73a4a

Different descriptions (1):
  'enhancement': api-server=New feature or request; web-app=New feature or request; data-tools=A new feature

5 difference(s) found.
```
sections.Notes:
- Names are compared ignoring case and punctuation, so `Good First Issue` and `good-first-issue` count as the same label spelled differently.
- Colours are compared as hex codes without case, so `D73A4A` equals `d73a4a`.
- A label with no description counts as `(none)`.
- The website demo reads the sample file; live comparisons work on your own computer.

tools.name: notion-db-sync
tools.summary: Sync a CSV file into a Notion database: add new rows, update changed ones. Dry run by default.

schema.description: Sync a CSV into a Notion database.

arguments.help: the CSV file (first row = column names)
Notion database id (or set it via --existing for a plan)
saved database query (JSON) instead of Notion
column that identifies a row (default: the title column)

sections.Purpose: Keep a Notion database in step with a spreadsheet. The tool reads a CSV, compares it with the rows already in a Notion database (matched on the title column, ignoring capitalisation), then adds the rows that are new and updates the cells that changed. It never deletes anything: rows that exist only in Notion are left alone. By default it only shows the plan.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
export NOTION_TOKEN=secret_...      # PowerShell: $env:NOTION_TOKEN = "secret_..."
python notion_db_sync.py tasks.csv --db DATABASE_ID            # show the plan
python notion_db_sync.py tasks.csv --db DATABASE_ID --apply    # make the changes
python notion_db_sync.py tasks.csv --existing saved-query.json # plan against a saved copy
```
Create an integration at notion.so/my-integrations, copy its token, and share the database with it (the `...` menu, then Connections). The database id is the 32-character part of its URL. The CSV's first row holds the column names, which must match the Notion property names. Supported property types are title, text, select, status, multi-select (use `;` between values), date, checkbox, number, URL, email and phone. Other columns are skipped and listed. The token is read from the environment and never printed. Writes are spaced by `--delay` seconds (Notion allows about three requests a second).
sections.Example:
```bash
python notion_db_sync.py notion-tasks.csv --existing notion-db.json
```
```
2 to add, 1 to update, 2 in Notion not in the CSV (left alone).
  + Plan the team offsite
  + Order new keyboard
  ~ Write the weekly report: Done, Status

Dry run - nothing changed. Add --apply to write these changes to Notion.
```
sections.Notes:
- Back up first if the database matters: see `notion-db-backup`.
- A row's key is its title; renaming a title in the CSV adds a new row rather than renaming the old one.
- `--existing` takes the JSON returned by Notion's database query, and it can never be combined with `--apply`.
- The website demo shows the plan from the sample database; real syncs work on your own computer.

tools.name: notion-page-exporter
tools.summary: Export Notion pages to markdown. Prints by default; --out-dir with --apply writes files.

schema.description: Export Notion pages to markdown.

arguments.help: Notion page ids (or full page URLs)
a saved block list (JSON) instead of Notion
write one .md file per page here

sections.Purpose: Get your Notion pages out as plain markdown files you own. The tool reads a page's blocks through the Notion API and converts them to markdown: headings, paragraphs with bold, italic, code and links, bulleted, numbered and to-do lists (including nested ones), quotes, callouts, code blocks, images, dividers and tables. Anything it can't convert is marked with a comment instead of being dropped silently.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
export NOTION_TOKEN=secret_...      # PowerShell: $env:NOTION_TOKEN = "secret_..."
python notion_page_exporter.py PAGE_ID_OR_URL [PAGE_ID_OR_URL ...]
python notion_page_exporter.py PAGE_ID --out-dir notes [--apply]
python notion_page_exporter.py --from-file saved-blocks.json --title "My page"
```
Create an integration at notion.so/my-integrations, copy its token, and share each page with it (the `...` menu, then Connections). You can paste a page's URL or its 32-character id. The markdown is printed; with `--out-dir` it lists the files it would write and `--apply` creates them (existing files are never overwritten). The token is read from the environment and never printed.
sections.Example:
```bash
python notion_page_exporter.py --from-file notion-blocks.json --title "Team wiki"
```
````
# Team wiki

# Project plan

We ship on **Friday**. Details in the [spec](https://example.com/spec) and the `checklist`.
sections.Goals:
- Launch the beta
- Collect feedback from *ten users*

1. Draft the announcement
2. Send it to the team

- [x] Book the venue
- [ ] Order snacks

> Perfect is the enemy of good.

```python
print('hello')
```

---

> Remember to back up the database.

- Sub-page: Meeting notes
````
sections.Notes:
- Sub-pages are listed as "Sub-page: name" but not exported; run the tool again with their ids.
- Images are linked, not downloaded; Notion's own file links expire after an hour.
- `--from-file` reads the JSON returned by Notion's "retrieve block children" call.
- The website demo converts the sample blocks; exporting real pages works on your own computer.

tools.name: notion-task-importer
tools.summary: Import tasks from a plain text file into a Notion database. Dry run by default.

schema.description: Import tasks from a text file into Notion.

arguments.help: text file, one task per line
saved database query (JSON) instead of Notion
treat this date as today, YYYY-MM-DD (for testing)

sections.Purpose: Turn a quick to-do list into Notion tasks. Write one task per line in a plain text file, with optional markers for the due date, tags and priority, and the tool adds each one as a new row in your Notion tasks database. Tasks whose title is already in the database are skipped, so you can run it again safely. By default it only shows what it would add.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
export NOTION_TOKEN=secret_...      # PowerShell: $env:NOTION_TOKEN = "secret_..."
python notion_task_importer.py tasks.txt --db DATABASE_ID            # show the plan
python notion_task_importer.py tasks.txt --db DATABASE_ID --apply    # create the tasks
python notion_task_importer.py tasks.txt --existing saved-query.json # plan against a saved copy
```
Task lines look like `- [ ] Write the report @2026-11-18 #work !high`. Markers: `@2026-11-18`, `@today`, `@tomorrow` or `@+3d` for the due date; `#tag` (any number); `!high`, `!medium` or `!low` for priority. `- [x]` marks a task as done; a leading `- `, `* ` or nothing at all works too. Lines starting with `# ` (hash and space) are comments.

Property names default to `Name`, `Status`, `Due`, `Tags` and `Priority`; change them with `--title-prop`, `--status-prop`, `--date-prop`, `--tags-prop` and `--priority-prop`. Status values are set with `--todo-value` and `--done-value` (for a checkbox property the box is simply ticked or not). Properties the database doesn't have are ignored and listed. Create an integration at notion.so/my-integrations and share the database with it; the token is read from the environment and never printed.
sections.Example:
```bash
python notion_task_importer.py tasks.txt --existing notion-db.json --today 2026-11-09
```
```
5 task(s) in the file: 5 to add, 0 already in Notion.
No such property in the database (ignored): Priority
  + Write the quarterly summary  [due 2026-11-18, tags work, priority high]
  + Buy birthday present  [due 2026-11-14, tags home]
  + Send invoice to Alice  [tags work, done]
  + Call the plumber  [priority high]
  + Water the plants  [due 2026-11-11, tags home]

Dry run - nothing added. Add --apply to create these tasks in Notion.
```
sections.Notes:
- Matching is by title, ignoring capitalisation.
- `--existing` takes the JSON returned by Notion's database query and cannot be combined with `--apply`.
- The website demo shows the plan from the sample database; real imports work on your own computer.

tools.name: markdown-to-notion
tools.summary: Turn a markdown file into Notion blocks and append them to a page. Dry run by default.

schema.description: Push a markdown file to a Notion page.

arguments.help: Notion page id or URL to append to
print the Notion blocks as JSON
actually add the blocks to the page

sections.Purpose: Write in markdown, publish in Notion. The tool converts a markdown file into native Notion blocks - headings, paragraphs, bold, italic, code, strikethrough and links, bulleted lists with nesting, numbered lists, to-do items, quotes, code blocks, dividers and images - and appends them to a page. By default it only shows what it would send.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
export NOTION_TOKEN=secret_...      # PowerShell: $env:NOTION_TOKEN = "secret_..."
python markdown_to_notion.py notes.md                          # show a summary
python markdown_to_notion.py notes.md --json                   # print the Notion blocks
python markdown_to_notion.py notes.md --page PAGE_ID --apply   # append to the page
```
Create an integration at notion.so/my-integrations, copy its token, and share the target page with it (the `...` menu, then Connections). `--page` accepts a page URL or its 32-character id. Blocks are added to the end of the page in batches of 100, spaced by `--delay` seconds. The tool only appends; it never edits or deletes what is already on the page. The token is read from the environment and never printed.
sections.Example:
```bash
python markdown_to_notion.py meeting-notes.md
```
```
meeting-notes.md: 15 top-level block(s), 15 in all
  3 bulleted list item, 2 paragraph, 2 heading 2, 2 numbered list item, 2 to do, 1 heading 1, 1 quote, 1 code, 1 divider

Dry run - nothing sent. Add --page PAGE_ID --apply to append these to a page.
```
sections.Notes:
- Consecutive lines of text are joined into one paragraph, as in standard markdown. Leave a blank line to start a new one.
- Long paragraphs are split automatically because Notion limits each text span to 2,000 characters.
- Headings deeper than `###` become Heading 3, and code languages Notion doesn't know become "plain text".
- Images are linked from their web address (`https://...`), not uploaded.
- Tables and raw HTML aren't converted and are sent as plain paragraphs.

tools.name: notion-db-backup
tools.summary: Back up a Notion database to a JSON file (read-only: nothing in Notion is changed).

schema.description: Back up a Notion database to JSON.

arguments.help: convert a saved database query instead
raw = all Notion returns (best for backups); simple = tidy rows
new file to write (default: a dated name)
print the JSON instead of saving

sections.Purpose: Keep your own copy of a Notion database. The tool reads every page of a database, following Notion's paging until the end, and saves it all to one JSON file: the database definition and each page with all of its properties. It only reads - nothing in Notion is changed - and it never overwrites an existing file, so you can run it daily and keep every copy.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
export NOTION_TOKEN=secret_...      # PowerShell: $env:NOTION_TOKEN = "secret_..."
python notion_db_backup.py DATABASE_ID [--format raw|simple] [--out backup.json]
python notion_db_backup.py DATABASE_ID --stdout
python notion_db_backup.py --from-file saved-query.json --format simple --stdout
```
Create an integration at notion.so/my-integrations, copy its token, and share the database with it (the `...` menu, then Connections). The database id is the 32-character part of its URL. `--format raw` (the default) keeps exactly what Notion returns, which is best for a backup; `--format simple` writes tidy rows (title text, select names, tag lists, true/false) that are easier to read or load into other tools. Without `--out` the file is named like `notion-backup-0123abcd-20261109.json`. The token is read from the environment and never printed.
sections.Example:
```bash
python notion_db_backup.py --from-file notion-db.json --format simple --stdout
```

- Page contents (the blocks inside each page) are not included; use `notion-page-exporter` for those.
- The backup of a large database can be many megabytes; the summary shows the size.
- Files stored in Notion are listed by link, and those links expire after an hour.

tools.name: ics-generator
tools.summary: Create a calendar (.ics) file with events from a CSV, ready for any calendar app.

schema.description: Create calendar .ics events from a CSV.

arguments.help: write to this new .ics file instead of printing
time zone of the times, e.g. Europe/London (default: none)
length when no end is given (60)

sections.Purpose: Put a list of events into any calendar app in one step. The tool reads a CSV (title, start, optional end, location and description) and writes a standard `.ics` file that Google Calendar, Outlook, Apple Calendar and most phone calendars can import. It handles timed events, all-day events, time zones, reminders and the awkward escaping and line-folding rules of the iCalendar format.
sections.Install:
Needs the `tzdata` package so Windows has a time zone database (it does nothing harmful on Linux or macOS):
```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```
sections.Usage:
```bash
python ics_generator.py events.csv [--out events.ics] [--tz Europe/London] [--utc] [--minutes 60] [--alarm 15]
```
CSV columns (a header row is required): `title`, `start`, and optionally `end`, `location`, `description`. The names `summary`, `name`, `begin`, `date`, `finish`, `place`, `notes` and `details` work too. Write times as `2026-11-16 09:30` and all-day events as just `2026-11-16`. A missing end becomes `--minutes` later (60 by default) or the next day for all-day events. With `--tz` the times carry that zone; add `--utc` to convert them to UTC, the most widely compatible choice. Without either they are "floating" local times. `--alarm 15` adds a reminder 15 minutes before each timed event. The result is printed, or saved with `--out` (an existing file is never overwritten). To import, open the file in your calendar app or use its Import option.
sections.Example:
```bash
python ics_generator.py events.csv --tz Europe/London --utc --alarm 10 --stamp 2026-11-01T08:00
```
```
BEGIN:VCALENDAR
VERSION:2.0
PRODID:-//daily-automation-scripts//ics-generator//EN
CALSCALE:GREGORIAN
X-WR-CALNAME:Events
BEGIN:VEVENT
UID:cae0c59315b3230a4541@daily-automation-scripts
DTSTAMP:20261101T080000Z
DTSTART:20261116T093000Z
DTEND:20261116T094500Z
SUMMARY:Team standup
LOCATION:Zoom
DESCRIPTION:Daily sync
BEGIN:VALARM
ACTION:DISPLAY
DESCRIPTION:Team standup
TRIGGER:-PT10M
END:VALARM
END:VEVENT
BEGIN:VEVENT
UID:ffa5261e8c0242691dfd@daily-automation-scripts
DTSTAMP:20261101T080000Z
DTSTART:20261116T123000Z
DTEND:20261116T133000Z
SUMMARY:Lunch\, with Alice
LOCATION:Cafe Roma
DESCRIPTION:Bring the contract\; discuss pricing
BEGIN:VALARM
ACTION:DISPLAY
DESCRIPTION:Lunch\, with Alice
```
sections.Notes:
- Rows that can't be converted (no title, bad date, end before start) are skipped with a message, and the exit code is 1.
- Each event gets a stable ID built from its title and start, so importing the same file twice updates events instead of duplicating them in most calendars.
- `--stamp` only exists so examples and tests give the same output every time.

tools.name: ics-agenda
tools.summary: Print a daily agenda from an .ics calendar file, including simple repeating events.

schema.description: Print a daily agenda from an .ics file.

arguments.help: time zone to show times in (UTC)

sections.Purpose: See your day without opening a calendar app. The tool reads any `.ics` calendar file (an export from Google Calendar, Outlook, Apple Calendar or a subscription download) and prints a clean agenda for a day or the next few days: all-day items first, then timed events with start and end, title and location. Repeating events (daily, weekly on chosen days, monthly, yearly, with counts, end dates and excluded dates) are expanded for you.
sections.Install:
Needs the `tzdata` package so Windows has a time zone database (it does nothing harmful on Linux or macOS):
```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```
sections.Usage:
```bash
python ics_agenda.py calendar.ics [--date 2026-11-16] [--days 7] [--tz Europe/London]
```
Without `--date` it shows today. Times are shown in `--tz` (UTC by default); events saved in another zone, or in UTC, are converted, and times with no zone are taken to be in the zone you chose. Cancelled events are left out. The file is only read, never changed.
sections.Example:
```bash
python ics_agenda.py agenda.ics --date 2026-11-16 --days 3
```
```
Monday 16 Nov 2026
  09:30-09:45  Team standup  @ Zoom
  12:30-13:30  Lunch, with Alice  @ Cafe Roma
  15:00-16:00  Weekly review

Tuesday 17 Nov 2026
  09:30-09:45  Team standup  @ Zoom

Wednesday 18 Nov 2026
  09:30-09:45  Team standup  @ Zoom
  16:00        Dentist  @ Main Street Clinic

6 item(s) over 3 day(s), times in UTC.
```
sections.Notes:
- Supported repeats: `DAILY`, `WEEKLY` (with `BYDAY`), `MONTHLY` and `YEARLY`, each with `INTERVAL`, `COUNT`, `UNTIL` and `EXDATE`. Rules like "the second Tuesday" are not expanded.
- Daylight-saving shifts in repeating events are approximate.
- Changed single occurrences of a repeating event (`RECURRENCE-ID`) are shown as originally scheduled.
- The agenda shows at most 31 days at a time.

tools.name: weekly-review
tools.summary: Generate a weekly review in markdown from your journal, habits, to-dos and notes.

schema.description: Generate a weekly review template.

arguments.help: any date in the week to review, YYYY-MM-DD (today)
write to this new markdown file instead

sections.Purpose: Start your weekly review with the facts already filled in. The tool builds a markdown review for any week from the files your other tools keep: the highlights from your journal, a habit grid for Monday to Sunday, finished and open to-dos (most urgent first), and the notes you captured. It ends with reflection questions and three empty slots for next week's priorities, ready to paste into Notion, Obsidian or any note app.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python weekly_review.py [--week-of 2026-01-07] [--journal journal.md] [--habits habits.json]
                        [--todos todos.json] [--notes notes.json] [--out review.md]
```
Every input is optional; sections are included only for the files you give. `--week-of` takes any date and reviews the Monday-to-Sunday week it falls in (default: this week). The files are the ones written by `journal-cli` (markdown with `## YYYY-MM-DD` days), `habit-tracker`, `todo-cli` and `quick-notes`. They are only read, never changed. The result is printed, or saved to a new file with `--out` (an existing file is never overwritten).
sections.Example:
```bash
python weekly_review.py --week-of 2026-01-07 --journal journal.md --habits habits.json --todos todos.json --notes notes.json
```
```
# Weekly review: 05 Jan - 11 Jan 2026
sections.From my journal:
**Monday 05 Jan**
- 09:10 Started the day with a long walk.
- 18:45 Finished the draft and sent it out.

**Tuesday 06 Jan**
- 08:30 Planned the week.
- 21:00 Read two chapters.
sections.To-dos:
Finished: 1 - still open: 3

- [x] Reply to Sam
- [ ] Write the weekly report (high)
- [ ] Renew passport (high)
- [ ] Book dentist appointment (normal)
sections.Notes:
- The to-do file has no dates, so it shows the current state of your list rather than what changed that week.
- Journal entries are matched by the date in each `## YYYY-MM-DD` heading.
- Reflection prompts are in the `PROMPTS` list at the top of the script if you'd like different questions.

tools.name: reading-list-manager
tools.summary: Keep a reading list: add books, mark them reading or finished, rate them, see your stats.

schema.description: Manage a reading list with statuses.

arguments.help: book title (add) or book numbers (the rest)
your rating, with finish or rate
only list books with this status
treat this date as today, YYYY-MM-DD (for testing)

sections.Purpose: Keep track of what you want to read, what you're reading and what you finished. Add books, move them through the statuses (to-read, reading, done), give finished ones a 1-5 rating, and see a summary of how much you read and what you liked best. Everything lives in one small JSON file you can back up or sync.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python reading_list_manager.py add "Deep Work" --author "Cal Newport"
python reading_list_manager.py list [--status to-read|reading|done]
python reading_list_manager.py start 3
python reading_list_manager.py finish 3 --rating 5
python reading_list_manager.py rate 3 --rating 4
python reading_list_manager.py remove 3
python reading_list_manager.py stats
```
`start`, `finish`, `rate` and `remove` take one or more book numbers (shown by `list`). The list is kept in `~/.reading-list.json`; point to another file with `--file`. `list` and `stats` only read it. Adding a title that is already there is refused.
sections.Example:
```bash
python reading_list_manager.py list --file reading-list.json
```
```
READING (1)
    2  The Pragmatic Programmer - Hunt & Thomas

TO-READ (2)
    3  Atomic Habits - James Clear
    4  Staff Engineer - Will Larson

DONE (2)
    1  Deep Work - Cal Newport  [5/5]
    5  Thinking, Fast and Slow - Daniel Kahneman  [4/5]
```
sections.Notes:
- `finish` records today's date, so `stats` can show how many books you finished each month.
- `--today` only exists so examples and tests give the same answer every time.
- Remove asks no questions; keep a copy of the JSON file if the list matters.
- Pair it with `notion-db-sync` to mirror the list in Notion.

tools.name: bookmark-deduper
tools.summary: Remove duplicate bookmarks from a browser HTML export. Dry run by default.

schema.description: Remove duplicate bookmarks from an HTML export.

arguments.help: bookmarks HTML file exported from your browser
new file to write the cleaned bookmarks to

sections.Purpose: Clean up a bookmark collection that has grown messy over the years. Export your bookmarks from your browser as an HTML file and the tool finds the ones that point to the same page, even when the address is written differently (`http` vs `https`, `www.` or not, a trailing slash, a `#fragment`, tracking parameters like `utm_source` and `fbclid`). By default it only lists the duplicates; with `--apply` it saves a cleaned copy and leaves your original untouched.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python bookmark_deduper.py bookmarks.html                              # show the duplicates
python bookmark_deduper.py bookmarks.html --out cleaned.html --apply   # save a clean copy
```
In Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari use "Export bookmarks" from the bookmark manager to get the HTML file, and "Import bookmarks" to load `cleaned.html` afterwards. The first copy of each page is kept (in folder order) and later copies are removed, together with their description lines. Different query strings such as `?page=2` count as different pages. The output is a new file; an existing file is never overwritten.
sections.Example:
```bash
python bookmark_deduper.py bookmarks.html
```
```
9 bookmark(s): 5 unique, 4 duplicate(s).
  duplicate (line 14) Python Documentation
    same page as line 8: Python docs
  duplicate (line 15) HN front page
    same page as line 10: Hacker News
  duplicate (line 17) An article again
    same page as line 16: An article
  duplicate (line 19) Hello World repo
    same page as line 9: Hello World

Dry run - nothing written. Add --out FILE --apply to save a cleaned copy.
```
sections.Notes:
- Folders that end up empty are kept; delete them in your browser if you like.
- Non-web links (`mailto:`, `javascript:`) are compared exactly as written.
- Always keep the original export until you've checked the cleaned file imports well.

tools.name: backup-script
tools.summary: Copy folders into a timestamped backup folder. Dry run by default.

schema.description: Copy folders to a timestamped backup folder.

arguments.help: skip matching files or folders, e.g. node_modules or '*.tmp'

sections.Purpose: Make a quick, dated copy of the folders you care about. Each run copies a folder into its own timestamped backup folder (`project-20261110-093000`), keeping file dates, empty folders and the folder layout. It checks every copied file's size, builds the backup under a temporary name and only renames it when everything succeeded, so a failed run never leaves a half-finished backup that looks complete. By default it only shows what it would do.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python backup_script.py FOLDER [FOLDER ...] --dest BACKUPS [--exclude PATTERN ...] [--apply]
```
`--exclude` takes names or patterns such as `node_modules`, `*.tmp` or `docs/private/*` (repeat it for several). Symbolic links are skipped rather than followed. The backup folder can't be inside the folder being backed up. An existing backup is never overwritten; run it again a second later or pick another `--dest`. Pair it with `backup-rotator` to prune old backups and `backup-verifier` to check the copy.
sections.Example:
```bash
python backup_script.py demo-project --dest backups-new --exclude LICENSE --now 2026-11-10T09:30:00
```
```
demo-project -> backups-new/demo-project-20261110-093000
  4 file(s), 681 B, 1 skipped
    would copy package.json
    would copy src/app.js
    would copy src/utils.js
    would copy tests/app.test.js

Dry run - nothing copied. Add --apply to make the backup.
```
sections.Notes:
- Add `--apply` to make the copy. Without it nothing is written.
- Copies keep modification times but not permissions or owners on every platform.
- A backup on the same disk doesn't protect you from the disk failing; use `--dest` on another drive or a synced folder.
- On the website demo the copy is made in your browser's temporary folder.

tools.name: incremental-backup
tools.summary: Back up only the files that are new or changed since the last run. Dry run by default.

schema.description: Incremental backup of one folder.

arguments.help: detect changes by content, not size and time (slower, exact)
overwrite changed files without keeping the old version

sections.Purpose: Back up a folder quickly by copying only what changed. The first run copies everything into the backup folder, which then mirrors your source. Later runs compare the source with a small record kept in the backup (`.backup-manifest.json`) and copy just the new and changed files. Nothing is ever deleted from the backup, and when a changed file is replaced its previous version is kept under `.history/<timestamp>/`, so a bad edit can't wipe out a good backup. By default it only shows the plan.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python incremental_backup.py FOLDER --dest BACKUP [--exclude PATTERN ...] [--hash] [--no-history] [--apply]
```
Changes are detected by size and modification time (with a 2-second tolerance for FAT drives and cloud folders); `--hash` compares file contents instead, which is slower but exact. Files you delete from the source stay in the backup. `--exclude` takes names or patterns such as `node_modules` or `*.tmp`. Symbolic links are skipped. The source and backup folders can't contain each other.
sections.Example:
```bash
python incremental_backup.py demo-project --dest mirror --exclude LICENSE
```
```
4 file(s) in demo-project: 4 new, 0 changed, 0 unchanged (681 B to copy).
  + package.json
  + src/app.js
  + src/utils.js
  + tests/app.test.js

Dry run - nothing copied. Add --apply to back up these files.
```
sections.Notes:
- Add `--apply` to copy. Without it nothing is written.
- The `.history` folder grows over time; `backup-rotator` can prune old backup folders, or delete old `.history` stamps by hand.
- Use `backup-verifier` to check the mirror against the source by hash.
- On the website demo the copy is made in your browser's temporary folder.

tools.name: zip-archiver
tools.summary: Zip folders and files with exclude patterns. Dry run by default.

schema.description: Zip folders with exclude patterns.

arguments.help: leave out matching names or paths, e.g. '*.log' or build
put a folder's contents at the top of the zip, not inside its name

sections.Purpose: Zip up a project without the clutter. Give it one or more folders (or files) and it builds a standard `.zip` that opens everywhere, leaving out whatever you exclude: build output, logs, `node_modules`, version-control folders and so on. By default it only shows what would go in; the archive is built under a temporary name and renamed when complete, so a failed run never leaves a broken zip.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python zip_archiver.py FOLDER [FOLDER_OR_FILE ...] --out archive.zip [--exclude PATTERN ...] [--exclude-common] [--apply]
```
`--exclude` takes names or patterns such as `build`, `*.log` or `docs/private/*` (repeat for several). `--exclude-common` adds `.git`, `node_modules`, `__pycache__`, `*.pyc`, `.venv`, `.idea`, `.DS_Store` and `Thumbs.db`. Folders are stored under their own name inside the zip; `--no-top-folder` puts their contents at the top instead. `--level 1-9` trades speed for size (6 by default). Symbolic links are skipped, and an archive created inside the folder it zips is left out of itself. An existing file is never overwritten.
sections.Example:
```bash
python zip_archiver.py demo-project --out demo.zip --exclude "*.md" --exclude LICENSE
```
```
4 file(s), 681 B -> demo.zip
  would add demo-project/package.json
  would add demo-project/src/app.js
  would add demo-project/src/utils.js
  would add demo-project/tests/app.test.js

Dry run - no zip created. Add --apply to create it.
```
sections.Notes:
- Add `--apply` to create the zip. Without it nothing is written.
- Pair it with `backup-rotator` to keep only the newest archives, and `backup-verifier` to check one against its source.
- Zips don't keep Unix permissions on every platform; use `tar-archiver` if you need that.
- On the website demo the zip is created in your browser's temporary folder.

tools.name: backup-rotator
tools.summary: Keep the newest N backups in a folder and prune the rest. Dry run by default.

schema.description: Keep the newest N backups, prune the rest.

arguments.help: the folder that holds the backups
which entries are backups, e.g. 'project-*' or '*.zip'
how many of the newest to keep
also keep the latest backup of each of the last M months

sections.Purpose: Stop old backups from filling your disk. Point the tool at the folder that collects your backups and tell it how many of the newest ones to keep; it lists which to keep and which to remove, oldest first, and how much space that frees. Backup age comes from the date in the name (`project-20261101-090000`, `backup_2026-11-01.zip`), falling back to the file's modified date. By default nothing is deleted.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python backup_rotator.py FOLDER --pattern "project-*" --keep 7 [--keep-monthly 6] [--apply]
```
`--pattern` is required and selects which entries are backups (files or folders directly inside `FOLDER`; patterns with slashes are refused), so anything else in the folder is never touched. `--keep` must be at least 1, so the newest backup can't be removed. `--keep-monthly M` additionally keeps the latest backup of each of the last M months, a simple way to hold on to older history cheaply. Symbolic links are removed themselves, never followed.
sections.Example:
```bash
python backup_rotator.py backups --pattern "project-*" --keep 3
```
```
5 backup(s) match 'project-*': keeping 3, removing 2.
  keep    project-20261105-090000  (2026-11-05 09:00, newest 3)
  keep    project-20261104-090000  (2026-11-04 09:00, newest 3)
  keep    project-20261103-090000  (2026-11-03 09:00, newest 3)
  remove  project-20261102-090000  (2026-11-02 09:00)
  remove  project-20261101-090000  (2026-11-01 09:00)

Dry run - nothing deleted. --apply would free 58 B.
```
sections.Notes:
- Add `--apply` to delete. Deleted backups don't go to the recycle bin, so read the list first.
- Works on any naming scheme that includes a date; names without one are ordered by modified time.
- Run it right after `backup-script` or `zip-archiver` to keep storage tidy.
- On the website demo the deletion happens in your browser's temporary folder.

tools.name: backup-verifier
tools.summary: Verify a backup (a folder or a .zip) against its source by comparing file hashes.

schema.description: Verify a backup against its source.

arguments.help: the backup: a folder or a .zip file
ignore matching names or paths on both sides
compare file sizes only (fast, but won't catch same-size changes)
also fail when the backup has files the source doesn't
folder prefix to remove from names inside a zip

sections.Purpose: A backup you haven't checked is a hope, not a backup. This tool compares a source folder with its backup (another folder, or a `.zip`) by SHA-256 hash and tells you exactly which files are missing from the backup, which have different content, and which exist only in the backup. The exit code is 0 when every source file is safely in the backup and 1 when something is wrong, so you can run it from a script or schedule after every backup.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python backup_verifier.py SOURCE BACKUP [--quick] [--strict] [--exclude PATTERN ...] [--strip PREFIX]
```
`BACKUP` can be a folder or a `.zip`. A zip that holds everything inside one top-level folder (as `zip-archiver` makes) is matched automatically; use `--strip "prefix/"` for other layouts. `--quick` compares sizes only, which is fast but can't catch an edit that keeps the same size. Extra files in the backup are reported but don't fail the check unless you add `--strict`. The bookkeeping files of `incremental-backup` (`.backup-manifest.json` and `.history`) are ignored. Nothing is changed; the tool only reads.
sections.Example:
```bash
python backup_verifier.py demo-project demo-backup
```
```
Compared 5 source file(s) with 5 in the backup by SHA-256.
Missing from the backup (1):
  LICENSE
Different in the backup (1):
  src/utils.js
Only in the backup (1):
  old-notes.log
PROBLEMS FOUND - this backup can't be trusted yet.
```
sections.Notes:
- Hashing reads every file, so verifying a large backup takes time; `--quick` is a first pass.
- Symbolic links are skipped on both sides.
- A passing check proves the backup matches the source now, not that the source itself is intact.

tools.name: folder-sync
tools.summary: One-way sync: make a target folder match a source folder. Dry run by default.

schema.description: One-way sync from SOURCE to TARGET.

arguments.help: the folder to copy from (never changed)
the folder that should end up matching it
also remove files from TARGET that aren't in SOURCE
compare size and modified time instead of file contents
let --delete run even when SOURCE has no files

sections.Purpose: Make one folder match another. This one-way sync copies new files and updated files from a source folder to a target folder, and can optionally delete files from the target that no longer exist in the source. The source is never changed. Each copy goes through a temporary file and is swapped in when complete, so an interrupted run can't leave a half-written file. By default it only shows the plan.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python folder_sync.py SOURCE TARGET [--delete] [--quick] [--exclude PATTERN ...] [--apply]
```
Without `--delete`, files that exist only in the target are listed with `?` and kept. With `--delete` they are listed with `-` and removed on `--apply`, and folders left empty are tidied away. By default files are compared by size and content hash, which is exact; `--quick` compares size and modified time (the source must be newer by more than 2 seconds) and is much faster on big trees. As a safeguard, `--delete` refuses to run when the source has no files at all, because that usually means a wrong path; add `--allow-empty` if you mean it. The two folders can't contain each other, and symbolic links are skipped.
sections.Example:
```bash
python folder_sync.py sync-source sync-target --delete
```
```
sync-source -> sync-target: 1 to add, 1 to update, 1 only in the target (to delete).
  + docs/new-chapter.md
  ~ readme.txt
  - old-only.txt

Dry run - nothing changed. Add --apply to sync.
```
sections.Notes:
- Add `--apply` to change the target. Without it nothing is written or deleted.
- This is a mirror, not a two-way sync: changes made only in the target are overwritten when the same file changes in the source.
- Deleted files don't go to the recycle bin; run without `--apply` first and read the list.
- On the website demo the sync happens in your browser's temporary folder.

tools.name: snapshot-differ
tools.summary: Take snapshots of folders and compare them: what was added, removed, changed or moved.

schema.description: Snapshot folders and compare snapshots.

arguments.help: compare: OLD and NEW (folders or snapshot .json files); snapshot: the folder to describe
record sizes only, no hashes (fast; misses same-size edits)

sections.Purpose: See exactly what changed in a folder between two points in time. Take a snapshot (a small JSON file listing every file with its size and SHA-256 hash) and compare it with the folder today, or with another snapshot. The report shows files that were added, removed, changed, and moved or renamed (matched by identical content), plus how much the total size changed. It's the fast answer to "what did that installer or sync tool just do to my folder?".
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python snapshot_differ.py snapshot FOLDER --out before.json [--exclude PATTERN ...] [--quick]
python snapshot_differ.py compare before.json FOLDER
python snapshot_differ.py compare before.json after.json
python snapshot_differ.py compare OLD_FOLDER NEW_FOLDER
```
`compare` takes any mix of folders and snapshot files. The exit code is 1 when there are differences and 0 when the snapshots match, which makes it easy to use in scripts. `--quick` records sizes only, which is much faster for huge folders but can't see an edit that keeps a file the same size (and can't detect moves). Snapshot files are new files; an existing one is never overwritten. Symbolic links are skipped.
sections.Example:
```bash
python snapshot_differ.py compare snapshot-old.json snapshot-new.json
```
```
OLD: 5 file(s) (2026-11-01T09:00:00)   NEW: 5 file(s) (2026-11-08T09:00:00)
Added (1):
  + docs/guide.md
Removed (1):
  - docs/old.md
Changed (1):
  ~ src/app.js
3 unchanged. Size change: -6 B.
```
sections.Notes:
- Snapshots record file contents only by hash; they don't store the files themselves.
- Empty folders and permissions aren't tracked.
- Pair it with `incremental-backup` or `folder-sync` to audit what a run changed.

tools.name: tar-archiver
tools.summary: Create compressed tar archives with a hash manifest, and verify or list them.

schema.description: Tar archives with a manifest.

arguments.help: create: folders/files to archive; list and verify: the archive

sections.Purpose: Make compressed tar archives you can check later. The tool bundles folders and files into a `.tar.gz`, `.tar.bz2`, `.tar.xz` or plain `.tar`, and puts a `MANIFEST.json` first inside it listing every file with its size and SHA-256 hash. Months later, `verify` re-reads the archive and tells you whether any file is damaged or missing. Unlike zip, tar keeps Unix permissions and timestamps, but the owner and group names are removed so nothing private is stored.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python tar_archiver.py create FOLDER [FOLDER_OR_FILE ...] --out backup.tar.gz [--exclude PATTERN ...] [--apply]
python tar_archiver.py list backup.tar.gz
python tar_archiver.py verify backup.tar.gz
```
The compression follows the extension you give `--out` (`.tar.gz`/`.tgz`, `.tar.bz2`, `.tar.xz` or `.tar`). Folders are stored under their own name. `create` only shows what it would do until you add `--apply`; the archive is built under a temporary name and renamed when complete, and an existing file is never overwritten. `list` prints the manifest, and `verify` exits with 1 if any file is missing or damaged. Symbolic links are skipped, and an archive created inside a folder it archives leaves itself out.
sections.Example:
```bash
python tar_archiver.py create demo-project --out demo.tar.gz --exclude "*.md"
```
```
5 file(s), 723 B -> demo.tar.gz (plus MANIFEST.json)
  would add demo-project/LICENSE
  would add demo-project/package.json
  would add demo-project/src/app.js
  would add demo-project/src/utils.js
  would add demo-project/tests/app.test.js

Dry run - no archive created. Add --apply to create it.
```
sections.Notes:
- Add `--apply` to create the archive. Without it nothing is written.
- Pair it with `backup-rotator` to keep only the newest archives.
- `verify` checks integrity against the manifest; it can't tell whether the original files were right to begin with.
- On the website demo the archive is created in your browser's temporary folder.

tools.name: backup-size-estimator
tools.summary: Estimate how big a backup will be, and whether it fits, before you run it. Read-only.

schema.description: Estimate backup size before you run it.

arguments.help: the folders you plan to back up
where the backup will go, to check free space
how many biggest files to list (5)

sections.Purpose: Know what a backup will cost before you start it. The tool scans the folders you plan to back up and reports how many files there are, the total size, which folders and files are biggest, and which file types take the space. It estimates how small a compressed archive would be (text compresses a lot, photos and videos hardly at all) and, if you name a destination, checks it has enough free space. It only reads: nothing is copied or changed.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python backup_size_estimator.py FOLDER [FOLDER ...] [--exclude PATTERN ...] [--dest BACKUP_FOLDER] [--top 5]
```
`--exclude` takes names or patterns such as `node_modules` or `*.tmp`; the report says how much space the exclusions save, so you can try patterns until the size is sensible. With `--dest` the tool reads the free space of the drive that folder is on (even if the folder doesn't exist yet) and says whether the backup fits as a plain copy, only if compressed, or not at all; the exit code is 1 in the last case. Symbolic links are skipped.
sections.Example:
```bash
python backup_size_estimator.py demo-project --exclude "*.md"
```
```
5 file(s) in 2 folder(s): 723 B
A plain copy needs about 723 B; a compressed archive about 199 B (a rough estimate).

Biggest folders:
       382 B  demo-project/src
       248 B  demo-project
        93 B  demo-project/tests

Biggest files:
       254 B  demo-project/src/app.js
       206 B  demo-project/package.json
       128 B  demo-project/src/utils.js
        93 B  demo-project/tests/app.test.js
        42 B  demo-project/LICENSE

By file type: .js 475 B, .json 206 B, (none) 42 B
```
sections.Notes:
- The compressed estimate is a rule of thumb (about 25% for text and code, 100% for already-compressed formats such as JPEG, MP4 and ZIP, 70% for everything else). Real results vary.
- Free-space checks can't know about quotas, other programs writing at the same time or network drives that report oddly.
- Pair it with `backup-script`, `zip-archiver` or `tar-archiver` once the numbers look right.

tools.name: sync-conflict-finder
tools.summary: Find sync-conflict copies left behind by Dropbox, OneDrive, Syncthing, Nextcloud and others.

schema.description: Find sync-conflict copies in a folder.

arguments.help: also treat 'name (1).ext' as a conflict when 'name.ext' exists

sections.Purpose: Cloud sync tools quietly leave extra copies when two devices change the same file at once, and nobody notices until something goes wrong. This tool scans a synced folder for those conflict copies - Dropbox and Nextcloud "conflicted copy" files, Syncthing `.sync-conflict-` files, and OneDrive's "name-COMPUTERNAME" copies - then compares each one with its original and tells you whether it is identical (safe to delete), different (worth a look) or an orphan (the original is gone). It only reports; it never deletes or moves anything.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python sync_conflict_finder.py FOLDER [--loose] [--exclude PATTERN ...]
```
The exit code is 1 when conflict copies exist and 0 when the folder is clean, so a scheduled job can alert you. OneDrive-style copies are only reported when the original file is in the same folder and the suffix looks like a computer name, to avoid false alarms on names like `summary-report.txt`. Add `--loose` to also report numbered copies such as `photo (1).jpg` (made by Google Drive and many browsers) when `photo.jpg` exists; this can flag legitimate files, which is why it's off by default. Symbolic links are skipped.
sections.Example:
```bash
python sync_conflict_finder.py cloud
```
```
5 conflict copy/copies found in cloud:

[IDENTICAL] budget-DESKTOP-4F2K9.xlsx
    OneDrive-style (computer name added); original: budget.xlsx
    same content as the original - safe to delete
[DIFFERENT] notes (Kaushik's conflicted copy 2026-11-03).txt
    Dropbox/Nextcloud conflicted copy; original: notes.txt
    differs from the original (44 B vs 45 B, copy is same age) - compare before deleting
[DIFFERENT] notes (conflicted copy 2026-11-02).txt
    Dropbox/Nextcloud conflicted copy; original: notes.txt
    differs from the original (25 B vs 45 B, copy is same age) - compare before deleting
[ORPHAN] orphan (conflicted copy 2026-10-01).txt
    Dropbox/Nextcloud conflicted copy; original: orphan.txt
    the original file is gone, so this copy may be the only one
[DIFFERENT] plan.sync-conflict-20261104-101500-ABCDEFG.md
    Syncthing conflict; original: plan.md
    differs from the original (25 B vs 7 B, copy is same age) - compare before deleting

1 identical, 3 different, 1 without an original. Nothing was changed or deleted.
```
sections.Notes:
- "Different" copies need a human: open both files, keep what you want, then delete the other by hand.
- Comparison is by content hash, so it is exact but reads both files.
- Run it after a long offline period or a reinstall, when conflicts are most likely.

tools.name: log-analyzer
tools.summary: Summarize a log file: levels, time span, busiest hours and the most common errors.

schema.description: Summarize one or more log files.

arguments.help: year to assume for syslog-style dates (this year)

sections.Purpose: Understand a log file in seconds instead of scrolling through thousands of lines. The tool reads one or more logs and reports how many entries there are and over what time span, how they split across levels (DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL), which hours were busiest, and which errors repeat most, grouped so that "timeout after 30 s" and "timeout after 45 s" count as the same problem. Stack traces and other continuation lines are attached to the entry above them instead of being counted as separate entries.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python log_analyzer.py app.log [more.log ...] [--top 5] [--year 2026]
```
It understands ISO timestamps (`2026-11-10 09:15:02,123` or `2026-11-10T09:15:02Z`), nginx/Apache dates (`[10/Nov/2026:09:15:02 +0000]`) and syslog dates (`Nov 10 09:15:02`, where `--year` supplies the missing year). Levels are recognised anywhere in the line, case-insensitively; `WARN` counts as WARNING, `ERR` as ERROR and `FATAL` as CRITICAL. The file is only read.
sections.Example:
```bash
python log_analyzer.py app.log --top 3
```
```
42 entries from 2026-11-10 08:00:23 to 2026-11-10 11:51:35
28 continuation line(s) such as stack traces were attached to the entry above them.

Levels:
  DEBUG          3    7.1%  ###
  INFO          22   52.4%  ########################
  WARNING       10   23.8%  ###########
  ERROR          6   14.3%  #######
  CRITICAL       1    2.4%  #

Busiest hours (top 3):
  2026-11-10 09:00      18  ########################
  2026-11-10 10:00      11  ###############
  2026-11-10 11:00       7  #########

Most common errors (top 3):
      3x  unhandled exception in worker #
      2x  payment gateway timeout after # s
      1x  database connection refused
```
sections.Notes:
- Lines before the first timestamped line are counted as stray and ignored.
- Lines with a timestamp but no level (such as web access logs) are counted under `(none)`; use `status-code-counter` for those.
- Big logs are read into memory, which is fine up to a few hundred megabytes.

tools.name: error-extractor
tools.summary: Pull the error entries out of log files, with surrounding lines and whole stack traces.

schema.description: Extract error entries from logs, with context.

arguments.help: extract lines matching this regex instead of levels
extra lines after, on top of the stack trace (0)
write the result to this new file

sections.Purpose: Get straight to what went wrong. The tool scans log files for error entries and prints each one with a few lines of context before it and its whole stack trace after it (the untimestamped lines that follow), merging overlapping entries so nothing is printed twice. Matching lines are marked with `>` and show their line numbers, like `grep` but aware of how log entries are laid out.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python error_extractor.py app.log [more.log ...] [--levels ERROR,CRITICAL] [--before 2] [--after 0]
python error_extractor.py app.log --pattern "timeout|refused" -i
python error_extractor.py app.log --count
python error_extractor.py app.log --out errors.txt
```
By default an entry is extracted when its timestamped line has the level ERROR, CRITICAL, FATAL or SEVERE; `--levels` changes that (for example `WARNING,ERROR`). `--pattern` extracts lines matching a regular expression instead. `--before` and `--after` add plain lines of context (the stack trace is always included). `--out` writes the result to a new file and never overwrites an existing one. The exit code is 1 when nothing matched, which suits scheduled checks. Log files are only read.
sections.Example:
```bash
python error_extractor.py app.log --before 1
```
```

>  9  2026-11-10 09:06:45,240 ERROR    [worker] database connection refused

--

> 17  2026-11-10 09:20:01,918 ERROR    [auth] payment gateway timeout after 943 s
