```
sections.Notes:
- Timestamps in ISO, nginx/Apache and syslog formats mark the start of an entry.
- With several files each result is labelled with its file name.
- For an overview rather than details, use `log-analyzer`.

tools.name: log-tail-filter
tools.summary: Show the end of a log file and keep following it, printing only lines that match a filter.

schema.description: Follow a log file and filter by pattern.

arguments.help: only show lines matching this regex
hide lines matching this regex (repeat for several)
matching lines to show from the end first (10)
stop after this many new matches

sections.Purpose: `tail -f` with a built-in filter, working the same on Windows, macOS and Linux. The tool prints the last few matching lines of a log file, then keeps watching and prints new lines as they are written, hiding everything that doesn't match. Filter by a regular expression, drop noisy lines, or show only a given level and above. It copes with log rotation: when the file is replaced by a shorter one it starts reading the new file from the top.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python log_tail_filter.py app.log -p "ERROR|timeout" [-x "healthcheck"] [-i] [--level WARNING] [-n 20]
python log_tail_filter.py app.log --level ERROR --no-follow
python log_tail_filter.py app.log -p payment --max-seconds 60
```
`-p` shows only lines matching a regex; `-x` hides lines matching one (repeat it for several); `--level WARNING` keeps WARNING, ERROR and CRITICAL; `-i` ignores case in the patterns. `-n` is how many matching lines from the end to show first (10). Following continues until you press Ctrl+C, or until `--max-seconds` or `--max-matches` is reached. With `--no-follow` it just prints the end and exits (code 1 if nothing matched). The log file is only read, never changed.
sections.Example:
```bash
python log_tail_filter.py app.log --no-follow --level ERROR -n 3
```
```
2026-11-10 09:56:48,405 ERROR    [db] unhandled exception in worker 445
2026-11-10 10:00:11,867 ERROR    [auth] payment gateway timeout after 676 s
2026-11-10 10:22:29,059 CRITICAL [worker] out of memory, restarting worker 743
```
sections.Notes:
- A line is shown only once it is complete, so you never see a half-written entry.
- Lines inside a stack trace have no level of their own, so a level filter hides them; use `-p` when you want traces.
- On the website demo only `--no-follow` makes sense, since the sample file never grows.

tools.name: nginx-log-parser
tools.summary: Parse nginx or Apache access logs (common and combined format) into a CSV file.

schema.description: Convert access logs to CSV.

arguments.help: write to this new CSV file instead of printing
only requests whose path contains this text
only this HTTP method, e.g. POST

sections.Purpose: Turn a web server access log into a spreadsheet. The tool reads nginx or Apache logs in the common and combined formats and writes a clean CSV with one row per request: time (ISO 8601 with its time zone), client IP, method, path, protocol, status, bytes sent, referrer, user agent and user. Open the result in Excel or Google Sheets, or load it into pandas, SQLite or any analysis tool. Lines that aren't in the expected format are counted and skipped rather than breaking the run.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python nginx_log_parser.py access.log [more.log ...] [--out requests.csv] [--status 5xx] [--method POST]
                           [--path-contains /api] [--columns time,ip,status,path]
```
Without `--out` the CSV is printed (the summary goes to stderr so it doesn't mix with the data); with it a new file is written and an existing file is never overwritten. `--status` takes an exact code (`404`) or a class (`5xx`). `--columns` picks and orders the columns from: `time, ip, method, path, protocol, status, bytes, referrer, user_agent, user`. The exit code is 1 when no rows matched. This handles the default `combined` log format; custom `log_format` lines with extra fields need a small change to the pattern.
sections.Example:
```bash
python nginx_log_parser.py access.log --status 5xx --columns time,ip,method,path,status
```
```
time,ip,method,path,status
2026-11-10T09:00:49+00:00,198.51.100.23,POST,/api/orders,500
2026-11-10T09:14:13+00:00,198.18.0.12,POST,/api/orders,500
```
sections.Notes:
- A dash (`-`) in the log becomes an empty cell, and a missing byte count becomes 0.
- Plain-text logs only; unzip rotated `.gz` files first (`gunzip access.log.1.gz`).
- Pair it with `top-ips-reporter` and `status-code-counter` for quick summaries without leaving the terminal.

tools.name: log-rotator
tools.summary: Rotate and compress big log files, keeping a few old copies. Dry run by default.

schema.description: Rotate and compress big log files.

arguments.help: log files, or folders of logs
rotate files at least this big, e.g. 10MB
remove the log after archiving it instead of emptying it in place

sections.Purpose: Stop log files from growing forever without needing `logrotate` (which isn't available on Windows). Point the tool at log files or folders of logs; any file over your size limit is compressed into `name.log.1.gz`, older archives shift up (`.1.gz` becomes `.2.gz`) and archives beyond your `--keep` limit are deleted. The compressed copy is read back and checked before the original is touched. By default it only shows what it would do.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python log_rotator.py LOG_OR_FOLDER [...] --max-size 10MB [--keep 5] [--pattern "*.log"] [--rename] [--apply]
```
Sizes can be written as `500KB`, `10MB` or `2G`. Folders are searched (not recursively) for files matching `--pattern`. By default the original log is emptied in place (so a running program keeps writing to the same file) and any lines written while it was being archived are preserved. With `--rename` the original is removed instead, which is better for programs that reopen their log after rotation; if the file grows during the copy, the rotation stops and you can run it again. Run it daily from cron or Task Scheduler.
sections.Example:
```bash
python log_rotator.py logs --max-size 2KB --keep 3
```
```
4 log file(s), 1 at least 2.0 KB.
  rotate  big.log  (5.0 KB) -> big.log.1.gz, original emptied in place
  skip    server-a.log  (542 B)
  skip    server-b.log  (542 B)
  skip    tiny.log  (33 B)

Dry run - nothing changed. Add --apply to rotate.
```
sections.Notes:
- Add `--apply` to rotate. Without it nothing is changed.
- Emptying a log in place can lose a line or two for programs that don't open their log in append mode; use `--rename` if that matters.
- Archives are standard gzip, readable with `gunzip`, 7-Zip or `log-analyzer` after unzipping.
- On the website demo the rotation happens in your browser's temporary folder.

tools.name: log-timeline
tools.summary: Bucket log events into a timeline so bursts and quiet gaps stand out.

schema.description: Bucket log events into a timeline.

arguments.help: count only lines matching this regex
year to assume for syslog-style dates

sections.Purpose: See when things happened. The tool groups the events in a log into time buckets (seconds, minutes, hours or days) and draws a text timeline with a bar for each bucket, a breakdown by level (`E3 W2 I10`), a marker on the busiest bucket and the empty gaps in between, so you can spot the exact minute an outage started, a quiet period when a service was down, or a traffic spike. Filter by level or a pattern to follow one kind of event.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python log_timeline.py app.log [more.log ...] [--bucket 10m] [--level ERROR] [--pattern REGEX] [--width 30] [--no-fill]
```
`--bucket` takes values like `30s`, `10m`, `1h` or `1d` (default `1h`); buckets are counted from midnight. Empty buckets are shown by default so gaps are visible (add `--no-fill` to hide them); a timeline is limited to 500 rows, so pick a bigger bucket for very long logs. It understands ISO timestamps, nginx/Apache dates and syslog dates (`--year` supplies the year for those). Lines without a timestamp, such as stack traces, are skipped and counted. The logs are only read.
sections.Notes:
- Letters: T trace, D debug, I info, N notice, W warning, E error, C critical.
- For web access logs the level breakdown is empty; the bars still show request volume over time.
- Combine with `log-analyzer` for totals and `error-extractor` for the details of a spike.

tools.name: top-ips-reporter
tools.summary: Rank the client IPs in a web access log by requests or bytes, and flag noisy ones.

schema.description: Rank client IPs in an access log.

arguments.help: group IPs by network, e.g. 24 for IPv4 /24 blocks
leave out an address (yourself, monitoring); repeat for several

sections.Purpose: Find out who is hitting your web server. The tool reads nginx or Apache access logs and ranks the client IP addresses by number of requests (or by data sent, or by errors), showing each one's share of all traffic, bytes served, number of error responses, when it was active and its most requested page. IPs that sent many requests with mostly errors are flagged, which is the usual signature of scanners and brute-force attempts.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python top_ips_reporter.py access.log [more.log ...] [--top 10] [--by requests|bytes|errors]
                           [--network 24] [--exclude-ip 203.0.113.9 ...]
```
`--network 24` groups addresses into /24 blocks (for IPv6 use a prefix such as `64`), which makes a distributed crawl easy to see. `--exclude-ip` leaves out your own address or monitoring checks (repeat for several). The common and combined log formats are supported; lines in other formats are counted and skipped. The log is only read; the tool never blocks anyone.
sections.Example:
```bash
python top_ips_reporter.py access.log --top 4
```
```
60 request(s) from 8 IP(s). Ranked by requests.

  #  Address        Requests   Share       Data  Errors
  1  198.51.100.23        20   33.3%   461.2 KB       3
       2026-11-10 09:00 to 09:44, most requested: /products/42
  2  203.0.113.7          13   21.7%   304.5 KB       1
       2026-11-10 09:02 to 09:44, most requested: /
  3  192.0.2.44           10   16.7%   211.4 KB       1
       2026-11-10 09:09 to 09:46, most requested: /
  4  192.0.2.5             7   11.7%   219.1 KB       0
       2026-11-10 09:05 to 09:39, most requested: /api/users
... and 4 more.
```
sections.Notes:
- Behind a proxy or CDN the log shows the proxy's address unless your server records the forwarded client address.
- A flagged IP isn't proof of abuse; check what it requested before blocking anything.
- Use `nginx-log-parser` to export the full detail as CSV, and `status-code-counter` for response-code totals.

tools.name: status-code-counter
tools.summary: Count HTTP status codes in an access log and show which pages cause the errors.

schema.description: Count HTTP status codes in an access log.

arguments.help: only this HTTP method, e.g. POST
only requests whose path contains this text
paths to list for each error code (3, use 0 to hide)
exit with 1 if server errors are more than this percent of requests

sections.Purpose: A quick health check for a website from its access log. The tool counts every HTTP status code (200, 301, 404, 500...) with its plain-English meaning, share of traffic and a bar, then rolls them up by class (success, redirect, client error, server error). For each error code it lists the pages responsible, so a spike of 404s or 500s points straight at the broken URL. It can also act as a guard in a script: `--fail-above-5xx` exits with 1 when too many requests ended in a server error.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python status_code_counter.py access.log [more.log ...] [--method POST] [--path-contains /api]
                              [--top-paths 3] [--fail-above-5xx 1.0]
```
`--method` and `--path-contains` narrow the count to part of your traffic. Query strings are removed from the paths shown, so `/missing?ref=1` and `/missing?ref=2` are the same page. `--top-paths 0` hides the error breakdown. Common and combined log formats are supported; other lines are counted and skipped. The log is only read.
sections.Example:
```bash
python status_code_counter.py access.log
```
```
60 request(s)

By status code:
  200 OK                         50   83.3%  ########################
  304 Not Modified                4    6.7%  ##
  401 Unauthorized                1    1.7%  #
  403 Forbidden                   2    3.3%  #
  404 Not Found                   1    1.7%  #
  500 Internal Server Error       2    3.3%  #

By class:
  2xx success            50   83.3%
  3xx redirect            4    6.7%
  4xx client error        4    6.7%
  5xx server error        2    3.3%

Paths behind the errors:
  401: /admin (1)
  403: /admin (2)
  404: /missing-page (1)
  500: /api/orders (2)

Client errors: 6.7%   Server errors: 3.3%
```
sections.Notes:
- A 304 "Not Modified" is normal for cached files and counts as a redirect class.
- Bots probing for `/admin` or `/wp-login.php` produce many harmless 404s; look at which paths they are before worrying.
- Use `top-ips-reporter` to see who is behind the errors.

tools.name: pattern-counter
tools.summary: Count regex matches across many log files (plain or .gz), per file and in total.

schema.description: Count regex matches across log files.

arguments.help: log files or folders of logs
what to count; repeat for several, e.g. -p timeouts=timeout
which files in a folder to read (*.log* also finds .log.1.gz)
values to list for patterns with a (group) (5, 0 = none)

sections.Purpose: Answer "how often did this happen?" across a whole folder of logs. Give the tool one or more regular expressions and it counts the matching lines in every log file, including rotated `.gz` archives, and prints a table with one row per file and one column per pattern, plus totals. If a pattern has a capture group such as `timeout talking to (\w+)`, it also lists the most common captured values, so you learn not just how many timeouts there were but which servers they involved.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python pattern_counter.py LOG_OR_FOLDER [...] -p "[NAME=]REGEX" [-p ...] [-i] [-r] [--glob "*.log*"] [--top 5]
```
Name a pattern with `NAME=` so its column is readable (`-p timeouts="timeout after \d+"`); without a name the regex itself is the heading. Folders are searched for `*.log*` (which includes `app.log.1.gz`); change that with `--glob`, and add `-r` to go through sub-folders. `-i` ignores case. Each line is counted once per pattern, however many times the pattern appears in it. The exit code is 1 when nothing matched or a file couldn't be read, so it can guard scheduled jobs. The logs are only read.
sections.Example:
```bash
python pattern_counter.py logs -p errors=ERROR -p payments=payments -p "slowest=handled request ([0-9]+)"
```
```
File            Lines  errors  payments  slowest
big.log            70       0         0        0
server-a.log       10       2         2        8
server-b.log       10       2         2        8
tiny.log            1       0         0        0
TOTAL              91       4         4       16

Top values for slowest: 0 (2), 1 (2), 2 (2), 4 (2), 5 (2)
```
sections.Notes:
- A line counts for a pattern if the regex matches anywhere in it, so anchor patterns with `^` or `\b` to be exact.
- `.gz` files are decompressed on the fly; nothing is written to disk.
- Use `error-extractor` to read the matching entries, and `log-timeline` to see when they happened.

tools.name: log-merger
tools.summary: Merge several log files into one, in timestamp order, keeping multi-line entries together.

schema.description: Merge logs in timestamp order.

arguments.help: prefix each line with its file name
drop entries before this time, e.g. '2026-11-10 09:05'
write the merged log to this new file
year to assume for syslog-style dates

sections.Purpose: Reconstruct what happened across several machines or services. The tool merges any number of log files into one, ordered by the timestamp of each entry, so a request that passed through the web server, the API and the database reads as one story. Multi-line entries such as stack traces stay attached to the line they belong to, equal timestamps keep the order of the files you listed, and an optional label shows which file each line came from.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python log_merger.py web.log api.log db.log [--label] [--since "2026-11-10 09:05"] [--until "2026-11-10 09:30"] [--out merged.log]
```
It understands ISO timestamps (`2026-11-10 09:15:02` or `2026-11-10T09:15:02Z`), nginx/Apache dates and syslog dates (`--year` supplies the missing year). Each file is sorted on its own first, so a log with a few out-of-order lines still merges correctly (the number fixed is reported). `--since` and `--until` keep a time window. Without `--out` the merged log is printed and the summary goes to stderr; with it a new file is written and an existing file is never overwritten. The original logs are only read.
sections.Example:
```bash
python log_merger.py logs/server-a.log logs/server-b.log --label --since "2026-11-10 09:02" --until "2026-11-10 09:06"
```
```
[server-a] 2026-11-10 09:02:00 INFO server-a handled request 2
[server-b] 2026-11-10 09:02:20 INFO server-b handled request 2
[server-a] 2026-11-10 09:03:00 ERROR server-a timeout talking to payments
[server-b] 2026-11-10 09:03:20 ERROR server-b timeout talking to payments
[server-a] 2026-11-10 09:04:00 INFO server-a handled request 4
[server-b] 2026-11-10 09:04:20 INFO server-b handled request 4
[server-a] 2026-11-10 09:05:00 INFO server-a handled request 5
[server-b] 2026-11-10 09:05:20 INFO server-b handled request 5
[server-a] 2026-11-10 09:06:00 INFO server-a handled request 6
```
sections.Notes:
- All timestamps are compared as written, so logs from machines in different time zones should be converted to one zone first.
- Lines before the first timestamp in a file stay at the top of that file's entries.
- Feed the merged file to `log-analyzer`, `log-timeline` or `error-extractor` for a whole-system view.

tools.name: port-scanner
tools.summary: Scan TCP ports on localhost or hosts you own; public addresses need explicit confirmation.

schema.description: TCP connect scan for hosts you own.

arguments.help: 22,80,443 or 1-1024 or common (default: a list of well-known ports)
show the first line a service sends
confirm you own the host or have written permission, to scan a public address
only describe what the ports are for; scan nothing

sections.Purpose: See which network services a machine is offering. The tool tries a TCP connection to each port you choose and reports the ones that answer, with the service normally found there (ssh, https, postgresql...) and a warning for ports that are risky to leave open, such as Telnet, Redis or an unprotected Docker API. It is meant for your own computer, your home network and servers you administer.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python port_scanner.py [HOST] [--ports 22,80,443 | 1-1024 | common] [--banner] [--timeout 0.5] [--threads 100]
python port_scanner.py --ports common --explain
```
With no host it scans `127.0.0.1`. `--ports common` (the default) tries about fifty well-known ports; ranges like `1-1024` and lists like `22,80,8000-8100` work too. `--banner` shows the first line a service sends, which often reveals its software and version. By default only loopback and private (LAN) addresses are scanned. A public address is refused unless you add `--i-own-this`, confirming that it is yours or that you have written permission: scanning other people's machines can be illegal and will be noticed. `--explain` just describes the ports without scanning anything.
sections.Example:
```bash
python port_scanner.py --ports 22,23,80,443,3306,6379,27017 --explain
```
```
   22  ssh
   23  telnet   ! telnet sends passwords in clear text
   80  http
  443  https
 3306  mysql
 6379  redis   ! Redis is often left open without a password
27017  mongodb   ! check that MongoDB requires authentication
```
sections.Notes:
- This is a plain "connect" scan: it completes a normal TCP connection and then closes it. UDP ports and stealth techniques are deliberately not included.
- A port that doesn't answer is either closed or filtered by a firewall; the tool can't tell which.
- The limit is 500 parallel connections and 10 seconds per port, so a scan can't be turned into a flood.
- The website demo can only use `--explain`; scanning needs a real network and works on your own computer.

tools.name: ssl-expiry-checker
tools.summary: Check when the TLS certificates of websites (or saved .pem files) expire.

schema.description: Check TLS certificate expiry.

arguments.help: treat this date as today, YYYY-MM-DD (for testing)

sections.Purpose: Never be surprised by an expired certificate. Give the tool a list of domains (or saved certificate files) and it reads each site's TLS certificate, then reports when it expires, how many days are left, who issued it, and whether the certificate actually covers the domain name. Each is marked OK, EXPIRING SOON, EXPIRED or NAME MISMATCH, and the exit code is 1 when anything needs attention, so a scheduled run can alert you.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install. The certificate is decoded by a small built-in parser, so no extra crypto package is needed.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python ssl_expiry_checker.py example.com example.org:8443 [--warn-days 30] [--timeout 8]
python ssl_expiry_checker.py site.pem fullchain.pem
```
`domain` connects on port 443 and `domain:port` on another port. A file ending in `.pem`, `.crt` or `.cer` is read directly (for a bundle, the first certificate, which is the site's own). The tool reads the certificate the server presents without rejecting it, so even an already-expired certificate can be examined and reported. It only reads; nothing is sent beyond the normal TLS handshake.
sections.Example:
```bash
python ssl_expiry_checker.py fullchain.pem expired.pem expiring.pem --today 2026-11-13
```
```
OK             fullchain.pem            expires 2027-01-01 (49 day(s) left)
               subject example.com; issuer Demo Intermediate CA 1
               names   example.com, www.example.com
EXPIRED        expired.pem              expires 2026-01-01 (316 day(s) ago)
               subject old.example.org; issuer Demo Intermediate CA 1
               names   old.example.org
EXPIRING SOON  expiring.pem             expires 2026-11-25 (12 day(s) left)
               subject shop.example.net; issuer Demo Intermediate CA 1
               names   shop.example.net
```
sections.Notes:
- `--warn-days` sets how early to warn (30 by default). `--today` exists only so examples and tests are repeatable.
- Names are matched against the certificate's Subject Alternative Names, including `*.example.com` wildcards (which cover one level only).
- This checks dates and names, not the whole trust chain; `cert-chain-viewer` shows the chain.
- The website demo reads the sample certificate files; live checks work on your own computer.

tools.name: dns-lookup
tools.summary: Look up DNS records (A, AAAA, MX, TXT, NS...) for a domain over DNS-over-HTTPS.

schema.description: Look up DNS records for a domain.

arguments.help: record types, comma separated (A, NS, CNAME, SOA, MX, TXT, AAAA, CAA)
which public DNS-over-HTTPS service to ask
read saved answers ({type: response}) instead of asking

sections.Purpose: Check how a domain is set up, from any computer without needing `dig` or `nslookup`. The tool asks a public DNS service for a domain's records (A and AAAA addresses, MX mail servers, TXT, NS name servers, CNAME aliases, SOA and CAA) and prints them in plain language: mail servers sorted by priority, and TXT records labelled when they are SPF, DKIM, DMARC or common verification entries. DNS errors such as "this domain does not exist" are explained instead of shown as codes.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python dns_lookup.py example.com [--types A,AAAA,MX,TXT,NS] [--resolver cloudflare|google]
python dns_lookup.py example.com --types MX,TXT --from-file saved-answers.json
```
Lookups use DNS-over-HTTPS (Cloudflare by default, or Google), because the standard library can't speak DNS directly for anything but addresses. The domain you ask about is sent to that service; nothing else is. `--from-file` reads answers saved earlier in the form `{"MX": <the JSON the service returned>, ...}`. The exit code is 1 when a lookup fails or the domain doesn't exist.
sections.Example:
```bash
python dns_lookup.py example.com --from-file dns-response.json
```
```
DNS records for example.com

A      93.184.216.34  (TTL 300s)
AAAA   2606:2800:21f:cb07:6820:80da:af6b:8b2c  (TTL 300s)
MX     priority 10  mail1.example.com  (TTL 300s)
       priority 20  mail2.example.com  (TTL 300s)
TXT    v=spf1 include:_spf.example.com ~all   [SPF: which servers may send mail for this domain]  (TTL 3600s)
       google-site-verification=abc123   [Google domain verification]  (TTL 3600s)
NS     a.iana-servers.net  (TTL 86400s)
       b.iana-servers.net  (TTL 86400s)
```
sections.Notes:
- Answers come from a public resolver's cache, so a recent DNS change can take up to the record's TTL to show.
- Only the record types listed above are supported.
- The website demo reads saved answers; live lookups work on your own computer.

tools.name: integrity-monitor
tools.summary: Detect changed, added and removed files against a stored baseline (a file integrity monitor).

schema.description: File integrity monitor.

arguments.help: init: record a baseline; check: compare; update: accept changes
name of an environment variable holding a secret used to sign the baseline, so tampering with the baseline itself is detected

sections.Purpose: Notice when files change that shouldn't. Record a baseline of a folder (every file's size and SHA-256 hash, plus permissions on Linux and macOS), then check against it later: the tool reports files that were modified, added or removed, and files whose permissions changed. It is the idea behind professional file-integrity monitors, useful for a web root that might get defaced, a configuration folder, or a server directory you want to keep an eye on. A baseline can be signed with a secret so tampering with the baseline itself is caught too.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python integrity_monitor.py init  FOLDER --baseline baseline.json [--exclude PATTERN ...] [--key-env VAR]
python integrity_monitor.py check FOLDER --baseline baseline.json [--key-env VAR]
python integrity_monitor.py update FOLDER --baseline baseline.json --apply
```
`init` writes a new baseline (never over an existing one). `check` compares and exits with 1 if anything differs, so a scheduled job can alert you, and with 2 if a signed baseline fails verification. After an expected change, `update` shows what it would accept; add `--apply` to rewrite the baseline, which also keeps the old one as `baseline.json.<time>.prev`. To sign the baseline, put a long secret in an environment variable (for example `export FIM_KEY=...`) and pass `--key-env FIM_KEY` to `init`, `check` and `update`. Store the baseline somewhere an attacker on the monitored machine can't edit it. The monitored folder is only read.
sections.Example:
```bash
python integrity_monitor.py check demo-project --baseline integrity-baseline.json
```
```
Compared 5 file(s) with the baseline of 2026-11-01T09:00:00: 4 unchanged.
  MODIFIED            src/utils.js
  REMOVED             docs/removed.md
2 change(s) found.
```
sections.Notes:
- Logs and caches change constantly; leave them out with `--exclude` (for example `--exclude logs --exclude "*.tmp"`).
- Hashes prove content changed, not why; investigate every MODIFIED or ADDED line you didn't expect.
- Permission changes are only tracked on Linux and macOS.
- Symbolic links are skipped.

tools.name: breach-password-checker
tools.summary: Check whether a password appears in known breaches, using Have I Been Pwned's k-anonymity API.

schema.description: Check a password against Have I Been Pwned without revealing it.

arguments.help: read the password from standard input instead of asking for it
check a SHA-1 hash (40 hex characters) instead of a password
read a saved range response instead of asking the API

sections.Purpose: Find out whether a password has already leaked, without handing it to anyone. The tool uses the free Have I Been Pwned "Pwned Passwords" service with its k-anonymity design: it hashes your password with SHA-1 on your own computer, sends only the **first five characters** of that hash, receives the few hundred hashes that start the same way, and looks for yours in that list locally. Neither your password nor your full hash ever leaves the machine, and the service can't tell which of the returned hashes you were checking.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python breach_password_checker.py                  # asks for the password; typing is hidden
echo 'my-password' | python breach_password_checker.py --stdin
python breach_password_checker.py --sha1 5BAA61E4C9B93F3F0682250B6CF8331B7EE68FD8
python breach_password_checker.py --sha1 HASH --range-file saved-range.txt
```
There is deliberately no `--password` option: a password typed on the command line is saved in your shell history and visible to other programs. The prompt hides what you type, and `--stdin` suits scripts and password managers. The result says how many times the password appears in breaches and the exit code is 1 when it does. Requests ask for "padding" so the size of the answer doesn't reveal anything either. Only the prefix is ever printed, never the password or the hash.
sections.Example:
```bash
python breach_password_checker.py --sha1 5BAA61E4C9B93F3F0682250B6CF8331B7EE68FD8 --range-file hibp-range.txt
```
```
Checked hash prefix 5BAA6.... (6 candidate hashes returned)
FOUND: this password has appeared 9,545,824 times in data breaches. Don't use it.
```
sections.Notes:
- The example hash is the SHA-1 of the word `password` and the range file is a saved, shortened response.
- "Not found" only means it isn't in the known breaches; short or predictable passwords are weak anyway.
- Never paste real passwords into websites that ask for them for "checking"; this tool is the safe way.
- The website demo can only use a saved range file; live checks work on your own computer.

tools.name: ssh-key-auditor
tools.summary: Review SSH keys for weak types, short lengths, age, missing passphrases and open permissions.

schema.description: Audit SSH keys.

arguments.help: note files older than this many days

sections.Purpose: Spot risky SSH keys before they become a problem. The tool reads your public keys, `authorized_keys` files and private key files and reports each key's type and length, its SHA-256 fingerprint and a verdict: **WEAK** for DSA keys and RSA keys under 2048 bits, a **NOTE** for RSA 2048 (fine, but ed25519 is better), and OK for ed25519, ECDSA, hardware-backed and RSA 3072+ keys. For private keys it checks whether a passphrase protects them and, on Linux and macOS, whether other users can read the file.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python ssh_key_auditor.py                 # audits ~/.ssh
python ssh_key_auditor.py ~/.ssh/authorized_keys /srv/keys [--max-age-days 365]
```
Give it files or folders (the default is `~/.ssh`; `known_hosts` and `config` are skipped). Private keys are only inspected, never uploaded or printed: the tool reads the first lines of the file to see whether it is encrypted, and ignores the secret part. `--max-age-days` adds a note for files not modified for a long time (keys don't record their creation date, so the file's date is used). The exit code is 1 when anything is WEAK. Nothing is changed; fix problems yourself, for example `ssh-keygen -t ed25519` to make a new key and `chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_rsa` for permissions.
sections.Example:
```bash
python ssh_key_auditor.py ssh-demo
```
```
authorized_keys
  [OK  ] ssh-ed25519 ed25519 - id_ed25519@demo-laptop SHA256:95Wqisu+3zXaqfBpDjPvxbSJnwQ4OjXu5PlT+2nZYGY
  [NOTE] ssh-rsa RSA 2048-bit is acceptable but ed25519 is stronger and shorter - id_rsa_old@demo-laptop SHA256:DeYxie+kyegwgks7q4FXv+gN87zwYIKBrNW5fxtPB7A

id_dsa.pub

id_ecdsa.pub

  [OK  ] ssh-ed25519 ed25519 - id_ed25519@demo-laptop SHA256:95Wqisu+3zXaqfBpDjPvxbSJnwQ4OjXu5PlT+2nZYGY

id_rsa_old.pub
  [NOTE] ssh-rsa RSA 2048-bit is acceptable but ed25519 is stronger and shorter - id_rsa_old@demo-laptop SHA256:DeYxie+kyegwgks7q4FXv+gN87zwYIKBrNW5fxtPB7A
id_rsa_pem

priv_locked

12 item(s) reviewed: 3 weak, 2 note(s). Nothing was changed.

sections.Notes:
- The example folder holds sample public keys and truncated fake private-key files; none of them is usable.
- A key with options such as `command="..."` or `no-pty` in `authorized_keys` is shown with those restrictions.
- On Windows, file permissions work differently, so the permission check is skipped.

tools.name: open-ports-lister
tools.summary: List the TCP ports this computer is listening on, and which program owns each one.

schema.description: List listening ports on this computer.

arguments.help: read saved output of netstat -ano, ss -ltnp or lsof instead
hide ports reachable only from this computer

sections.Purpose: Know what your computer is offering to the network. The tool lists every TCP (and on Windows and Linux, UDP) port the machine is listening on, the program that owns it, and whether it can be reached only from this computer or from other machines on the network. Risky services that are reachable from outside, such as a database, Redis, RDP or SMB, are flagged. It works on Windows, macOS and Linux by running the system's own read-only tools.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install. It uses `netstat` and `tasklist` on Windows, `lsof` on macOS and `ss` on Linux, which are normally already there.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python open_ports_lister.py [--only-exposed]
python open_ports_lister.py --parse saved-output.txt
```
Ports bound to `127.0.0.1` or `::1` are "this computer" only; `0.0.0.0` and `::` mean every network interface, and a specific address such as `192.168.1.20` is reachable on that network. `--only-exposed` hides the local-only ones. On Linux and macOS, run it with `sudo` to see the program names of other users' services. `--parse` reads saved output of `netstat -ano` (Windows), `ss -ltnup` (Linux) or `lsof -nP -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN` (macOS) from a file, for example one collected on a server you can't run Python on. Nothing is changed.
sections.Example:
```bash
python open_ports_lister.py --parse ss.txt
```
```
 Port  Proto  Reachable from    Service       Program
   22  tcp    all interfaces    ssh           sshd (pid 812)
   80  tcp    all interfaces    http          nginx (pid 1044)
  443  tcp    all interfaces    https         nginx (pid 1044)
 3306  tcp    all interfaces    mysql         mysqld (pid 1200)   <-- risky to expose
 5432  tcp    this computer     postgresql    postgres (pid 990)
 6379  tcp    this computer     redis         redis-server (pid 1010)

6 listening port(s): 4 reachable from other computers, 2 local only.
1 exposed service(s) are usually better kept local or behind a firewall.
```
sections.Notes:
- Being reachable on the network doesn't mean reachable from the internet: your router and firewall still sit in between.
- Combine with `port-scanner` to see the same ports from the outside.
- The website demo reads the saved listings; listing real ports works on your own computer.

tools.name: whois-lookup
tools.summary: Look up who registered a domain, when it expires and which name servers it uses (WHOIS).

schema.description: WHOIS lookup for a domain.

arguments.help: read saved WHOIS text instead of asking
print the full WHOIS text as well
don't ask the registrar's own server for extra detail
treat this date as today, YYYY-MM-DD (for testing)

sections.Purpose: See who is behind a domain and when it runs out. The tool performs a WHOIS lookup - first asking IANA which registry manages the domain's ending (.com, .org, .uk...), then that registry, and then the registrar's own server for extra detail - and turns the answer into a tidy summary: registrar, creation, update and expiry dates (with the days remaining), status flags, name servers, DNSSEC and, where the registry still publishes it, the organisation and abuse contact. It works without the `whois` command that Windows doesn't include.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python whois_lookup.py example.com [--raw] [--no-follow] [--timeout 10]
python whois_lookup.py --from-file saved-whois.txt
```
`--raw` also prints the full WHOIS text the servers returned. `--no-follow` stops at the registry and skips the registrar's server. Lookups use the plain WHOIS protocol on TCP port 43, so a firewall that blocks that port will block the tool. Registries differ in what they publish, and since 2018 personal details are usually hidden ("redacted"), so a missing owner name is normal. The exit code is 1 when no details could be found or the lookup failed.
sections.Example:
```bash
python whois_lookup.py --from-file whois.txt --today 2026-11-13
```
```
Domain:        EXAMPLE.COM
Registrar:     Example Registrar, Inc.
Created:       1995-08-14
Updated:       2026-08-14
Expires:       2027-08-13 (273 day(s) left)
Organisation:  Internet Assigned Numbers Authority
Country:       US
DNSSEC:        signedDelegation
Abuse contact: abuse@registrar.example
Status:        clientDeleteProhibited
               clientTransferProhibited
Name servers:  a.iana-servers.net
               b.iana-servers.net
```
sections.Notes:
- Use `dns-lookup` for a domain's DNS records and `ssl-expiry-checker` for its certificate.
- Some registries limit how many lookups you can make; don't script thousands of them.
- The website demo reads saved WHOIS text; live lookups work on your own computer.

tools.name: security-header-checker
tools.summary: Grade a website's HTTP security headers (A+ to F) and explain how to improve them.

schema.description: Grade a site's security headers.

arguments.help: a URL, or a saved header dump (e.g. from curl -I -L)
exit with 1 if the grade is worse than this (C)

sections.Purpose: Find out how well a website protects its visitors through its HTTP response headers. The tool grades a site from A+ to F and explains each check in plain language: HSTS (forces HTTPS), Content-Security-Policy (blocks injected scripts, and is marked down for `unsafe-inline` and wildcards), clickjacking protection, `nosniff`, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy, cross-origin isolation, cookie flags (`Secure`, `HttpOnly`, `SameSite`) and whether the server advertises its software version. Each line says what's missing and how many points it cost.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python security_header_checker.py https://example.com [--min-grade C]
python security_header_checker.py saved-headers.txt
```
Give a URL (the page is requested once and only its headers are read) or a saved dump such as the output of `curl -sI -L https://example.com > headers.txt`; for a redirect chain the final response is graded. The exit code is 1 when the grade is worse than `--min-grade` (C by default), which makes it usable as a CI check for your own site. Only request sites you own or are allowed to test.
sections.Example:
```bash
python security_header_checker.py site-headers.txt
```
```
Security headers: grade C (64%)

  [PASS] HSTS                     20/20  HSTS enabled for 365 days
  [WARN] Content-Security-Policy  15/25  CSP allows 'unsafe-inline', which weakens it
  [PASS] Clickjacking             10/10  Framing is restricted (clickjacking protection)
  [PASS] MIME sniffing            10/10  X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
  [WARN] Referrer-Policy           5/10  Referrer-Policy 'no-referrer-when-downgrade' still leaks full URLs to other sites
  [FAIL] Permissions-Policy        0/5   No Permissions-Policy (camera, microphone, location... aren't restricted)
  [FAIL] Isolation                 0/5   No Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy / Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy
  [WARN] Cookies                   4/10  session lacks Secure/SameSite; theme lacks HttpOnly
  [WARN] Info disclosure           0/5   Reveals software details: Server: nginx/1.24.0, X-Powered-By: Express
```
sections.Notes:
- The score is a guide, not a certificate: a site can score A+ and still have other weaknesses, and a low score doesn't mean it has been hacked.
- Weights: CSP 25, HSTS 20, and 10 each for framing, `nosniff`, referrer policy and cookies; the rest 5.
- Use `header-inspector` to see every header, and `ssl-expiry-checker` for the certificate.
- The website demo grades saved header files; checking a live site works on your own computer.

tools.name: cert-chain-viewer
tools.summary: Print a site's (or a .pem file's) TLS certificate chain: who issued each certificate and when.

schema.description: Show a TLS certificate chain.

arguments.help: host (example.com or example.com:8443) or a .pem file
treat this date as today, YYYY-MM-DD (for testing)

sections.Purpose: See the whole trust chain behind a website's HTTPS certificate. For each certificate - the server's own, the intermediate CA that signed it and the root - the tool prints who it was issued to and by, the validity dates with the days left, the key type and size (RSA 2048-bit, EC P-256...), the signature algorithm, serial number, SHA-256 fingerprint and the host names it covers. It also checks that every certificate was issued by the next one in the list and flags broken links and expired certificates. It needs no OpenSSL.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python cert_chain_viewer.py example.com [--timeout 8]
python cert_chain_viewer.py example.com:8443
python cert_chain_viewer.py fullchain.pem [--today 2026-11-13]
```
Give a host (optionally with a port) to connect and read what the server presents, or a `.pem`/`.crt` file such as `fullchain.pem` from your web server. On Python 3.13+ the chain is exactly what the server sent; on older versions the tool reads the server's certificate and follows its "CA Issuers" links to find the parents. The exit code is 1 if any certificate has expired, a link in the chain doesn't match, or nothing could be read.
sections.Example:
```bash
python cert_chain_viewer.py fullchain.pem --today 2026-11-13
```
```
3 certificate(s), from fullchain.pem. Signatures are not verified here.

[1] example.com  (server certificate)
    issuer     Demo Intermediate CA 1
    valid      2026-10-01 to 2027-01-01 (49 day(s) left)
    key        RSA 2048-bit, signed with sha256WithRSA
    serial     6299EDFAA36ECBCD0AEB04BAE222FF9A2087D65B
    SHA-256    FB:78:36:4B:2F:3D:69:86:F5:8E:54:85:42:99:73:58:10:46:0D:98:F5:74:37:77:AB:4C:E3:BB:A1:47:EF:F0
    names      example.com, www.example.com
    link       issued by the next certificate

[2] Demo Intermediate CA 1  (intermediate CA)
    issuer     Demo Root CA
    valid      2024-01-01 to 2030-01-01 (1145 day(s) left)
    key        RSA 3072-bit, signed with ecdsa-with-SHA256
    serial     133624FE770202EB53CCA968438578CC9C13B694
    SHA-256    EB:A5:93:7C:00:32:77:97:5B:50:84:AC:33:2E:DF:86:8E:B3:6D:D3:A2:4F:55:E5:03:F4:62:BB:20:BB:B5:B8
    link       issued by the next certificate

[3] Demo Root CA  (root CA)
    issuer     Demo Root CA
    valid      2026-11-13 to 2036-11-10 (3650 day(s) left)
    key        EC P-384, signed with ecdsa-with-SHA256
    serial     3AFC5C4915EC05372E9A7F862247588D5284227F
    SHA-256    3B:A5:09:4A:26:A7:19:3D:FD:71:7C:84:96:BD:46:5B:C2:4B:12:DA:E0:71:49:D9:78:A6:D4:3A:3A:B7:09:CA
    link       self-signed root (the end of the chain)
