sections.Notes:
- Signatures are not cryptographically verified and the root isn't checked against a trust store; this tool shows the chain, it doesn't vouch for it.
- A server normally leaves out the root, so "not self-signed: the chain doesn't include its root" is expected for live hosts.
- Use `ssl-expiry-checker` to monitor several certificates' expiry dates.
- The website demo reads certificate files; checking a live host works on your own computer.

tools.name: image-compressor
tools.summary: Compress images in bulk with a quality setting, keeping only results that are smaller.

schema.description: Compress a folder of images.

arguments.help: also shrink images whose longest side is bigger (0 = keep size)
really write the files (default is a dry run)

sections.Purpose: Shrink a whole folder of photos so they upload and load faster. Each JPEG/WebP is re-encoded at the quality you choose, PNGs are re-saved with maximum lossless compression, and large images can also be scaled down with `--max-side`. A file is only written when the result is actually smaller; otherwise it is reported as "already small" and left alone.
sections.Install:
Needs Pillow:
```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```
sections.Usage:
```bash
python image_compressor.py FOLDER [--quality 80] [--max-side PX] [-o OUTDIR] [--apply]
```
Dry run by default: it works out the savings but writes nothing. With `--apply` the compressed copies go into `FOLDER/compressed` (or `-o`). Originals are never changed and existing results are never overwritten.
sections.Example:
```bash
python image_compressor.py . --quality 40 --apply
```
```
gps-photo.jpg: 4.8 KB -> 1.8 KB (-62%) 320x220
Holiday Photo 01.JPG: 3.9 KB -> 1.9 KB (-53%) 320x200
Holiday Photo 02.JPG: 2.7 KB -> 958 B (-66%) 300x200
logo.png: 840 B -> 630 B (-25%) 240x120
keep palette-demo.png: already small (286 B), not worth recompressing
photo-portrait.jpg: 3.3 KB -> 1.5 KB (-54%) 300x200
Screenshot 2026-03-01 at 09.30.15.png: 386 B -> 313 B (-19%) 160x100
Screenshot 2026-03-02 at 14.05.00.png: 387 B -> 314 B (-19%) 160x100
Compressed 7 image(s), saving 8.9 KB.
```
sections.Notes:
- Quality 70-85 is a good balance for photos; below 50 you will start to see blocky areas.
- Photos are turned the right way up using their rotation flag; other metadata such as camera details is dropped by the re-encode.
- Use `exif-stripper` if you only want to remove location data, and `image-resizer` for exact sizes.

tools.name: image-watermarker
tools.summary: Add a text watermark to every image in a folder.

schema.description: Add a text watermark to a folder of images.

arguments.help: really write the files (default is a dry run)

sections.Purpose: Stamp a text watermark (a copyright line, a name, "DRAFT") onto every image in a folder. The text is white with a soft dark shadow so it stays readable on both light and dark pictures, and you control the corner, size and transparency.
sections.Install:
Needs Pillow 10.1 or newer:
```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```
sections.Usage:
```bash
python image_watermarker.py FOLDER --text "(c) Me 2026" [--position bottom-right] [--opacity 50] [--size 5] [-o OUTDIR] [--apply]
```
`--position` is one of `bottom-right`, `bottom-left`, `top-right`, `top-left` or `center`. `--size` is the text height as a percentage of the image width. Dry run by default; `--apply` writes the marked copies into `FOLDER/watermarked` (or `-o`) and never overwrites a file.
sections.Example:
```bash
python image_watermarker.py . --text "(c) Kaushik 2026" --position bottom-left --apply
```
```
gps-photo.jpg -> watermarked\gps-photo.jpg (320x220)
Holiday Photo 01.JPG -> watermarked\Holiday Photo 01.JPG (320x200)
Holiday Photo 02.JPG -> watermarked\Holiday Photo 02.JPG (300x200)
logo.png -> watermarked\logo.png (240x120)
palette-demo.png -> watermarked\palette-demo.png (200x100)
photo-portrait.jpg -> watermarked\photo-portrait.jpg (300x200)
Screenshot 2026-03-01 at 09.30.15.png -> watermarked\Screenshot 2026-03-01 at 09.30.15.png (160x100)
Screenshot 2026-03-02 at 14.05.00.png -> watermarked\Screenshot 2026-03-02 at 14.05.00.png (160x100)
Watermarked 8 image(s).
```
sections.Notes:
- Originals are never touched; JPEG results are saved without transparency.
- A watermark deters casual copying but can be cropped out; it is not protection.
- Use `contact-sheet-maker` to review a whole folder of results at a glance.

tools.name: contact-sheet-maker
tools.summary: Build one contact sheet (a grid of labelled thumbnails) from a folder of images.

schema.description: Make a contact sheet from a folder of images.

arguments.help: really write the sheet (default is a dry run)

sections.Purpose: See a whole folder of pictures on one page. The tool crops every image to a square thumbnail, arranges them in a grid with the file name underneath, and saves a single contact sheet you can browse, print or send for approval. Photos shot in portrait mode are turned the right way up first.
sections.Install:
Needs Pillow 10.1 or newer:
```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```
sections.Usage:
```bash
python contact_sheet_maker.py FOLDER [--columns 4] [--thumb 160] [--no-labels] [-o SHEET.png] [--apply]
```
Dry run by default: it reports the grid size and what it would create. With `--apply` it writes `FOLDER/contact-sheet.png` (or `-o`) and refuses to overwrite an existing file. The sheet is never counted as one of its own inputs, so you can re-run it safely after moving the old one away.
sections.Example:
```bash
python contact_sheet_maker.py sprites/ --columns 3 --thumb 96 --apply
```
```
6 image(s) in a grid of 3 column(s): 320x252 pixels -> sprites\contact-sheet.png
Saved sprites\contact-sheet.png.
```
sections.Notes:
- Thumbnails are cropped to squares so the grid stays tidy; originals are untouched.
- Unreadable files are skipped with a message. The exit code is 1 when there is nothing to show or the sheet already exists.
- Use `thumbnail-generator` if you want a separate small file per image instead.

tools.name: exif-stripper
tools.summary: Remove EXIF and location data from photos by saving clean copies.

schema.description: Remove EXIF/GPS data from photos.

arguments.help: really write the files (default is a dry run)

sections.Purpose: Photos quietly carry extra information: the GPS position where they were taken, the camera and phone model, the exact time, and the editing software. Before you post a picture online, this tool shows what each photo reveals and saves clean copies with the pixels only. Orientation is applied first, so portrait photos still look right.
sections.Install:
Needs Pillow 10.1 or newer:
```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```
sections.Usage:
```bash
python exif_stripper.py FOLDER [-o OUTDIR] [--quality 95] [--apply]
```
Dry run by default: it lists what would be removed from each photo and writes nothing. With `--apply` the clean copies go into `FOLDER/clean` (or `-o`); originals are never modified and existing copies are never overwritten.
sections.Example:
```bash
python exif_stripper.py . --apply
```
```
gps-photo.jpg: removes GPS location, camera Canon EOS 90D, date 2026:03:01 09:30:15, software Demo Editor 2.1
Holiday Photo 01.JPG: removes camera DemoCam D100
Holiday Photo 02.JPG: removes camera DemoCam D100
logo.png: no metadata found
palette-demo.png: no metadata found
photo-portrait.jpg: removes camera DemoCam D100
Screenshot 2026-03-01 at 09.30.15.png: no metadata found
Screenshot 2026-03-02 at 14.05.00.png: no metadata found
Cleaned 8 photo(s); 4 carried metadata.
```
sections.Notes:
- JPEG copies are re-encoded (default quality 95), which is visually near-identical but not bit-for-bit.
- Colour profiles are dropped too, so colours can shift slightly on wide-gamut photos.
- Use `image-metadata-reader` to look at a single photo's full metadata first.

tools.name: audio-metadata-reader
tools.summary: Read tags and duration from audio files (MP3, FLAC and WAV) without any extra library.

schema.description: Read audio tags and duration.

sections.Purpose: Find out what is inside your music files without opening a player: title, artist, album, year, track number, genre and the length of each file, plus bitrate, sample rate and channels. It reads MP3 (ID3v2 and ID3v1 tags), FLAC (Vorbis comments) and WAV files with the Python standard library alone, so there is nothing to install.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python audio_metadata_reader.py FILE_OR_FOLDER [FILE_OR_FOLDER ...]
```
Folders are scanned for `.mp3`, `.flac` and `.wav` files (not subfolders). The exit code is 1 if any file couldn't be read. The last line adds up the total playing time, handy for an album or a playlist folder.
sections.Example:
```bash
python audio_metadata_reader.py audio-demo/
```
```
morning-raga.mp3  [0:03, 128 kbps, 44.1 kHz, stereo]
    Title   Morning Raga
    Artist  Demo Quartet
    Album   Sunrise Sessions
    Year    2025
    Track   3/9
    Genre   Classical
night-drive.flac  [3:20, 44.1 kHz, stereo]
    Title   Night Drive
    Artist  Synth Collective
    Album   Neon Roads
    Year    2024
    Track   1
    Genre   Electronic
tone.wav  [0:02, 8 kHz, mono]
    (no tags)

3 file(s), 3:25 in total.
```
sections.Notes:
- MP3 length is worked out from the file size and the first frame's bitrate, so it is exact for constant-bitrate files and an estimate for variable-bitrate ones.
- Other formats (M4A, OGG, Opus) aren't supported; use `video-info-reporter` (via ffprobe) for those.
- The tool only reads; it never changes tags. Use a tag editor such as Mp3tag or MusicBrainz Picard to edit them.

tools.name: video-info-reporter
tools.summary: Report codec, resolution, size and duration of video files using ffprobe.

schema.description: Report video details using ffprobe.

sections.Purpose: Get the key facts about video files in one glance: duration, file size, overall bitrate, the video codec with its resolution, frame rate and pixel format, the audio codec with sample rate and channel layout, subtitles, and the title/creation date if the file has them. It asks FFmpeg's `ffprobe` for the data, so it understands virtually every format.
sections.Install: Needs FFmpeg (which includes `ffprobe`) on your PATH: `winget install ffmpeg`, `brew install ffmpeg` or `sudo apt install ffmpeg`. No Python packages are required.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python video_info_reporter.py FILE_OR_FOLDER [...]
python video_info_reporter.py --from-json probe.json
```
Folders are scanned for common video extensions. `--from-json` reads output you saved earlier with `ffprobe -v error -print_format json -show_format -show_streams video.mp4 > probe.json`, which is useful on a machine without FFmpeg. The exit code is 1 if any file couldn't be read.
sections.Example:
```bash
python video_info_reporter.py --from-json ffprobe-holiday.json
```
```
holiday.mp4
  Duration   2:05
  Size       73.6 MB
  Bitrate    4922 kbps overall
  Video      h264, 1920x1080, 29.97 fps, yuv420p
  Audio      aac, 48 kHz, stereo
  Title      Holiday in Goa
  Creation time 2026-03-01T09:30:15.000000Z

1 video(s), 2:05 in total.
```
sections.Notes:
- If `ffprobe` isn't installed the tool says so instead of crashing.
- Use `video-frame-grabber` to save pictures from a video.
- The website demo reads saved ffprobe output; real videos are analysed on your own computer.

tools.name: similar-image-finder
tools.summary: Find near-duplicate images (resized, recompressed, brightened) with perceptual hashes.

schema.description: Find near-duplicate images.

arguments.help: most differing bits (out of 64) to still count as similar (6)

sections.Purpose: Find pictures that look the same even though the files differ: a photo and its resized copy, a re-saved or recompressed version, a slightly brightened edit. Exact-duplicate tools miss these because the bytes are different. This one computes a small "perceptual fingerprint" (a 64-bit difference hash) of every image and groups the ones whose fingerprints are nearly identical, marking the largest version of each group.
sections.Install:
Needs Pillow:
```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```
sections.Usage:
```bash
python similar_image_finder.py FOLDER [--threshold 6] [-r]
```
`--threshold` is how many of the 64 bits may differ (default 6; 0 means practically identical, higher finds looser matches but also more false alarms). `-r` includes subfolders. The tool only reports: it never moves or deletes anything, so you decide which copies to keep.
sections.Example:
```bash
python similar_image_finder.py similar-demo/
```
```
Group 1: 3 similar images (largest marked *)
 * beach-bright.jpg             640x440  10.2 KB  (reference)
   beach-small.jpg              160x110  2.1 KB  3 bit(s) different
   beach.jpg                    640x440  9.7 KB  2 bit(s) different

Checked 5 image(s): 1 group(s), 2 possible duplicate(s). Nothing was changed.
```
sections.Notes:
- The largest image (by pixels, then file size) is marked `*` as the likely original to keep.
- Cropped or heavily edited versions, or photos of the same scene from a different angle, will not match.
- Use `duplicate-file-finder` for byte-for-byte duplicates.

tools.name: palette-extractor
tools.summary: Extract the dominant colors of an image as hex codes with their share of the picture.

schema.description: Find an image's dominant colors.

arguments.help: print JSON instead of a table
also save a strip of the colors as an image

sections.Purpose: Pull the main colors out of a picture, for designing a matching website, choosing a theme or just seeing what a photo is made of. You get each color as a hex code and RGB value, how much of the image it covers, a plain-English name (navy, orange, beige...) and a small bar, ordered from the most to the least common. Transparent areas count as white.
sections.Install:
Needs Pillow:
```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```
sections.Usage:
```bash
python palette_extractor.py IMAGE [-n 5] [--json] [--swatch strip.png]
```
`-n` sets how many colors to find (1-16, default 5). `--json` prints machine-readable output. `--swatch` also saves a strip image with the colors in proportion; it refuses to overwrite an existing file.
sections.Notes:
- Colors are found by median-cut quantisation on a reduced copy of the image, so it is fast even for large photos.
- Gradients and photographs produce "average" colors rather than exact pixel values.
- Use `grayscale-converter` or `image-converter` to change the image itself.

tools.name: video-frame-grabber
tools.summary: Save still frames from a video at regular intervals using FFmpeg.

schema.description: Save frames from a video at intervals.

arguments.help: video length in seconds (skips ffprobe; handy for planning)
really save the frames (default is a dry run)

sections.Purpose: Turn a video into a set of still pictures: one frame every N seconds, for thumbnails, storyboards, slides from a recorded talk or a quick visual summary. It uses FFmpeg to seek straight to each moment, so it is fast even on long videos, and it names each picture with its timestamp.
sections.Install: Needs FFmpeg (including `ffprobe`) on your PATH: `winget install ffmpeg`, `brew install ffmpeg` or `sudo apt install ffmpeg`. No Python packages are required.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python video_frame_grabber.py VIDEO [--every 10] [--start 0] [--count N] [--format jpg|png] [-o OUTDIR] [--apply]
```
Dry run by default: it works out the timestamps and file names and shows the plan without running FFmpeg. With `--apply` the frames are saved into `./frames` (or `-o`). `--duration SECONDS` tells the tool the video's length so the plan works without `ffprobe`. Existing frames are skipped (FFmpeg is run with `-n`, so nothing is ever overwritten).
sections.Example:
```bash
python video_frame_grabber.py holiday.mp4 --duration 95 --every 30
```
```
holiday.mp4: 0:01:35 long, one frame every 30s
  0:00:00 -> holiday_00000000ms.jpg
  0:00:30 -> holiday_00030000ms.jpg
  0:01:00 -> holiday_00060000ms.jpg
  0:01:30 -> holiday_00090000ms.jpg
Would save 4 frame(s) to frames. Use --apply to do it.
```
sections.Notes:
- Names look like `holiday_00030000ms.jpg` (milliseconds into the video) so they sort in order.
- The last frame is always before the end of the video; a frame at exactly the end would be empty.
- Use `video-info-reporter` to see a video's length and codecs first, and `contact-sheet-maker` to view the frames together.
- The website demo shows the plan; saving real frames works on your own computer.

tools.name: sprite-sheet-builder
tools.summary: Pack a folder of images into one sprite sheet plus a JSON map of where each frame sits.

schema.description: Pack images into a sprite sheet.

arguments.help: really write the files (default is a dry run)

sections.Purpose: Combine many small images into one picture (a sprite sheet) plus a JSON file saying where each one sits. Game engines and websites load one image instead of dozens, which is faster, and the JSON "atlas" tells your code the x, y, width and height of every frame. Frames of different sizes are centred in equal-sized cells on a tidy grid.
sections.Install:
Needs Pillow:
```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```
sections.Usage:
```bash
python sprite_sheet_builder.py FOLDER [--columns N] [--padding 2] [--name spritesheet] [--apply]
```
Frames are packed in file-name order, so name them `frame-01.png`, `frame-02.png`... for animations. By default the grid is as square as possible. Dry run by default: it prints the layout. With `--apply` it writes `NAME.png` and `NAME.json` into the folder and refuses to overwrite earlier ones (use `--name` for a new sheet).
sections.Example:
```bash
python sprite_sheet_builder.py sprites/ --columns 3 --apply
```
```
6 frame(s), cell 36x36, sheet 116x78
  frame-01.png             at (4, 4) 32x32
  frame-02.png             at (44, 2) 28x36
  frame-03.png             at (78, 5) 36x30
  frame-04.png             at (4, 42) 32x32
  frame-05.png             at (46, 46) 24x24
  frame-06.png             at (79, 41) 34x34
Saved spritesheet.png and spritesheet.json in sprites.
```
sections.Notes:
- Transparency is kept, so use PNG frames for sprites.
- A sheet from an earlier run is never packed into the next one.
- Use `contact-sheet-maker` for a labelled preview grid instead of a sheet for programs.

tools.name: markdown-link-checker
tools.summary: Check the links inside markdown files: local files, #anchors and (optionally) web URLs.

schema.description: Check links in markdown files.

arguments.help: what links starting with / point to (current folder)

sections.Purpose: Find broken links in your documentation before your readers do. The tool reads markdown files (or whole folders of them) and checks every link and image: that the file it points to exists, that a `#section` anchor matches a real heading in the target page (using GitHub's anchor rules), that reference-style links like `[text][ref]` have a definition, and, if you ask, that web links still answer. Links inside code blocks and `inline code` are ignored.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python markdown_link_checker.py PATH [PATH ...] [--external] [--root DIR] [--timeout 8]
```
Each `PATH` is a markdown file or a folder (searched recursively). Local links are resolved relative to the file they are in; links starting with `/` are resolved from `--root`. Web links are only requested with `--external` (one HEAD request each, falling back to GET for servers that refuse HEAD). The exit code is 1 when any link is broken, so it works in CI.
sections.Example:
```bash
python markdown_link_checker.py handbook/
```
```
handbook\index.md:4  BROKEN  roadmap.md  (file not found)
handbook\index.md:11  BROKEN  #faq  (no heading with that anchor)
handbook\index.md:13  BROKEN  images/team.jpg  (file not found)
handbook\setup.md:9  BROKEN  [oops]  (undefined reference link)

Checked 3 file(s): 4 broken link(s). Web links were not checked (use --external).
```
sections.Notes:
- `mailto:`, `tel:` and similar links are skipped.
- Each web address is requested once per run even if it appears many times.
- Use `markdown-toc-generator` to build contents lists whose anchors this tool can then verify.

tools.name: markdown-to-html
tools.summary: Convert a markdown file into a single, styled, self-contained HTML page.

schema.description: Convert markdown to an HTML page.

arguments.help: HTML file to create (next to the input)
really write the file (default is a dry run)

sections.Purpose: Turn a markdown file into a single self-contained web page you can open in a browser, email or publish. It handles headings (with anchor ids), paragraphs, bold/italic/strikethrough, links and images, inline code and fenced code blocks, bullet, numbered and task lists, block quotes, tables and horizontal rules. The page has clean built-in styling that follows the reader's light or dark mode, and all text is HTML-escaped.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python markdown_to_html.py FILE.md [-o OUT.html] [--title TEXT] [--no-style] [--apply]
```
Dry run by default: it converts in memory and reports the title and size. With `--apply` it writes `FILE.html` next to the input (or `-o`) and refuses to overwrite an existing file. The title comes from the first `# heading` unless you pass `--title`.
sections.Example:
```bash
python markdown_to_html.py meeting-notes.md --apply
```
```
meeting-notes.md -> meeting-notes.html: "Team meeting", 1,827 characters, 3 heading(s)
Saved meeting-notes.html.
```
sections.Notes:
- Nested lists and raw HTML blocks are not supported; this is a deliberately small converter for everyday notes and READMEs.
- Use `markdown-to-pdf` when you need a PDF instead.

tools.name: readme-linter
tools.summary: Check a README for missing sections and common mistakes, and score it.

schema.description: Lint a README file.

sections.Purpose: Review a README the way a new visitor would. The linter checks for a title and a short description, install, usage, license and contributing sections, at least one code example, heading levels that don't skip, duplicate headings, empty links, leftover TODO text, a sensible length and a table of contents on long files. Each check is marked PASS, WARN or FAIL and the file gets a score out of 100.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python readme_linter.py README.md [--min-score 60]
```
The exit code is 1 when the score is below `--min-score` or any check FAILs, so it can guard a pull request. Headings inside code blocks are ignored.
sections.Example:
```bash
python readme_linter.py README.md
```
```
README.md: score 55/100

  [PASS] Title: Demo Project
  [FAIL] No short description under the title (what is this and who is it for?)
  [PASS] Has the install section
  [PASS] Has the usage section
  [FAIL] Missing the license section
  [WARN] Missing the contributing section
  [WARN] Missing the features or overview section
  [WARN] No code blocks: show a command or snippet people can copy
  [PASS] Heading levels are in order
  [WARN] Duplicate headings: usage
  [PASS] No TODO/placeholder text
  [WARN] Only 13 words; most READMEs need more detail

2 problem(s), 5 suggestion(s).
```
sections.Notes:
- Section names are matched loosely ("Getting started" counts as install, "Examples" as usage).
- A high score means the README is complete, not that it is well written; read it too.
- Use `markdown-link-checker` to verify the links in it.

tools.name: text-summarizer
tools.summary: Make an extractive summary: pick the most important sentences of a long text.

schema.description: Summarise a text file by picking key sentences.

sections.Purpose: Get the gist of a long article, report or email without reading all of it. The tool scores every sentence by how many of the text's most frequent meaningful words it contains (ignoring common words like "the" and "and"), gives a small bonus to the first sentence of each paragraph, and prints the best few in their original order. It works fully offline and needs no AI service.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python text_summarizer.py FILE.txt [-n 3] [--bullets]
```
`-n` is how many sentences to keep (default 3). `--bullets` prints one bullet per sentence instead of a paragraph. A line at the end shows how much of the text was kept. The exit code is 1 when the text is too short to summarise.
sections.Example:
```bash
python text_summarizer.py article-long.txt -n 3 --bullets
```
```
- Solar power is growing faster than any other source of electricity.
- Solar panels produce no electricity at night and very little during storms.
- In the coming years, experts expect solar power to supply a quarter of the world's electricity.

Kept 3 of 18 sentence(s): 39 of 245 words (15%).
```
sections.Notes:
- This is *extractive*: it quotes existing sentences rather than rewriting them, so the result is accurate but can read a little choppy.
- Sentences are split at `. ! ?` followed by a capital letter; common abbreviations like "Dr." and "e.g." don't count as sentence ends.
- Use `keyword-extractor` to list the main topics instead.

tools.name: keyword-extractor
tools.summary: Pull the top keywords (and optionally two-word phrases) out of one or more documents.

schema.description: Extract keywords from documents.

sections.Purpose: List what each document is mainly about. The tool counts the meaningful words in every text or markdown file (dropping common words such as "the" and "with") and shows the most frequent ones. When you give it several documents it weights the words so that terms found in every document rank lower and words special to one document rank higher (a simple TF-IDF), which is exactly what you want for tagging a folder of notes or articles.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python keyword_extractor.py FILE_OR_FOLDER [...] [--top 8] [--phrases]
```
Folders are searched recursively for `.txt`, `.md`, `.markdown` and `.rst` files. `--top` sets how many keywords to show per document. `--phrases` looks for repeated two-word phrases ("wind turbines") instead of single words.
sections.Example:
```bash
python keyword_extractor.py articles/ --top 4
```
```
batteries.txt  (23 words)
    batteries                x2
    battery                  x1
    changes                  x1
    falling                  x1
solar.txt  (25 words)
    solar                    x4
    panels                   x2
    cheaper                  x1
    evening                  x1
wind.txt  (26 words)
    wind                     x5
    farms                    x2
    air                      x1
    blows                    x1

Keywords are weighted so that words found in every document rank lower.
```
sections.Notes:
- Words must be at least three letters long; numbers are ignored.
- The ranking is by weighted score, the count (`x3`) shows how often the word appears.
- Use `word-counter` for a plain frequency table and `text-summarizer` for the key sentences.

tools.name: wordlist-spellcheck
tools.summary: Find words that are not in a word list, with spelling suggestions.

schema.description: Find unknown words against a word list.

arguments.help: one word per line (default: system list)
extra accepted words (names, jargon); can be repeated

sections.Purpose: Catch typos by checking every word of a document against a list of valid words. Anything not in the list is reported with the lines it appears on and up to three "did you mean" suggestions. Because it uses a plain word list, it is easy to adapt: use a dictionary for your language, add your own names and jargon with `--allow`, and it works the same on Windows, macOS and Linux.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. You need a word list: a text file with one word per line. On Linux and macOS the tool finds `/usr/share/dict/words` automatically; otherwise pass `--wordlist` (free lists such as SCOWL or `words_alpha.txt` work well).
sections.Usage:
```bash
python wordlist_spellcheck.py FILE [FILE ...] [--wordlist words.txt] [--allow mine.txt] [--ignore-capitalized]
```
Web addresses, email addresses, `inline code` and ALL-CAPS words are skipped. `--allow` adds extra accepted words and can be repeated. `--ignore-capitalized` skips names and places. The exit code is 1 when unknown words are found.
sections.Example:
```bash
python wordlist_spellcheck.py draft.txt --wordlist wordlist-small.txt
```
```
draft.txt: 9 unknown word(s)
  jumpd          line 1        did you mean: jumps
  chek           line 2        did you mean: check
  befor          line 2        did you mean: before, for
  leter          line 2        did you mean: letter
  freind         line 2        did you mean: friend
  thier          line 3        did you mean: there, their, other
  watter         line 3        did you mean: water
  kaushik        line 4
  zorblax        line 4

9 word(s) to check against wordlist-small.txt (143 known words).
```
sections.Notes:
- The tool only reports; it never edits your file.
- A word list can't judge grammar or the wrong-but-valid word ("their" vs "there").
- The demo list here is tiny on purpose; use a full dictionary for real work.

tools.name: docx-to-markdown
tools.summary: Convert Word (.docx) files to markdown: headings, bold/italic, links, lists and tables.

schema.description: Convert .docx files to markdown.

arguments.help: write FILE.md files into this folder instead of printing

sections.Purpose: Turn Word documents into clean markdown you can edit in any text editor, commit to git or publish on the web. Unlike a plain-text extractor, it keeps the document's structure: title and headings, **bold** and *italic* text, hyperlinks, bullet and numbered lists (including nested levels) and tables. It reads the `.docx` file directly, so Word does not need to be installed.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python docx_to_markdown.py FILE.docx [FILE.docx ...] [-o OUTDIR]
```
Without `-o` the markdown is printed (with a `<!-- name -->` marker between several files). With `-o` each file is written as `OUTDIR/NAME.md`; existing files are never overwritten. If the document has a Title style, it becomes `#` and Heading 1 becomes `##`. The exit code is 1 if a file can't be read.
sections.Example:
```bash
python docx_to_markdown.py report.docx
```
```
# Quarterly Report
sections.Summary:
Sales grew **12 percent** this quarter, driven by *new customers*. Read the [full dashboard](https://example.com/dashboard).

### Highlights

- Launched the mobile app
- Opened two new offices
- Hired **eight** engineers

### Next steps

1. Finish the audit
2. Plan the next release

| Region | Sales | Growth |
| --- | --- | --- |
| North | 120 | 10% |
| South | 95 | 14% |

Prepared by the finance team.
```
sections.Notes:
- Images, comments, footnotes and text boxes are not converted; use `docx-text-extractor` if you only need the text.
- Old `.doc` files must be saved as `.docx` first.
- Convert the result to a web page with `markdown-to-html`.

tools.name: readability-scorer
tools.summary: Score how easy a text is to read: Flesch reading ease, grade levels and more.

schema.description: Score the readability of text files.

arguments.help: exit with 1 if any file's average grade is above this

sections.Purpose: Find out how hard your writing is to read. The tool counts sentences, words and syllables and computes five well-known scores: Flesch reading ease (higher is easier; 60-70 is plain English), and the Flesch-Kincaid, Gunning fog, Coleman-Liau, SMOG and ARI grade levels (the US school grade needed to understand the text), plus their average. Use it to keep documentation, emails or web copy at the level your audience expects.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python readability_scorer.py FILE [FILE ...] [--target-grade 9]
```
`--target-grade` makes the exit code 1 when a file's average grade is above the target, so it can check writing in CI. Syllables are estimated with rules for English, so scores are approximate, and very short texts (under a few sentences) are unreliable.
sections.Example:
```bash
python readability_scorer.py plain-english.txt article-long.txt
```
```
plain-english.txt: 42 words, 9 sentences (4.7 words each, 0% long words)
  Reading ease   117.5  very easy (about 5th grade)
  Flesch-Kincaid grade  0.0
  Gunning fog    grade  1.9
  Coleman-Liau   grade  0.0
  SMOG           grade  3.1
  ARI            grade  0.0
  Average grade   0.0
article-long.txt: 245 words, 18 sentences (13.6 words each, 15% long words)
  Reading ease    53.5  fairly difficult (10th-12th grade)
  Flesch-Kincaid grade  9.2
  Gunning fog    grade 11.3
  Coleman-Liau   grade 11.9
  SMOG           grade 11.2
  ARI            grade  9.3
  Average grade  10.6
```
sections.Notes:
- Scores favour short sentences and short words; a low grade doesn't guarantee a clear text.
- Headings and bullet points without full stops count as sentence breaks only at blank lines.
- Use `word-counter` for basic counts and `text-summarizer` for the main points.

tools.name: srt-shifter
tools.summary: Shift subtitle (.srt) timings forward or backward by an offset.

schema.description: Shift .srt subtitle timings.

arguments.help: offset such as 2.5, -1.2s, 1500ms or -00:00:01,500 (write --shift=-2 for a negative value)
only shift cues starting at or after this time (default: all)
really write the file (default is a dry run)

sections.Purpose: Fix subtitles that appear too early or too late. The tool moves every cue in an `.srt` file by an offset you give (for example 2.5 seconds later, or 1 second earlier), optionally only from a certain time onwards, and writes a new, correctly numbered file. Cues pushed before 00:00:00 are clamped or dropped.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python srt_shifter.py MOVIE.srt --shift 2.5 [--after 00:10:00] [-o OUT.srt] [--apply]
python srt_shifter.py MOVIE.srt --shift=-1.5 --apply
```
Offsets can be `2.5` or `+2.5s` (seconds), `1500ms`, `1m30s` or a clock time such as `00:00:01,500`. For a negative offset write `--shift=-1.5` with an equals sign. `--after` limits the shift to cues starting at or after that time (use it when only the second half is out of sync). Dry run by default: it previews the first cues. With `--apply` it creates `MOVIE.shifted.srt` (or `-o`) and never overwrites an existing file; your original is untouched.
sections.Example:
```bash
python srt_shifter.py subtitles.srt --shift 2.5 --apply
```
```
5 cue(s), shifting by +2.5s
  00:00:01,000 -> 00:00:03,500  Welcome back to the channel.
  00:00:04,000 -> 00:00:06,500  Today we are building
  00:00:08,100 -> 00:00:10,600  First, create a new folder.
  00:01:02,500 -> 00:01:05,000  Now let's run it!
  01:00:00,000 -> 01:00:02,500  See you next time.
Saved subtitles.shifted.srt (5 cue(s)).
```
sections.Notes:
- Files with Windows line endings or a byte-order mark are handled.
- Only the timings change; the subtitle text is copied as it is.
- If the drift grows over the film (not a fixed offset), the frame rates differ; a stretch factor is outside this tool.

tools.name: glossary-builder
tools.summary: Build a glossary from the **bold** terms and their definitions in markdown notes.

schema.description: Build a glossary from bold terms in notes.

arguments.help: also list bold terms that have no definition

sections.Purpose: Turn your study notes or documentation into a glossary. Write definitions as you go in the form `**Term**: what it means` (or `**Term** - what it means`, with or without a leading bullet) and the tool gathers them from one or more markdown files into an alphabetical glossary grouped by letter. Terms defined twice are merged, and bold words that have no definition are counted so you know what is left to explain.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python glossary_builder.py NOTES.md [MORE.md ...] [--format md|csv|json] [--include-undefined] [-o glossary.md]
```
The result is printed unless you give `-o` (which refuses to overwrite an existing file). `--include-undefined` also lists bold terms that have no definition, marked "(no definition yet)". Text in code blocks is ignored. The exit code is 1 if no definitions were found.
sections.Example:
```bash
python glossary_builder.py study-notes.md --include-undefined
```
```
# Glossary
sections.B:
**Bandwidth**  
how much data a connection can carry per second.
sections.D:
**DNS**  
translates names such as example.com into IP addresses.
sections.L:
**Latency**  
the time a message takes to travel from sender to receiver.
sections.P:
**Packet**  
a small chunk of data sent across a network.
sections.U:
**UDP**  
faster but without delivery guarantees.

**router**  
(no definition yet)

**firewall**  
(no definition yet)

**OSI model**  
(no definition yet)

**bold words**  
(no definition yet)

1 term(s) were defined more than once (first definition kept).
```
sections.Notes:
- When a term is defined more than once, the first definition is kept and a note says so.
- Terms are matched without regard to capital letters.
- CSV and JSON output are handy for flashcard apps and spreadsheets.

tools.name: dockerfile-linter
tools.summary: Flag common Dockerfile mistakes: unpinned images, running as root, leaky layers and more.

schema.description: Lint a Dockerfile.

arguments.help: comma-separated rule ids to skip, e.g. DL012

sections.Purpose: Catch the Dockerfile mistakes that cause slow builds, big images and security problems, before you build. The linter reads your Dockerfile (including multi-line `RUN` commands) and flags: images with no tag or `:latest`, a container that runs as root, `apt-get install` without `-y`, missing cache cleanup, `pip install` without `--no-cache-dir`, `ADD` where `COPY` is meant, `cd` instead of `WORKDIR`, relative `WORKDIR`, `sudo`, `curl ... | sh`, secrets such as `ENV ADMIN_PASSWORD=...`, port 22, duplicate `CMD`/`ENTRYPOINT`, a missing `HEALTHCHECK`, and copying all source before installing dependencies (which defeats layer caching).
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python dockerfile_linter.py Dockerfile [--strict] [--ignore DL012,DL014]
```
Each finding shows the line number, a severity (ERROR, WARN or INFO), a rule id and a plain explanation. The exit code is 1 when there is any ERROR; with `--strict` warnings fail too. `--ignore` skips rules you disagree with.
sections.Example:
```bash
python dockerfile_linter.py Dockerfile
```
```
Dockerfile:1  WARN  DL001  'ubuntu' has no tag, so it means :latest; pin a version
Dockerfile:1  WARN  DL002  No USER instruction: the container runs as root
Dockerfile:1  INFO  DL012  No HEALTHCHECK defined
Dockerfile:3  ERROR DL004  apt-get install without -y waits for input and fails
Dockerfile:3  WARN  DL004  Remove /var/lib/apt/lists/* in the same RUN
Dockerfile:3  WARN  DL004  Run 'apt-get update' in the same RUN as install
Dockerfile:3  INFO  DL004  Add --no-install-recommends to keep the image smaller
Dockerfile:4  ERROR DL011  ADMIN_PASSWORD looks like a secret baked into the image
Dockerfile:5  WARN  DL013  WORKDIR 'app' is relative; use an absolute path
Dockerfile:6  WARN  DL003  Use COPY instead of ADD for plain files (ADD has hidden extras)
Dockerfile:7  WARN  DL005  pip install without --no-cache-dir keeps its cache
Dockerfile:7  WARN  DL006  Use WORKDIR instead of 'cd' inside RUN
Dockerfile:8  ERROR DL009  Piping a download into a shell runs unverified code
Dockerfile:9  WARN  DL010  Port 22 suggests SSH in a container; use docker exec instead
Dockerfile:11  WARN  DL007  2 CMD instructions; only the last one has an effect

3 error(s), 10 warning(s), 2 suggestion(s).
```
sections.Notes:
- Only the last stage of a multi-stage build is checked for `USER`.
- This is a quick static check, not a replacement for a full tool like hadolint or a vulnerability scanner.
- Use `env-template-generator` to keep secrets out of files you commit.

tools.name: env-template-generator
tools.summary: Make a .env.example from a real .env: same keys and comments, secret values removed.

schema.description: Create a .env.example from a .env file.

arguments.help: file to create (default: <env file>.example next to it)
keep harmless values (true/false, port numbers, localhost...)
really write the file (default is a dry run)

sections.Purpose: Create a safe `.env.example` from your real `.env` file, so teammates know which settings the project needs without ever seeing your passwords. Every variable and comment is kept in the same order, but the values are removed (or replaced with a placeholder). If an example file already exists, the tool doesn't touch it; it tells you which variables are missing from it and which are no longer used.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python env_template_generator.py .env [--keep-safe] [--placeholder TEXT] [-o OUTPUT] [--apply]
```
Dry run by default: it prints the template and says what it would write. With `--apply` it creates `.env.example` next to the input (or `-o`). `--keep-safe` keeps harmless values such as `true`, `8080` or `localhost` but still removes anything that looks secret (keys containing PASS, SECRET, TOKEN, KEY..., or URLs with credentials). Quotes, `export` prefixes and trailing comments are handled. The exit code is 1 if an existing example file is missing variables.
sections.Example:
```bash
python env_template_generator.py app.env --keep-safe
```
```
app.env: 5 variable(s), 4 value(s) removed

API_KEY=
DB_PASSWORD=
NAME=
EMPTY=
TOKEN=

app.env.example already exists and was not touched.
  Missing from it: NAME, EMPTY
  Only in it (not in app.env): SMTP_HOST
```
sections.Notes:
- Run it in CI to make sure `.env.example` never falls behind `.env`.
- The real `.env` is only read, never changed. Remember to keep it in `.gitignore`.
- Use `secret-scanner` to look for secrets that slipped into other files.

tools.name: requirements-checker
tools.summary: Report which pinned packages in a requirements.txt are behind their latest PyPI release.

schema.description: Check pinned requirements for newer versions.

arguments.help: JSON file {package: latest version} to use instead of asking PyPI

sections.Purpose: See which of your pinned Python packages have newer releases. The tool reads `package==version` lines from a requirements file, looks up each package's latest version on PyPI and tells you whether the update is a major, minor or patch change, so you can plan upgrades before an old version becomes a security problem. Lines without `==` (such as `numpy>=1.24`), comments and `-r` includes are ignored.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python requirements_checker.py requirements.txt [--latest latest.json] [--timeout 10]
```
By default each package is looked up on PyPI over the internet. `--latest` reads a saved JSON file such as `{"flask": "3.0.3"}` instead, which works offline and in tests. Set the `PYPI_URL` environment variable to use a private index that serves the same JSON API. The exit code is 1 when any package is outdated.
sections.Example:
```bash
python requirements_checker.py requirements-demo.txt --latest latest-versions.json
```
```
!  flask              2.0.1      -> 3.0.3      major update
!  requests           2.31.0     -> 2.32.3     minor update
!  Jinja2             3.1.2      -> 3.1.4      patch update
!  pytest             7.4.0      -> 8.3.3      major update
?  internal-tool      0.4.2      could not check (not in the version file)

5 pinned package(s): 4 outdated, 1 unchecked.
```
sections.Notes:
- Versions are compared numerically, and pre-releases sort before the release.
- Packages the tool can't look up (private packages, no network) are listed with `?` and don't fail the run.
- A newer version isn't always safe to install; read the changelog for major updates.
- The website demo uses a saved version file; live lookups work on your own computer.

tools.name: ci-config-validator
tools.summary: Validate GitHub Actions workflow files: structure, pinned actions and risky patterns.

schema.description: Validate GitHub Actions workflow files.

sections.Purpose: Catch mistakes in your GitHub Actions workflow files before pushing them and waiting for a failed run. The validator parses each workflow and checks that it has `on` and `jobs`, that every job has `runs-on` and `steps`, that `needs` points to real jobs, that every step has `uses` or `run` (not both) and no duplicate `id`. It also warns about actions without a version or pinned to a moving branch like `@main`, outdated actions such as `checkout@v2`, untrusted text like a pull-request title used directly inside `run:` (a command-injection risk), and missing `permissions` or `timeout-minutes`.
sections.Install:
Needs PyYAML:
```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```
sections.Usage:
```bash
python ci_config_validator.py PATH [PATH ...] [--strict]
```
Give workflow files or a folder such as `.github/workflows` (searched recursively for `.yml` and `.yaml`). Findings are listed per file as ERROR, WARN or INFO with their location (for example `jobs.test.steps[3]`). The exit code is 1 on any ERROR, or on warnings too with `--strict`.
sections.Example:
```bash
python ci_config_validator.py workflows/
```
```
workflows\ci.yml: 10 finding(s)
  ERROR jobs.test.steps[5] (Bad step): a step can have 'uses' or 'run', not both
  ERROR jobs.deploy: missing 'runs-on'
  ERROR jobs.deploy: needs 'build', but there is no such job
  ERROR jobs.deploy.steps[2]: duplicate step id 'ship' (also steps[1])
  WARN  jobs.test.steps[1]: actions/checkout@v2 is old; the current major is v4
  WARN  jobs.test.steps[2]: 'actions/setup-python@main' follows a moving branch; pin a tag or commit sha
  WARN  jobs.test.steps[4] (Greet the author): untrusted text (PR title, branch, comment...) in 'run' can inject commands; pass it through env
  INFO  file: no 'permissions': the token gets the repository default
  INFO  jobs.test: no 'timeout-minutes' (a stuck job runs up to 6 hours)
  INFO  jobs.deploy: no 'timeout-minutes' (a stuck job runs up to 6 hours)
workflows\release.yml: OK

2 file(s): 4 error(s), 3 warning(s), 3 suggestion(s).
```
sections.Notes:
- This checks structure and common risks; it does not run the workflow or know every action's inputs.
- The list of "current" action versions is small and built in; update it in the script when new majors appear.
- Use `dockerfile-linter` for the Dockerfiles your workflows build.

tools.name: makefile-target-lister
tools.summary: List the targets of a Makefile with their descriptions, grouped by ##@ section headings.

schema.description: List the documented targets of a Makefile.

sections.Purpose: Turn a Makefile into a readable help screen. The tool lists every target with its description and its dependencies, grouped under section headings, so newcomers can see what `make test` or `make deploy` do without reading the recipes. Descriptions come from a `## text` comment on the target line, or from the comment line directly above it. Variables, pattern rules (`%.o: %.c`) and special targets like `.PHONY` are ignored.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python makefile_target_lister.py [Makefile] [--all]
```
Write documentation like this in your Makefile:
```make
##@ Development
test: ## Run the tests
	pytest
```
`##@ Name` starts a new section. By default only documented targets are shown; `--all` also lists the rest as "(no description)". Targets that are not declared in `.PHONY` are marked `[file target]` since they normally produce a file. The exit code is 1 if nothing documented was found.
sections.Example:
```bash
python makefile_target_lister.py Makefile --all
```
```
Development
  install  Install the dependencies
  test     Run the test suite
  lint     Check the code style
  build    Build the distributable package  (needs: lint, test)

Housekeeping
  clean    Remove build output and caches
  run      (no description)
  docker   Build the Docker image

7 target(s) listed.
```
sections.Notes:
- Works with any `make` (GNU, BSD, Windows `nmake`-style files are not supported).
- Multiple targets on one line (`a b: ## doc`) share the description.
- Use `markdown-toc-generator` for the same kind of help for documentation files.

tools.name: port-conflict-checker
tools.summary: Check whether ports are free before starting services, and spot duplicates in compose files.

schema.description: Check ports before starting services.

arguments.help: docker-compose file whose published ports should be checked
only look for duplicates, don't test the ports on this machine

sections.Purpose: Avoid the "port is already allocated" error when starting your services. Give the tool the ports you need (or a `docker-compose.yml`) and it reports two kinds of trouble: **duplicates**, where two services publish the same host port (it understands `"8000:80"`, `127.0.0.1:9090:9090`, ranges such as `6380-6382:6380-6382` and `/udp`), and **ports already in use** on this machine, found by trying to bind them.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python port_conflict_checker.py 8000 8080-8082
python port_conflict_checker.py --compose docker-compose.yml [--host 0.0.0.0] [--static]
```
Without `--static` each TCP port is also tested on this computer: `FREE` ports aren't listed as problems, `IN USE` means another program is listening, and `NO PERMISSION` means the port needs administrator rights (or, on Windows, is reserved). `--static` skips the machine check and only looks for duplicates. The exit code is 1 when any problem is found, so it works as a pre-flight check in scripts.
sections.Example:
```bash
python port_conflict_checker.py --compose docker-compose.yml --static
```
```
5432/tcp DUPLICATE (docker-compose.yml:db and docker-compose.yml:cache) docker-compose.yml:cache, docker-compose.yml:db
   6380/tcp ok                                 docker-compose.yml:cache
   6381/tcp ok                                 docker-compose.yml:cache
   6382/tcp ok                                 docker-compose.yml:cache
   8000/tcp DUPLICATE (docker-compose.yml:web and docker-compose.yml:api) docker-compose.yml:api, docker-compose.yml:web
   8443/tcp ok                                 docker-compose.yml:web
   9090/tcp ok                                 docker-compose.yml:api

7 port(s) checked: 2 problem(s). Machine check skipped (--static).
```
sections.Notes:
- Container-only ports (`"3000"` with no host side) are skipped because Docker picks a random host port.
- Binding a port briefly and releasing it is safe, but a service could still grab the port a moment later.
- Use `open-ports-lister` to see which programs are listening right now.
- The website demo runs the duplicate check only; testing ports works on your own computer.

tools.name: health-check-poller
tools.summary: Poll health-check URLs several times and report failures, slow responses and uptime.

schema.description: Poll health-check URLs and report failures.

arguments.help: text the response body must contain
append every check to this CSV log
summarise a CSV log instead of polling

sections.Purpose: Check whether your services are really up, not just once but over a short period. The tool requests each health-check URL several times, records the status code and response time, and tells you for every URL whether it is **UP**, **SLOW**, **DEGRADED** (some checks failed) or **DOWN**, with the uptime percentage, average and slowest response, and the last error. It can also require a specific status (`200`, `2xx`, `204`...) or a piece of text in the response.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python health_check_poller.py URL [URL ...] [--count 3] [--interval 2] [--timeout 5] \
    [--expect 2xx] [--contains TEXT] [--slow 1000] [--csv log.csv]
python health_check_poller.py --summarise log.csv
```
Each round checks every URL once, then waits `--interval` seconds. `--csv` appends every check to a log file (creating it with a header if needed), and `--summarise` reads such a log later and prints the same summary without polling, which is handy for a report over many runs. The exit code is 1 when any URL is not UP, so it works in deployment scripts. Only poll services you own or are allowed to test.
sections.Example:
```bash
python health_check_poller.py --summarise health-results.csv
```
```
Summary:
  DEGRADED https://example.com/health  5/6 ok (83%), avg 368 ms, max 1210 ms  last error: HTTP 503
  UP       https://api.example.com/ping  6/6 ok (100%), avg 39 ms, max 44 ms
  DOWN     https://legacy.example.com/status  0/3 ok (0%), no response  last error: connection refused
```
sections.Notes:
- A response slower than `--slow` milliseconds makes a URL SLOW even if it returned 200.
- Redirects are followed; connection errors and timeouts count as failures with the error text.
- The website demo summarises a saved log; polling live URLs works on your own computer.

tools.name: cron-explainer
tools.summary: Explain cron expressions in plain English and show when they will run next.

schema.description: Explain cron expressions in plain English.

arguments.help: explain every line of a crontab file
how many future runs to show (3)

sections.Purpose: Read cron schedules without squinting at five numbers. Give the tool an expression such as `30 8 * * 1-5` or a whole crontab file and it explains each one in plain English ("At 08:30, on Monday through Friday") and lists the next times it will run, so you can check a schedule before relying on it. It understands `*`, ranges (`9-17`), lists (`1,15`), steps (`*/10`, `1-5/2`), month and weekday names (`JAN`, `MON-FRI`), Sunday as 0 or 7, and the macros `@hourly`, `@daily`, `@weekly`, `@monthly`, `@yearly` and `@reboot`.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python cron_explainer.py "*/15 9-17 * * 1-5" [more expressions] [--next 3] [--from "2026-11-18 09:30"]
python cron_explainer.py --file crontab.txt
```
Put each expression in quotes. With `--file`, comments, blank lines and `NAME=value` settings are skipped and the command is shown next to its schedule. `--from` sets the starting time for the "next runs" (default: now, in local time). If a day of the month and a weekday are both given, cron runs on days matching either one, and the explanation says so. The exit code is 1 if any expression is invalid.
sections.Example:
```bash
python cron_explainer.py --file crontab.txt --from "2026-11-18 09:30" --next 2
```
```
*/15 * * * *   /usr/bin/sync-data.sh
  Every 15 minutes, every day
  next: Wed 18 Nov 2026 09:45; Wed 18 Nov 2026 10:00

0 2 * * *   /usr/local/bin/backup.sh
  At 02:00, every day
  next: Thu 19 Nov 2026 02:00; Fri 20 Nov 2026 02:00

30 8 * * 1-5   /home/me/standup-reminder.sh
  At 08:30, on Monday through Friday
  next: Thu 19 Nov 2026 08:30; Fri 20 Nov 2026 08:30

0 0 1 * *   /usr/local/bin/monthly-report.sh
  At 00:00, on day 1 of the month
  next: Tue 01 Dec 2026 00:00; Fri 01 Jan 2027 00:00

0 9,17 * * MON,WED,FRI   /usr/local/bin/check-inbox.sh
  At 09:00 and 17:00, on Monday, Wednesday and Friday
  next: Wed 18 Nov 2026 17:00; Fri 20 Nov 2026 09:00

@daily   /usr/local/bin/rotate-logs.sh
  At 00:00, every day
  next: Thu 19 Nov 2026 00:00; Fri 20 Nov 2026 00:00

0 0 29 2 *   /usr/local/bin/leap-day.sh
  At 00:00, on day 29 of the month in February
  next: Tue 29 Feb 2028 00:00; Sun 29 Feb 2032 00:00
```
sections.Notes:
- Times are shown in the machine's local time; cron itself uses the server's timezone.
- Seconds fields (6-field Quartz or Spring expressions) are not supported.
- A schedule that can never match (like 31 February) says "never".

tools.name: docker-image-reporter
tools.summary: Report the sizes of local Docker images: the biggest ones, dangling images and totals.

schema.description: Report local Docker image sizes.

arguments.help: read saved output of: docker images --format '{{json .}}'

sections.Purpose: Find out what is eating your disk space. The tool lists your local Docker images from the biggest to the smallest with their age, flags the large ones (over 500 MB), counts the "dangling" images (untagged leftovers from rebuilds that `docker image prune` can remove) and points out repositories that keep several big old tags.
sections.Install: Needs Docker installed and running (for live use). No Python packages are required.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python docker_image_reporter.py [--top 10]
python docker_image_reporter.py --from-file images.jsonl
```
Without options it runs `docker images --format "{{json .}}"` for you. `--from-file` reads output you saved earlier, for example on another machine: `docker images --format "{{json .}}" > images.jsonl`. `--top` limits how many images are listed. The tool only reads; it never removes anything.
sections.Example:
```bash
python docker_image_reporter.py --from-file docker-images.jsonl --top 6
```
```
IMAGE                           SIZE  CREATED        ID

sections.Notes:
- Docker reports sizes in decimal units (1 GB = 1000 MB), and the tool does too.
- Images share layers, so the total is the sum of the listed sizes and the real disk use is usually lower. `docker system df` shows the true figure.
- If Docker isn't installed the tool says so instead of crashing.
- The website demo reads a saved list; your real images are reported on your own computer.

tools.name: release-tagger
tools.summary: Work out the next semantic version from commit messages, and optionally create the git tag.

schema.description: Suggest the next version from commit messages.

arguments.help: saved commit subjects, one per line (instead of reading git)
create the annotated git tag (never pushed)

sections.Purpose: Decide the next version number from what changed, and tag it. The tool finds the latest version tag, reads the commit messages since then and applies the Conventional Commits rules of semantic versioning: a `feat:` means a minor release, `fix:` or `perf:` a patch release, and anything with `!` (like `feat!:`) or a `BREAKING CHANGE:` line a major release. Other commits (docs, chore, refactor...) don't need a release on their own. It prints the changes grouped by kind and the next version, and can create the annotated tag for you.
sections.Install: Needs `git` on your PATH for repositories. No Python packages are required.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python release_tagger.py [--repo DIR] [--apply]
python release_tagger.py --log-file commits.txt --current v1.4.2
```
Dry run by default. With `--apply` the tool creates an annotated tag such as `v1.5.0` in the repository (listing the changes in its message) but never pushes it; it prints the `git push origin v1.5.0` command to run yourself and refuses to touch a tag that already exists. A repository with no tags starts from `v0.0.0`. For a saved list of commit subjects (`git log --format=%s > commits.txt`) pass `--log-file` and `--current`; `--apply` only works on a real repository.
sections.Example:
```bash
python release_tagger.py --log-file commits.txt --current v1.4.2
```
```
Current version: v1.4.2   (8 commit(s) since)

Breaking changes:
  - feat!: remove the deprecated v1 endpoints

Features:
  - feat(api): add pagination to the list endpoint

Fixes:
  - fix: handle empty responses from the billing service
  - fix(ui): correct the dark mode contrast on buttons

Other (no release on their own):
  - docs: explain the retry settings
  - chore: bump dependencies
  - refactor: split the settings module
  - Update README wording

Next version: v2.0.0  (major bump)
Dry run. Use --apply to create the tag in the repository.
```
sections.Notes:
- Commit messages that don't follow the convention count as "other", so they never cause a release.
- Pre-release suffixes (`-rc.1`) aren't handled; the tool works with plain `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` tags.
- Use `commit-message-linter` to keep your commit messages in the right format.

tools.name: clipboard-history-logger
tools.summary: Log clipboard changes to a searchable file, then list or search the history.

schema.description: Log, list and search clipboard history.

arguments.help: history file (clipboard-history.jsonl in your home folder)
also log text that looks like a password, key or card number

sections.Purpose: Never lose something you copied. The tool watches your clipboard and appends every new piece of text to a history file with a timestamp, then lets you list recent entries or search the whole history ("what was that command I copied on Thursday?"). By default it **skips anything that looks sensitive** (passwords, API keys, private keys, long token-like strings and credit-card numbers) so secrets don't end up in a file.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. It uses your system's clipboard tool: PowerShell on Windows, `pbpaste` on macOS, and `wl-paste`, `xclip` or `xsel` on Linux (install one of them).
sections.Usage:
```bash
python clipboard_history_logger.py watch [--log FILE] [--interval 1] [--seconds 600] [--count 20]
python clipboard_history_logger.py list [--last 10]
python clipboard_history_logger.py search TERM
```
`watch` checks the clipboard every `--interval` seconds until you press Ctrl-C (or `--seconds` / `--count` is reached). The history is a JSON-lines file, `clipboard-history.jsonl` in your home folder unless you pass `--log`. `--include-sensitive` turns the secret filter off; `--max-chars` limits how much of each entry is kept. Only text is recorded, not images or files. `search` exits with 1 when nothing matches.
sections.Example:
```bash
python clipboard_history_logger.py search flask --log clipboard-log.jsonl
```
```
2026-11-20 09:12:30  pip install flask requests
2026-11-21 09:20:37  Thanks for the update - I'll review the flask docs tomorrow.

2 match(es) in 7 saved entries.
```
sections.Notes:
- The history file is plain text and unencrypted: anything that passes the filter can be read by anyone with access to your account. Delete it whenever you like.
- The secret filter is a best effort, not a guarantee. Don't rely on it for highly sensitive material.
- The website demo searches a saved history; watching the clipboard works on your own computer.

tools.name: snippet-manager
tools.summary: Store text snippets (email replies, code, addresses) and paste them via the clipboard.

schema.description: Keep and paste text snippets.

arguments.help: snippet file (snippets.json in your home folder)
read the text for add from this file
really delete (default is a dry run)

sections.Purpose: Keep the text you type again and again (email replies, your address, SQL queries, code) in one place and get it back in a second. Save a snippet with a name, then `copy` it to the clipboard and paste it anywhere. Snippets can contain `{date}`, `{time}` and `{datetime}` placeholders that are filled in when you show or copy them, and the tool counts how often you use each one.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Copying uses your system's clipboard tool: `clip` on Windows, `pbcopy` on macOS, and `wl-copy`, `xclip` or `xsel` on Linux. If none is found, the text is printed instead.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python snippet_manager.py add NAME "text to save" [--file FILE] [--overwrite]
python snippet_manager.py list
python snippet_manager.py show NAME
python snippet_manager.py copy NAME
python snippet_manager.py search WORD
python snippet_manager.py delete NAME [--apply]
```
Snippets live in `snippets.json` in your home folder, or the file you give with `--store`. `add` refuses to replace an existing snippet unless you pass `--overwrite`. `delete` only says what it would remove until you add `--apply`. A mistyped name suggests close matches.
sections.Example:
```bash
python snippet_manager.py list --store snippets.json
```
```
address               39 chars  used 4x  Kaushik 12 Park Street Bengaluru 560001
meeting-reply         90 chars  used 9x  Thanks for the invite. I can join on {date} at {ti
sig                   37 chars  used 31x  Best regards, Kaushik svk@example.com
sql-active            62 chars  used 2x  SELECT * FROM users WHERE active = 1 ORDER BY crea

4 snippet(s) in snippets.json.
```
sections.Notes:
- The store is a readable JSON file, easy to back up or sync with a cloud folder.
- Use `text-expander` if you'd rather type short abbreviations that expand inside text files.
- The website demo lists and shows saved snippets; copying to the clipboard works on your own computer.

tools.name: active-window-logger
tools.summary: Log which application (and window title) has focus over time, to a CSV file.

schema.description: Log the focused application over time.

arguments.help: CSV log (window-log.csv in your home folder)
log only the application, not the window title (more private)

sections.Purpose: Record which application you are using and for how long, as raw material for a screen-time report or a timesheet. The tool checks the focused window every couple of seconds and writes a CSV row (`time,app,title`) each time the focus changes, such as switching from your editor to the browser. A log like this feeds `screen-time-report`, which adds up the time per application.
sections.Install:
Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Platform support:
- **Windows:** works out of the box (uses the Windows API).
- **macOS:** uses `osascript`; allow your terminal under System Settings > Privacy & Security > Accessibility to read window titles.
- **Linux:** needs `xdotool` and an X11 session (Wayland doesn't allow reading the active window).
sections.Usage:
```bash
python active_window_logger.py watch [--log FILE] [--interval 2] [--seconds 3600] [--count 50] [--no-titles]
python active_window_logger.py show [--last 15]
```
`watch` runs until you press Ctrl-C (or `--seconds` / `--count` is reached) and appends to `window-log.csv` in your home folder unless you pass `--log`. `--no-titles` records only the application name, which is more private because window titles can contain document names, email subjects and web page titles. `show` prints the latest rows.
sections.Example:
```bash
python active_window_logger.py show --log window-log.csv --last 8
```
```
2026-11-20 17:30:00  LockApp        Lock screen
2026-11-21 09:00:00  Chrome         Inbox - Mail
2026-11-21 09:20:00  Code           main.py - project
2026-11-21 10:15:00  Terminal       git status
2026-11-21 10:20:00  Code           main.py - project
2026-11-21 11:05:00  Slack          #team-chat
2026-11-21 11:20:00  Chrome         Docs - API reference
2026-11-21 12:00:00  LockApp        Lock screen

Showing 8 of 23 logged window change(s).
```
sections.Notes:
- The log is plain text and may contain sensitive titles; keep it private or use `--no-titles`.
- Only changes are logged, so the file stays small. A long gap between rows usually means the computer was idle or locked.
- The website demo shows a saved log; logging the live window works on your own computer.

tools.name: screen-time-report
tools.summary: Summarise application usage from an active-window log (time,app,title CSV).

schema.description: Report time spent per application.

arguments.help: longest gap in minutes to count as use; longer is idle (5)
extra apps to leave out, comma-separated

sections.Purpose: See where your computer time goes. The tool reads the log written by `active-window-logger` and adds up how long each application had focus, per day, with a share of the day and a small bar. Each log row lasts until the next one; a long gap (more than `--idle-gap` minutes, 5 by default) is treated as you being away and counted only up to that limit, and lock screens are never counted. Useful for timesheets, focus reviews or just curiosity.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python screen_time_report.py window-log.csv [--date 2026-11-20] [--top 8] [--idle-gap 5] [--by-title] [--ignore Spotify,Slack]
```
The input is a CSV with the columns `time,app,title` (ISO times). `--date` limits the report to one day, `--top` limits how many applications are listed per day, `--by-title` splits applications by window title (to see which documents or sites took the time) and `--ignore` leaves out applications. With several days in the log a combined total is added. The exit code is 1 when there is no usage to report.
sections.Example:
```bash
python screen_time_report.py window-log.csv --date 2026-11-20 --idle-gap 30
```
```
2026-11-20  total 4h 51m
  Code                                3h 30m   72%  ##################
  Chrome                                 53m   18%  #####
  Slack                                  18m    6%  ##
  Terminal                                6m    2%  #
  Spotify                                 4m    1%  #

Based on 23 log row(s) covering 27h 00m; gaps over 30 min and lock screens count as idle.
```
sections.Notes:
- A larger `--idle-gap` counts more of the quiet periods as use; a smaller one is stricter. Pick the value that matches how you work.
- The last row of a log has no end time, so it adds nothing until a newer row follows it.
- Pair it with `active-window-logger` to produce the log.

tools.name: wallpaper-rotator
tools.summary: Rotate the desktop wallpaper through the pictures in a folder.

schema.description: Change the wallpaper from a folder of pictures.

arguments.help: next: in order, random, daily: one per day (next)
remembers the last picture (.wallpaper-rotator.json in your home)
really change the wallpaper (default is a dry run)

sections.Purpose: Keep your desktop fresh by cycling through a folder of pictures. Run it by hand or from a scheduler (Task Scheduler, cron, launchd) and it picks the next picture and sets it as your wallpaper. Three modes: **next** goes through the folder in order and starts over, **random** picks a different picture each time, and **daily** shows one picture per day (the same all day).
sections.Install:
Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Setting the wallpaper uses the operating system:
- **Windows:** built in (png, jpg and bmp).
- **macOS:** built in (uses `osascript`).
- **Linux:** needs GNOME's `gsettings` (also sets the dark-mode picture) or `feh`.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python wallpaper_rotator.py FOLDER [--mode next|random|daily] [--seed N] [--state FILE] [--apply]
```
Dry run by default: it shows which picture is next and what it would run, and changes nothing. With `--apply` it sets the wallpaper and remembers the picture in a small state file (`.wallpaper-rotator.json` in your home folder, or `--state`) so `next` continues from there. `--seed` makes random choices repeatable. Supported files: `.png`, `.jpg`, `.jpeg`, `.bmp`.
sections.Example:
```bash
python wallpaper_rotator.py wallpapers/
```
```
3 picture(s) in wallpapers; mode next.
Next wallpaper: sunrise-1.png
Would run: SystemParametersInfoW SPI_SETDESKWALLPAPER ...
Dry run. Use --apply to change it.
```
sections.Notes:
- Original pictures are never modified.
- To rotate every hour on Windows, create a Task Scheduler task that runs `python wallpaper_rotator.py FOLDER --apply`.
- The website demo can only show the plan; changing the real wallpaper works on your own computer.

tools.name: reminder-scheduler
tools.summary: Schedule one-off terminal reminders: '25m', '15:30', or a list of them from a file.

schema.description: Schedule one-off reminders in the terminal.

arguments.help: read 'when message' lines from a file
pretend it is this time, 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM' (for planning)

sections.Purpose: Set quick reminders without opening any app. Tell it when and what ("25m  Stand up", "15:30  Submit the timesheet") and it waits in the terminal, then rings the terminal bell and prints the message. You can set one reminder from the command line, or load a whole day of them from a file. Handy for a Pomodoro, a meeting or "move the laundry".
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install. `--notify` additionally uses `osascript` (macOS), `notify-send` (Linux) or `msg` (Windows) if available.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python reminder_scheduler.py 25m "Stand up and stretch"
python reminder_scheduler.py 15:30 "Submit the timesheet" [--notify]
python reminder_scheduler.py --file reminders.txt [--plan] [--now "2026-11-21 09:00"]
```
Times can be relative (`25m`, `1h30m`, `90s`, `in 2h`), a clock time today or tomorrow (`15:30`) or a full date (`2026-11-22 09:00`). A reminders file has one `when message` per line; blank lines and `#` comments are ignored. `--plan` prints the schedule without waiting. Keep the terminal window open while you wait; Ctrl-C cancels everything.
sections.Example:
```bash
python reminder_scheduler.py --file reminders.txt --plan --now "2026-11-21 09:00"
```
```
4 reminder(s), starting 2026-11-21 09:00:00:
  Sat 21 Nov 09:25  (in 0h 25m)  Stand up and stretch
  Sat 21 Nov 10:00  (in 1h 00m)  Join the team call
  Sat 21 Nov 15:30  (in 6h 30m)  Submit the timesheet
  Sat 21 Nov 18:00  (in 9h 00m)  Go home!
Plan only; run without --plan to wait for them.
```
sections.Notes:
- Reminders only live while the program runs; if you close the window or shut down, they are gone.
- A clock time that has already passed today means tomorrow at that time.
- Use `countdown-timer` for a simple countdown and `snippet-manager` for reusable text.

tools.name: folder-watcher
tools.summary: Watch a folder and run a command whenever new (or changed) files appear.

schema.description: Run a command when files appear in a folder.

arguments.help: command to run per file, e.g. "python convert.py {path}" ({path} {name} {stem} {ext} {dir})
treat files already in the folder as new
stop watching after this many seconds
wait until a file hasn't changed for this many seconds (2)
really run the command (default is a dry run)

sections.Purpose: Automate "when a file lands here, do this". The tool watches a folder and, for every new (or changed) file, runs a command of your choice: convert a CSV, upload a report, resize a photo, start a backup. It waits until a file has stopped changing before acting, so it doesn't grab half-written files, and it ignores temporary files (`*.tmp`, `*.part`, `*.crdownload`, hidden files).
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python folder_watcher.py FOLDER --run "python process.py {path}" [--pattern "*.csv"] [--events new|changed|both]
                         [-r] [--include-existing] [--once] [--seconds N] [--interval 2] [--settle 2] [--apply]
```
Placeholders in `--run`: `{path}` (full path), `{name}`, `{stem}`, `{ext}` and `{dir}`. The command is split into words first and the file name is filled in afterwards, so names with spaces are safe and no shell is involved. **Dry run by default:** events and the commands that would run are printed; add `--apply` to really run them. By default only files that appear after the watch starts count; `--include-existing` also handles the files already there, and `--once` checks once and stops. Without `--once` it keeps watching until you press Ctrl-C (or `--seconds` runs out).
sections.Example:
```bash
python folder_watcher.py incoming/ --run "python process.py {path}" --once --settle 0
```
```
Watching incoming for new '*' files (dry run: commands are only shown)...
new     notes.txt
  would run: python process.py incoming\notes.txt
new     orders.csv
  would run: python process.py incoming\orders.csv
new     report.pdf
  would run: python process.py incoming\report.pdf
3 event(s) handled. Use --apply to run the command.
```
sections.Notes:
- It polls the folder every `--interval` seconds, so it needs no extra libraries and works the same on every system.
- A command's exit code is shown after each run; a failing command doesn't stop the watcher.
- Be careful what you run with `--apply`: the command receives whatever file arrives in the folder.
- Use `download-watcher` to sort a Downloads folder automatically.

tools.name: download-watcher
tools.summary: Sort files in your Downloads folder into subfolders (Images, Documents...) as they arrive.

schema.description: Sort downloaded files into folders by type.

arguments.help: the folder to sort (your Downloads folder)
keep running and sort new files
stop watching after this many seconds
leave files alone that changed in the last N seconds (5)
really move the files (default is a dry run)

sections.Purpose: Keep your Downloads folder tidy without thinking about it. The tool sorts the files in a folder into subfolders by type: Images, Documents, Data, Archives, Audio, Video, Installers, Code and Other. It leaves downloads that are still in progress (`.crdownload`, `.part`, `.tmp`, hidden files) and files that changed in the last few seconds alone, so it never moves a half-finished download. If a file with the same name is already in the destination, the new one gets `(1)`, `(2)`... so nothing is overwritten.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python download_watcher.py [FOLDER] [--watch] [--interval 10] [--seconds N] [--settle 5] [--apply]
```
`FOLDER` defaults to your `Downloads` folder. **Dry run by default:** it lists where each file would go. With `--apply` the files are moved. One pass is made unless you add `--watch`, which keeps sorting new arrivals every `--interval` seconds until you press Ctrl-C (or `--seconds` runs out). Existing subfolders are never touched.
sections.Example:
```bash
python download_watcher.py downloads/ --settle 0
```
```
backup.zip -> Archives/
data.csv -> Data/
holiday.jpg -> Images/
invoice.docx -> Documents/
movie.mp4 -> Video/
mystery -> Other/
notes.txt -> Documents/
report-q3.pdf -> Documents/
Screenshot 2026-11-20.png -> Images/
setup-1.2.exe -> Installers/
song.mp3 -> Audio/
skip big-file.iso.crdownload: download in progress or hidden

Would move 11 file(s): 1 Archives, 1 Audio, 1 Data, 3 Documents, 2 Images, 1 Installers, 1 Other, 1 Video. Use --apply to do it.
```
sections.Notes:
- Moves stay inside the same folder, so they are quick and keep the files' dates.
- Because moving is easy to reverse by hand, the tool doesn't keep an undo log; review the dry run first.
- The categories are listed in the script (`CATEGORIES`) if you want to add your own file types.
- Use `folder-watcher` to run your own command on new files instead.

tools.name: screenshot-indexer
tools.summary: Index screenshots with the text found in them (OCR) so you can search them later.

schema.description: Index and search screenshots by their text.

arguments.help: the folder to index, or the words to search for
really write the index file (default is a dry run)

sections.Purpose: Find a screenshot by what is written in it. The tool builds a small search index of a folder of screenshots (size, date from the file name, and the text visible in the picture) and lets you search it later: `search "invoice 4821"` lists every screenshot containing those words, with a snippet of the text. Re-indexing is incremental, so only new or changed pictures are processed.
sections.Install:
Needs Pillow:
```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```
