For the text, the tool uses (in this order) a **sidecar file** next to the picture (`shot.png.txt` or `shot.txt`, with text from any OCR program or app) or, if [Tesseract](https://github.com/tesseract-ocr/tesseract) is installed and on your PATH, runs it for you. Without either, pictures are still indexed by name, size and date, but not by their text.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python screenshot_indexer.py index FOLDER [--index screenshots-index.json] [--apply]
python screenshot_indexer.py search "words to find" [--index screenshots-index.json]
```
`index` is a dry run until you add `--apply`, which writes the JSON index. `search` needs every word to appear (in the text or the file name) and exits with 1 when nothing matches. Pictures that disappeared from the folder stay in the index until you delete the index file.
sections.Example:
```bash
python screenshot_indexer.py index screenshots/ --index shots-index.json --apply
```
```
shot-invoice.png: 320x180, 10 word(s) of text [sidecar]  Invoice #4821 Total due: 1,250.00 USD by...
shot-login-error.png: 320x180, 10 word(s) of text [sidecar]  Error 403 Access denied. Please sign in ...
shot-meeting.png: 320x180, 9 word(s) of text [sidecar]  Team standup Agenda: release plan, flask...

3 image(s): 3 new, 0 updated, 0 unchanged.
Saved shots-index.json.
```
sections.Notes:
- OCR is never perfect; search for distinctive words rather than whole sentences.
- The index contains the text of your screenshots, which may include private information; keep it private.
- The website demo reads the sidecar text files; Tesseract OCR runs on your own computer.

tools.name: text-expander
tools.summary: Expand abbreviations (btw, ;sig, addr) in text files using a map file.

schema.description: Expand abbreviations in text files.

arguments.help: abbreviation map: 'abbr = text' lines or a JSON object
really change the files (default is a dry run); a .bak copy is kept

sections.Purpose: Type less. Define short abbreviations once (`btw` for "by the way", `;sig` for your signature, `addr` for your address) and the tool expands them everywhere in your text files. Abbreviations are matched as whole words, longer ones win over shorter ones, and the replacement can span several lines and include `{date}`, `{time}` or `{datetime}`.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python text_expander.py FILE [FILE ...] --map abbreviations.txt [--ignore-case] [--apply]
```
The map file has one `abbreviation = replacement` per line (use `\n` for a line break; `#` starts a comment), or it can be a JSON object. **Dry run by default:** each file is reported with the number of replacements and the first changed line; add `--apply` to rewrite the files. Before changing a file the tool saves a backup next to it (`note.txt.bak`, or a time-stamped one if that exists), so you can always go back.
sections.Example:
```bash
python text_expander.py expand-demo.txt --map expander-map.txt
```
```
expand-demo.txt: 5 replacement(s) (;date x1, ;sig x1, addr x1, btw x1, omw x1)
  - btw the report is ready; omw to the office now.
  + by the way the report is ready; on my way to the office now.

Dry run. Use --apply to change the files.
```
sections.Notes:
- Matching is case-sensitive unless you pass `--ignore-case`.
- An abbreviation inside a longer word is left alone (`btw` doesn't change `abtwx`), and so is text like `;sig2`.
- Use `snippet-manager` to keep longer reusable text and copy it to the clipboard.

tools.name: csv-schema-validator
tools.summary: Validate a CSV file against a schema of column types and rules, or infer a schema from it.

schema.description: Validate a CSV file against a schema.

arguments.help: print a schema guessed from the CSV instead of validating

sections.Purpose: Catch bad data before it reaches your database or report. You describe what each column should look like in a small JSON schema (type, required, unique, minimum/maximum, allowed values, a pattern, a date format) and the tool checks every row, listing the exact line, column, value and reason for each problem. If you don't have a schema yet, `--infer` writes a first draft from the data itself.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python csv_schema_validator.py data.csv schema.json [--max-errors 20]
python csv_schema_validator.py data.csv --infer > schema.json
```
A schema looks like this:
```json
{"strict": true,
 "columns": {
   "id":     {"type": "int", "required": true, "unique": true, "min": 1},
   "email":  {"type": "str", "pattern": "^[^@\s]+@[^@\s]+$"},
   "status": {"type": "str", "allowed": ["active", "inactive"]},
   "joined": {"type": "date", "format": "%Y-%m-%d"}}}
```
Types are `str`, `int`, `float`, `bool`, `date` and `datetime`. Other rules: `required`, `unique`, `min`, `max`, `min_length`, `max_length`, `allowed`, `pattern`. Empty cells are fine unless the column is `required`. With `"strict": true`, columns that aren't in the schema are reported too. The exit code is 1 if anything is wrong, so it can gate a pipeline.
sections.Example:
```bash
python csv_schema_validator.py customers.csv customers-schema.json
```
```
line 9    id           '7' is a duplicate (first seen on line 8)
line 11   email        'not-an-email' does not match the pattern ^[^@\s]+@[^@\s]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,}$
line 12   name         is required but empty
line 13   age          '150' is above the maximum of 120
line 14   status       'pending' is not one of active, inactive
line 15   signup_date  '12/31/2024' is not a valid date (expected format %Y-%m-%d)
line 16   score        'n/a' is not a valid float

16 row(s) checked: 7 problem(s) on 7 row(s) - id (1), email (1), name (1), age (1), status (1), signup_date (1), score (1), 0 structure problem(s).
```
sections.Notes:
- Line numbers are lines of the file (the header is line 1).
- `--infer` is only a guess: review it, then tighten it by hand (for example add `allowed` lists or a `pattern`).
- Use `data-profiler` to understand a dataset first, and `json-schema-validator` for JSON documents.

tools.name: data-profiler
tools.summary: Profile a CSV dataset: types, missing values, unique counts and value distributions.

schema.description: Profile a CSV dataset.

sections.Purpose: Get to know a dataset in seconds. For every column of a CSV file the profiler shows the detected type (integer, decimal, date, true/false or text), how many values are present and missing, how many are unique, and a summary suited to the type: minimum, quartiles, median, mean, standard deviation and a text histogram for numbers; length and the most common values for text. It also warns about things worth a look: mostly-empty columns, constant columns, identifier-like columns, and numeric columns polluted with stray text.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python data_profiler.py data.csv [--columns age,status] [--top 5] [--bins 6] [--delimiter ";"]
```
Missing values are empty cells and the markers `NA`, `N/A`, `null`, `none`, `nan`, `-` and `?`. `--top` sets how many common values are listed and `--bins` how many histogram bars numbers get. A summary line gives the number of rows and duplicate rows.
sections.Example:
```bash
python data_profiler.py customers.csv --columns age,status,score
```
```
customers.csv: 16 rows x 9 columns, 0 duplicate row(s)

age  [int]  16 values, 0 missing, 15 unique
    min 27  p25 29.25  median 35  p75 44  max 150  mean 42.94  std 29.52
           27 - 47.50     #################### 14
        47.50 - 68        #                    1
           68 - 88.50                          0
        88.50 - 109                            0
          109 - 129.50                         0
       129.50 - 150       #                    1

status  [text]  16 values, 0 missing, 3 unique
    length 6-8 (average 6.4)
    common: active (12), inactive (3), pending (1)

score  [float]  14 values, 2 missing, 14 unique
    min 58  p25 71.25  median 80.25  p75 86.62  max 91  mean 78.54  std 9.82
           58 - 63.50     #####                1
        63.50 - 69        #####                1
           69 - 74.50     ##########           2
        74.50 - 80        ###############      3
           80 - 85.50     ###############      3
        85.50 - 91        #################### 4

0 of 3 column(s) have something worth a look.
```
sections.Notes:
- Types are guessed from the values, so one stray text value turns a number column into text (and the profiler warns you about it).
- For files with millions of rows use a tool built for scale; this one reads the file into memory.
- Use `csv-schema-validator` to turn what you learn into enforceable rules.

tools.name: sqlite-csv-importer
tools.summary: Load one or more CSV files into tables of a SQLite database.

schema.description: Load CSV files into a SQLite database.

arguments.help: table name (only with a single CSV; default: file name)
what to do when the table already exists (fail)
really write to the database (default is a dry run)

sections.Purpose: Turn CSV files into SQL tables you can query. Each CSV becomes a table in a SQLite database (a single portable file): column names are cleaned into safe SQL names, the type of each column (INTEGER, REAL or TEXT) is worked out from the data, empty cells and markers like `NA` become real NULLs, and values with leading zeros (zip codes, phone numbers, ids) are kept as text so the zeros aren't lost.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python sqlite_csv_importer.py a.csv [b.csv ...] --db mydata.db [--table NAME] [--if-exists fail|replace|append] [--apply]
```
**Dry run by default:** it shows each table, its columns and types and the row count, without touching the database. Add `--apply` to write. The table is named after the file unless you pass `--table` (single file only). If a table already exists the import stops (`fail`), unless you choose `replace` (drop and recreate) or `append` (only when the columns match). Then query the result with `sqlite-query-cli`.
sections.Example:
```bash
python sqlite_csv_importer.py customers.csv orders.csv --db demo.db --apply
```
```
customers.csv -> table customers (create): 16 row(s)
    id                   INTEGER
    name                 TEXT
    email                TEXT
    phone                TEXT
    age                  INTEGER
    status               TEXT
    signup_date          TEXT
    country              TEXT
    score                REAL
    done: table 'customers' now has 16 row(s)
orders.csv -> table orders (create): 12 row(s)
    order_id             INTEGER
    customer_id          INTEGER
    product              TEXT
    qty                  INTEGER
    price                REAL
    ordered_at           TEXT
    done: table 'orders' now has 12 row(s)
```
sections.Notes:
- Dates stay as text in ISO form (`2024-03-12`), which SQLite can sort and compare correctly.
- Rows shorter than the header are padded with NULLs; a header-only file creates an empty table.
- The database file is created if needed; existing tables you don't mention are left alone.

tools.name: sqlite-query-cli
tools.summary: Run SQL against a SQLite file and print the result as a table, CSV, JSON or markdown.

schema.description: Run SQL against a SQLite database.

arguments.help: one SQL statement, e.g. 'SELECT * FROM users'
list tables and their row counts
rows to print in table format, 0 for all (50)
allow statements that change the database
with --write: keep the changes (default only shows their effect)

sections.Purpose: Ask questions of a SQLite database from the terminal, without installing a database tool. Run any SQL query and get a neat aligned table (or CSV, JSON or markdown for other programs), list the tables with their row counts, or print their `CREATE` statements. The database is opened **read-only** by default, so a mistyped `DELETE` can't hurt anything.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install (SQLite is built into Python).
sections.Usage:
```bash
python sqlite_query_cli.py shop.db "SELECT * FROM customers LIMIT 5" [--format table|csv|json|markdown] [--limit 50]
python sqlite_query_cli.py shop.db --tables
python sqlite_query_cli.py shop.db --schema
python sqlite_query_cli.py shop.db "UPDATE customers SET country = 'IN' WHERE id = 1" --write [--apply]
```
One statement per call. Table output right-aligns numbers, shows missing values as `NULL`, shortens very long text and prints the first `--limit` rows (0 for all). Statements that change data need `--write`, and even then they are a **dry run** that reports how many rows would change; add `--apply` to keep the changes. The exit code is 1 when the SQL fails.
sections.Example:
```bash
python sqlite_query_cli.py shop.db "SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.order_id) AS orders, ROUND(SUM(o.qty * o.price), 2) AS spent FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id GROUP BY c.id ORDER BY spent DESC"
```
```
name          | orders | spent
--------------+--------+------
Ben Carter    |      2 | 87.05
Asha Rao      |      3 |  80.4
Diego Alvarez |      2 |  67.0
Emma Wilson   |      2 |  48.0
Chloe Martin  |      1 |  44.0
Farid Khan    |      1 |   9.5

6 row(s)
```
sections.Notes:
- Create a database from CSV files with `sqlite-csv-importer`, or from logs with `log-to-sqlite`.
- Quote the whole query so your shell doesn't treat `*` or `;` specially.
- Only SQLite files are supported (not MySQL or PostgreSQL).

example.query: SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.order_id) AS orders, ROUND(SUM(o.qty * o.price), 2) AS spent FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id GROUP BY c.id ORDER BY spent DESC

tools.name: json-schema-validator
tools.summary: Validate JSON files against a JSON Schema (a practical subset of drafts 6 and 7).

schema.description: Validate JSON files against a JSON Schema.

sections.Purpose: Check that JSON files have the shape you expect: the right fields, types and values. Write the rules once in a JSON Schema and the tool validates one file or a whole folder, listing every problem with its exact location (`$.address.zip`, `$.tags[1]`) in plain words. It implements the commonly used parts of JSON Schema (drafts 6 and 7) itself, so there is nothing to install.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python json_schema_validator.py schema.json FILE_OR_FOLDER [...] [--max-errors 10]
```
Folders are searched recursively for `.json` files. Supported keywords: `type` (including lists of types), `enum`, `const`, `required`, `properties`, `patternProperties`, `additionalProperties`, `items` (one schema or a list), `minItems`, `maxItems`, `uniqueItems`, `minLength`, `maxLength`, `pattern`, `format` (email, uri, date, date-time, ipv4, uuid), `minimum`, `maximum`, `exclusiveMinimum`, `exclusiveMaximum`, `multipleOf`, `minProperties`, `maxProperties`, `allOf`, `anyOf`, `oneOf`, `not`, `if`/`then`/`else` and local `$ref` references (`#/definitions/...` or `#/$defs/...`). Unknown keywords are ignored. The exit code is 1 if any file is invalid or unreadable.
sections.Example:
```bash
python json_schema_validator.py person.schema.json people/
```
```
ada.json: valid
bob.json: valid
broken.json: 8 problem(s)
  $.name is shorter than 1 character(s)
  $.email does not match the pattern ^[^@\s]+@[^@\s]+\.[a-z]{2,}$
  $.age is string, expected integer
  $.role must be one of "admin", "editor", "viewer"
  $.tags[1] is a duplicate of an earlier item
  $.nickname is not an allowed property
  $.address is missing the required property 'city'
  $.address.zip does not match the pattern ^\d{5,6}$

2 of 3 file(s) valid.
```
sections.Notes:
- Remote `$ref` addresses (http://...) are not fetched and give an error.
- Booleans are not numbers, and `3.0` counts as an integer, as the standard says.
- Use `csv-schema-validator` for CSV files.

tools.name: data-anonymizer
tools.summary: Mask emails, names, phone numbers and other personal data in a CSV file.

schema.description: Mask personal data in a CSV file.

arguments.help: mask this column as one of: email, name, phone, card, ip, hash, redact, year, scrub
never mask this column, even if it looks personal
secret text that makes the masking yours
really write the file (default is a dry run)

sections.Purpose: Share a dataset without sharing people's details. The tool finds the personal columns of a CSV (emails, names, phone numbers, IP addresses, card numbers, national ids) from their headers and values, and masks them: emails become `user_6de6d529@example.com`, names become made-up names, phone numbers keep only their last two digits, cards keep the last four. The same input always gives the same output (for a given `--salt`), so rows about the same person still match and joins keep working.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python data_anonymizer.py data.csv [--mask COLUMN:KIND] [--keep COLUMN] [--no-auto] [--salt SECRET] [-o OUT.csv] [--apply]
```
Kinds: `email`, `name`, `phone`, `card`, `ip`, `hash`, `redact`, `year` (keeps only the year of a date) and `scrub` (replaces emails and phone numbers found inside free text). **Dry run by default:** it lists the detected columns and previews the first rows. With `--apply` it writes `NAME.anonymized.csv` (or `-o`) and never overwrites an existing file. Use `--mask` to name columns the tool missed, `--keep` for ones it shouldn't touch and `--no-auto` to mask only what you name.
sections.Example:
```bash
python data_anonymizer.py customers.csv
```
```
customers.csv: 16 row(s), 3 column(s) to mask
  name           as name    (detected) - 15 value(s) changed
  email          as email   (detected) - 16 value(s) changed
  phone          as phone   (detected) - 15 value(s) changed

Preview (first rows):
  name         'Asha Rao'                   -> 'Casey Tate'
  email        'asha.rao@example.com'       -> 'user_6de6d529@example.com'
  phone        '+91 98765 43210'            -> '+XX XXXXX XXX10'

  name         'Ben Carter'                 -> 'Reese Hayes'
  email        'ben.carter@example.org'     -> 'user_e2c846fb@example.com'
  phone        '(555) 201-3344'             -> '(XXX) XXX-XX44'

  name         'Chloe Martin'               -> 'Sage Tate'
  email        'chloe.m@example.com'        -> 'user_8e9f506d@example.com'
  phone        '555-310-8899'               -> 'XXX-XXX-XX99'

Dry run. Use --apply to write customers.anonymized.csv.
```
sections.Notes:
- This is **pseudonymisation**, not a guarantee of anonymity: other columns (age, country, dates) can still identify someone when combined. Review the result before sharing.
- Keep your `--salt` secret; anyone who knows it can test guesses against the masked values.
- Empty cells stay empty, and the original file is never modified.

tools.name: csv-differ
tools.summary: Show which rows were added, removed or changed between two CSV files.

schema.description: Compare two CSV files row by row.

arguments.help: column(s) that identify a row, comma-separated (default: the first column)
treat 66 and 66.0, 'Yes' and 'yes' and extra spaces as equal

sections.Purpose: See exactly what changed between two versions of a CSV file. You choose the column(s) that identify a row (an id, an email, or a combination) and the tool reports the rows that were **added**, the rows that were **removed**, and the rows that were **changed**, with the old and new value of every field that differs. It also notes columns that appeared or disappeared. Handy for comparing exports from two dates, checking a data cleanup, or reviewing a pipeline's output.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python csv_differ.py old.csv new.csv [--key id] [--ignore updated_at,score] [--loose] [--max 20] [--format text|csv]
```
`--key` takes one or more column names separated by commas (default: the first column); it must be unique in both files, otherwise the tool says so and stops. `--ignore` leaves columns out of the comparison. `--loose` treats `66` and `66.0`, `Yes` and `yes`, and extra spaces as equal. `--format csv` prints a machine-readable list (`change,key,column,old,new`) instead of the report. The exit code is 0 when the files match, 1 when they differ and 2 on problems such as a duplicate key.
sections.Example:
```bash
python csv_differ.py customers-v1.csv customers-v2.csv --key id
```
```
customers-v1.csv (6 rows) -> customers-v2.csv (6 rows), key: id

Added (1):
  + 16  name=Omar Haddad, email=omar.haddad@example.com, status=active, score=70.0

Removed (1):
  - 5  name=Emma Wilson, email=emma.wilson@example.com, status=active, score=79.5

Changed (2):
  ~ 1
      email: 'asha.rao@example.com' -> 'asha.rao@newmail.example'
  ~ 3
      status: 'inactive' -> 'active'
      score: '65.5' -> '66.0'

1 added, 1 removed, 2 changed.
```
sections.Notes:
- Row order doesn't matter; only the key decides which rows belong together.
- Large lists are cut at `--max` entries per section; use `--format csv` to get everything.
- Use `data-profiler` to understand one file and `csv-schema-validator` to check it against rules.

tools.name: parquet-converter
tools.summary: Convert CSV to Parquet and back, with a size and schema report.

schema.description: Convert between CSV and Parquet.

arguments.help: file to create (default: same name with the other extension)
really write the file (default is a dry run)

sections.Purpose: Convert between CSV and Parquet, the compact column-oriented format used by data tools like pandas, Spark and DuckDB. Parquet files are typically several times smaller than the CSV they came from, remember column types (numbers stay numbers, dates stay dates) and load much faster. The tool detects the direction from the file extension, shows the columns, their types and missing-value counts, and reports the size change after converting.
sections.Install:
Needs pandas and a Parquet engine:
```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```
sections.Usage:
```bash
python parquet_converter.py data.csv [-o data.parquet] [--compression snappy|gzip|zstd|none] [--apply]
python parquet_converter.py data.parquet -o data.csv --apply
```
**Dry run by default:** it reads the file, prints the schema and says what it would create. With `--apply` it writes the converted file next to the source (or at `-o`) and never overwrites an existing file. `--delimiter` sets the separator for CSV input (use `.tsv` files for tabs). The exit code is 1 when a file can't be read or written.
sections.Example:
```bash
python parquet_converter.py orders.csv --apply
```
```
orders.csv: 12 row(s) x 6 column(s), 452 B
  order_id             int64           
  customer_id          int64           
  product              str             
  qty                  int64           
  price                float64         
  ordered_at           str             

Saved orders.parquet: 4.1 KB (832% larger than the original).
```
sections.Notes:
- Parquet pays off with more data: tiny files like the demo can even grow because of the format's fixed overhead.
- Column types come from pandas' guess; empty cells in a whole-number column make it decimal (`float64`).
- Use `csv-to-json` or `json-to-csv` for text formats, and `sqlite-csv-importer` for a database.
- The website demo uses the `fastparquet` engine; on your computer `pyarrow` is used.

tools.name: log-to-sqlite
tools.summary: Load web-server access logs and application logs into SQLite so you can query them with SQL.

schema.description: Load log files into a SQLite database.

arguments.help: start the log tables from scratch instead of adding to them
really write to the database (default is a dry run)

sections.Purpose: Turn log files into something you can ask questions of. The tool reads web-server access logs (the common Apache/nginx "combined" format) and application logs (`2026-11-10 08:40:09,475 WARNING [api] message`), recognises each line automatically and stores it in a SQLite database with proper columns: time, IP, method, path, status and bytes for access logs; time, level, component and message for application logs. Stack traces that follow an error line are attached to that error's message. Then use SQL ("which pages returned errors?", "how many warnings per hour?").
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python log_to_sqlite.py app.log access.log --db logs.db [--replace] [--apply]
```
Two tables are used: `access_logs` and `app_logs`. **Dry run by default:** it only reports how many lines of each kind it found (and how many it didn't recognise). With `--apply` the rows are added; new files are appended to what is already there, or use `--replace` to start the tables from scratch. Timestamps are stored as ISO text (`2026-11-10T09:00:06`), so SQL can sort and filter them. After loading it prints a short summary. Query the result with `sqlite-query-cli`.
sections.Example:
```bash
python log_to_sqlite.py app.log access.log --db logs.db --apply
```
```
app.log: 0 access line(s), 42 application line(s)
access.log: 60 access line(s), 0 application line(s)

Saved to logs.db:
  access_logs: 60 row(s)
  app_logs: 42 row(s)
    INFO      22
    WARNING   10
    ERROR     6
    DEBUG     3
    CRITICAL  1
    status codes: 200 x50, 304 x4, 500 x2, 403 x2

Try: sqlite_query_cli.py logs.db "SELECT path, COUNT(*) FROM access_logs WHERE status >= 500 GROUP BY path"
```
sections.Notes:
- Running `--apply` twice on the same files adds the rows twice; use `--replace` to reload.
- Lines that match no known format (and aren't part of a stack trace) are counted but not stored.
- For quick reports without a database, see `log-analyzer`, `nginx-log-parser` and `top-ips-reporter`.

tools.name: pipeline-runner
tools.summary: Run a chain of data steps (read, filter, join, group, sort, write...) from a YAML file.

schema.description: Run a data pipeline from a YAML file.

arguments.help: really write the output files (default is a dry run)

sections.Purpose: Describe a small data-cleaning job in a YAML file and run it with one command, repeatably. A pipeline is a list of steps applied in order to a CSV table: read it, filter rows, compute new columns, join another file, group and total, sort, trim, and write the result. Because the steps live in a file, you can review them, keep them in git and rerun them whenever the data changes, without writing code.
sections.Install:
Needs PyYAML (JSON pipeline files work too):
```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```
sections.Usage:
```bash
python pipeline_runner.py pipeline.yml [--apply]
```
```yaml
name: top orders report
steps:
  - read: orders.csv
  - filter: {column: qty, op: ">=", value: 2}
  - add_column: {name: total, expr: "qty * price"}
  - sort: {by: total, desc: true}
  - select: [order_id, product, qty, price, total]
  - limit: 5
  - write: top-orders.csv
```
Steps: `read` (path or `{file, delimiter}`), `filter` (`column`, `op`, `value`; ops `== != > >= < <= contains startswith endswith matches is_empty not_empty`), `select`, `drop`, `rename` (`{old: new}`), `sort` (`by`, `desc`), `dedupe` (columns), `limit`, `fill` (`column`, `value`), `add_column` (`name` plus `expr`, `template` such as `"{first} {last}"`, or `value`), `group` (`by`, `agg: {column: sum|mean|min|max|count}`), `join` (`file`, `on`, optional `right_on`, `how: left|inner`) and `write`. Expressions allow only numbers, column names and `+ - * / % //`. **Dry run by default:** everything runs in memory and a preview is shown; `write` only creates its file with `--apply`, and never overwrites an existing file. A failing step stops the run and names its number.
sections.Example:
```bash
python pipeline_runner.py pipeline.yml
```
```
Pipeline: top orders report

 1. read orders.csv                                                        -> 12 row(s), 6 column(s)
 2. filter {"column": "qty", "op": ">=", "value": 2}                       -> 8 row(s), 6 column(s)
 3. add_column {"name": "total", "expr": "qty * price"}                    -> 8 row(s), 7 column(s)
 4. sort {"by": "total", "desc": true}                                     -> 8 row(s), 7 column(s)
 5. select ["order_id", "product", "qty", "price", "total"]                -> 8 row(s), 5 column(s)
 6. limit 5                                                                -> 5 row(s), 5 column(s)
 7. write top-orders.csv                                                   -> 5 row(s), 5 column(s)

Result (first 5 of 5 row(s)):
  order_id | product   | qty | price | total
  ---------+-----------+-----+-------+------
  1011     | Backpack  | 3   | 39.9  | 119.7
  1007     | Backpack  | 2   | 39.9  | 79.8
  1004     | Notebook  | 10  | 4.5   | 45
  1005     | Desk lamp | 2   | 22.0  | 44
  1006     | Pen set   | 4   | 7.25  | 29

Would write top-orders.csv (5 row(s)). Use --apply to do it.
```
sections.Notes:
- All values are read as text; comparing and sorting treat numbers as numbers when both sides look numeric.
- Column names in expressions must not contain spaces (use a `rename` step first).
- Use `csv-differ` to compare a pipeline's output between runs and `csv-schema-validator` to check it.

tools.name: async-url-checker
tools.summary: Check thousands of URLs concurrently (asyncio) with global and per-host limits.

schema.description: Check many URLs concurrently.

arguments.help: URLs or text files with one URL per line
save the results to this new CSV file
report on a saved CSV instead of checking
validate the list; make no requests

sections.Purpose: Check a very long list of web addresses quickly and politely. The tool uses Python's `asyncio` to keep many requests in flight at once (50 by default), with a separate limit per website (5) so one server is never hammered. For each URL it reports the final status, the response time and where redirects lead, retries short-lived failures (5xx errors and network hiccups) with a growing pause, and sums everything up. It can save the results to a CSV file and later summarise that file without touching the network again.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python async_url_checker.py urls.txt [more.txt https://extra.example/] [--concurrency 50] [--per-host 5]
                            [--timeout 10] [--retries 1] [--method HEAD|GET] [--no-follow]
                            [--only-problems] [--csv results.csv]
python async_url_checker.py --plan urls.txt
python async_url_checker.py --summarise results.csv [--slow 2000] [--only-problems]
```
Inputs are URLs or text files with one URL per line (`#` starts a comment); duplicates and invalid lines are removed and counted. `HEAD` requests (the default) are fast and fall back to `GET` for servers that refuse them. `--plan` only validates the list. `--csv` saves `url,status,ms,final_url,error` to a new file (never overwriting). The exit code is 1 if any URL is broken, so it works as a link check in CI. Only check sites you own or are allowed to test, and keep the limits modest.
sections.Example:
```bash
python async_url_checker.py --summarise link-check-results.csv
```
```
OK            200    84 ms  https://example.com/  
OK            200   131 ms  https://example.com/products  
REDIRECT      301    62 ms  https://example.com/old-page  -> https://example.com/new-page
CLIENT ERROR  404    77 ms  https://example.com/missing  HTTP 404
OK            200   210 ms  https://www.python.org/  
OK            200  2450 ms  https://slow.example.net/report    (slow)
FAILED          0      ---  https://down.example.org/  connection refused
SERVER ERROR  503   320 ms  https://example.com/api/health  HTTP 503
OK            200    96 ms  https://example.com/about  

9 URL(s): 5 ok, 1 redirect, 1 client error, 1 server error, 1 failed.
Response times: median 131 ms, slowest 2450 ms.
```
sections.Notes:
- Statuses: OK, REDIRECT (the final address differs), CLIENT ERROR (4xx), SERVER ERROR (5xx) and FAILED (no answer).
- Requests run in worker threads managed by asyncio, so no extra libraries are needed.
- Use `bulk-url-checker` for a simpler thread-pool version and `broken-link-finder` to find links inside a page.
- The website demo summarises a saved results file; checking live URLs works on your own computer.

tools.name: parallel-downloader
tools.summary: Download many files in parallel, resuming partial downloads and never overwriting files.

schema.description: Download many files in parallel, with resume.

arguments.help: URLs or text files with one URL per line
really download (default only shows the plan)

sections.Purpose: Download a list of files several at a time, and pick up where an interrupted download left off. Files are saved as `NAME.part` while they download and renamed to `NAME` only when complete, so you never end up with a half-finished file that looks finished. If a `.part` file exists from an earlier run, the tool asks the server to continue from that point (an HTTP `Range` request); if the server can't resume, it starts that file again cleanly. Files that already exist are never overwritten, and two URLs with the same file name get `(1)`, `(2)`... added.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python parallel_downloader.py file-urls.txt [https://more.example/a.zip] [-o downloads] [--workers 4]
                              [--timeout 30] [--retries 2] [--apply]
```
URLs can be given directly or in text files with one per line (`#` starts a comment). **Dry run by default:** it prints each file's name and state (`new`, `resume from 2.0 KB`, `exists, skipped`) without touching the network. Add `--apply` to download with `--workers` at a time. Each failed file is retried (resuming) up to `--retries` times, and the final line counts what succeeded and failed; the exit code is 1 if anything failed. Only download files you have the right to download.
sections.Example:
```bash
python parallel_downloader.py file-urls.txt -o dl
```
```
4 file(s) to dl/ (1 invalid line(s) skipped)
  report-q3.pdf                      resume from 2.0 KB     https://downloads.example.com/reports/report-q3.pdf
  logo.png                           exists, skipped        https://downloads.example.com/images/logo.png
  export-2026-11.csv                 new                    https://downloads.example.com/data/export-2026-11.csv
  archive-ef9a75                     new                    https://downloads.example.com/archive?id=77&format=zip
  skipping invalid: ftp://files.example.com/old.iso

Dry run: 3 to download with 4 at once. Use --apply to start.
```
sections.Notes:
- File names come from the URL path (`q3%20report.pdf` becomes `q3 report.pdf`); a URL with no usable name gets a short hash name.
- When the server reports the file size, the finished download is checked against it.
- Use `image-downloader` to grab pictures from a page and `rate-limited-fetcher` when you need to be gentler with a server.
- The website demo shows the plan; downloading works on your own computer.

tools.name: api-recorder
tools.summary: Record API responses to JSON fixture files that tests can replay.

schema.description: Record API responses as JSON fixtures.

arguments.help: spec file (JSON or YAML) of calls
record only the call with this name
list the fixtures already recorded in the output folder
really call the API and write fixtures (default is a plan)

sections.Purpose: Capture real API responses once and reuse them in tests, demos or offline development. You list the calls in a small spec file; the tool makes each request and saves a JSON **fixture** with the request, the status, the response time, the headers and the body (parsed as JSON when it is JSON). Secrets are protected: tokens are read from environment variables (`${API_TOKEN}`), and `Authorization`, cookies and API-key headers are replaced with `<redacted>` in the saved files.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+ (JSON specs). Reading a YAML spec needs PyYAML: `pip install pyyaml`.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python api_recorder.py api-calls.json [-o fixtures] [--only NAME] [--refresh] [--apply]
python api_recorder.py --list [-o fixtures]
```
A spec looks like this:
```json
{"base_url": "https://api.example.com/v1",
 "headers": {"Authorization": "Bearer ${API_TOKEN}"},
 "calls": [{"name": "list-users", "path": "/users?limit=2"},
           {"name": "create-user", "method": "POST", "path": "/users", "body": {"name": "Test"}},
           {"name": "health", "url": "https://status.example.com/health"}]}
```
**Dry run by default:** it prints each call and whether its fixture is new or already exists, and makes no requests. With `--apply` it calls the API and writes one `NAME.json` per call into the output folder. Existing fixtures are kept unless you add `--refresh`. If a `${VARIABLE}` isn't set, `--apply` stops and names it. `--list` summarises the fixtures already recorded. Only record APIs you are allowed to call, and remember that fixtures contain response data.
sections.Example:
```bash
python api_recorder.py api-calls.json
```
```
list-users           GET    https://api.example.com/v1/users?limit=2  [exists, kept]
get-user-1           GET    https://api.example.com/v1/users/1  [new]
create-user          POST   https://api.example.com/v1/users  [new]
health               GET    https://status.example.com/health  [new]

Note: variables not set here: API_TOKEN (needed with --apply).

Plan only: 3 call(s) would be recorded into fixtures. Use --apply to do it.
```
sections.Notes:
- Response headers such as `Set-Cookie` are redacted too, but review a fixture before committing it: the body may contain personal data.
- Non-JSON responses are stored as text.
- Use `mock-server` to serve recorded responses and `api-smoke-tester` to check a live API.
- The website demo shows the plan and keeps recorded fixtures untouched; recording works on your own computer.

tools.name: api-smoke-tester
tools.summary: Run smoke tests against REST endpoints described in a JSON file.

schema.description: Smoke-test REST endpoints from a JSON file.

arguments.help: use this base URL instead of the file's
run only the test with this name
check the file and list the tests; make no requests

sections.Purpose: Answer "is my API alive and behaving?" in a few seconds, from a plain JSON file. Each test names an endpoint and what you expect: the status code, fields in the JSON response (nested paths like `data.user.id`), text in the body, a response header, and a maximum response time. The tool runs the tests in order and prints PASS or FAIL with the reason, which makes it a good post-deploy check or CI step.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python api_smoke_tester.py smoke-tests.json [--base-url https://staging.example.com] [--only NAME] [--fail-fast] [--timeout 10]
python api_smoke_tester.py smoke-tests.json --validate
```
```json
{"base_url": "https://api.example.com",
 "headers": {"Authorization": "Bearer ${API_TOKEN}"},
 "tests": [
   {"name": "health", "path": "/health", "expect_status": 200, "max_ms": 500},
   {"name": "user 1", "path": "/users/1", "expect_json": {"name": "Ada", "tags.0": "*"}},
   {"name": "create", "method": "POST", "path": "/users", "body": {"name": "Zed"},
    "expect_status": 201, "expect_contains": "Zed"}]}
```
`expect_status` defaults to 200. In `expect_json` a value of `"*"` means "the field must exist". `expect_header` checks that a header contains some text (case-insensitively). Header values can use `${ENV_VARS}`, so tokens stay out of the file. `--validate` checks the file and lists the tests without making any request. The exit code is 1 if any test fails. Only test APIs you own or are allowed to test.
sections.Example:
```bash
python api_smoke_tester.py smoke-tests.json --validate
```
```
ok  GET    health                 https://api.example.com/health  [status, max_ms]
ok  GET    users list             https://api.example.com/users  [status, json, header]
ok  GET    user 1                 https://api.example.com/users/1  [json]
ok  GET    missing user           https://api.example.com/users/999  [status]
ok  POST   create                 https://api.example.com/users  [status, contains]

5 test(s) look valid. No requests were made.
```
sections.Notes:
- Mistakes in the file (unknown settings, duplicate names, a missing URL) are reported before anything runs.
- A test that can't reach the server fails with the reason, rather than stopping the whole run.
- Use `latency-benchmark` for response-time statistics and `health-check-poller` for repeated checks.
- The website demo validates the test file; running the tests works on your own computer.

tools.name: webhook-receiver
tools.summary: A local server that logs incoming webhooks, checks their signatures, and shows the log.

schema.description: Receive, log and inspect webhooks.

arguments.help: show: the log to read; verify: the saved payload
shared secret for HMAC SHA-256 signature checks
verify: the signature to check, e.g. sha256=ab12...
answer 401 when a signature is present but wrong
show: only entries whose path contains this

sections.Purpose: See exactly what a service sends to your webhook URL while you develop. `serve` starts a small local server that accepts any request, answers it (200 by default), prints one line per request and appends the full details (method, path, headers, parsed body, size) to a log file. If you give it the shared secret, it checks each request's HMAC SHA-256 signature (the `X-Hub-Signature-256` style used by GitHub and many others) and marks it valid or INVALID, optionally answering 401 for bad signatures. `show` reads a log back, and `verify` checks a saved payload against a signature when you are debugging.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install. To receive webhooks from the internet you also need a tunnel such as ngrok or Cloudflare Tunnel pointing at your port.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python webhook_receiver.py serve [--port 8000] [--log webhook-log.jsonl] [--secret SHARED_SECRET]
                                 [--status 200] [--reject-invalid] [--max-requests N]
python webhook_receiver.py show webhook-log.jsonl [--path /hooks/github] [--last 20]
python webhook_receiver.py verify payload.json --secret SHARED_SECRET --signature sha256=...
```
The server listens on `127.0.0.1` (your computer only) unless you pass `--host`. `Authorization`, `Cookie` and API-key headers are replaced with `<redacted>` in the log, but bodies are stored as received, so treat the log as sensitive. `show` exits with 1 if the log contains an INVALID signature; `verify` exits with 1 when the signature doesn't match.
sections.Example:
```bash
python webhook_receiver.py show webhook-log.jsonl
```
```
09:00:12  POST   /hooks/github      valid       61 B  {"ref": "refs/heads/main", "commits": 3}
09:03:40  POST   /hooks/stripe      none        44 B  {"type": "invoice.paid", "amount": 4900}
09:07:05  POST   /hooks/github      INVALID     38 B  {"action": "opened", "number": 42}
09:15:31  GET    /health            none         0 B  (no body)
09:21:02  POST   /hooks/form        none        32 B  name=Ada&email=ada%40example.com

5 request(s), 1 with an INVALID signature; showing the last 5.
```
sections.Notes:
- Signatures are computed over the raw request body, which is why `verify` reads the file as bytes; re-formatting the JSON changes the signature.
- Bodies over 1 MB are cut off.
- Use `mock-server` to pretend to be an API and `api-recorder` to capture real API responses.
- The website demo shows a saved log; running the server works on your own computer.

tools.name: rate-limited-fetcher
tools.summary: Fetch URLs politely: a request rate limit, retries with backoff, and respect for Retry-After.

schema.description: Fetch URLs politely with rate limits.

arguments.help: URLs or text files with one URL per line
also save each response body here
really make the requests (default only shows the plan)

sections.Purpose: Fetch web pages the way a considerate visitor would. The tool keeps a minimum gap between requests to the same website (so `--rate 1` means at most one request per second per site), and when a server pushes back it **backs off**: on a 429 or 5xx answer or a network error it waits and tries again, pausing longer each time (1s, 2s, 4s... with a little random jitter so many clients don't all return at once). If the server sends a `Retry-After` header, that exact wait is used instead. Responses can be saved to a folder.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python rate_limited_fetcher.py urls.txt [https://more.example/page] [--rate 1] [--retries 3] [--backoff 1]
                               [--timeout 15] [-o pages] [--apply]
```
URLs can be given directly or in text files with one per line (`#` starts a comment). **Dry run by default:** it prints the schedule (when each request would start) and an estimate of the total time, and makes no request. Add `--apply` to fetch. Successful pages are saved into `-o` (existing files are never overwritten). The exit code is 1 if any URL ultimately failed. Always check a site's terms and `robots.txt` first, and keep the rate low; see `sitemap-crawler` for a robots-aware crawl.
sections.Example:
```bash
python rate_limited_fetcher.py urls.txt --rate 2
```
```
4 URL(s) on 3 site(s), 2 request(s)/second per site, up to 3 retries (1 invalid skipped)
  t+  0.0s  https://example.com
  t+  0.5s  https://example.com/
  t+  0.0s  https://www.python.org/
  t+  0.0s  http://example.org/page?utm_source=news&id=7

Plan only: about 0.5s without retries (retries wait 1s, 2s, 4s... or the server's Retry-After). Use --apply to fetch.
```
sections.Notes:
- Statuses that are retried: 408, 425, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504, and network errors. Other 4xx answers (such as 404) are final.
- The limit is per site, so URLs on different sites are fetched without waiting for each other.
- Use `async-url-checker` when you only need to know whether URLs work, and `parallel-downloader` for big files.
- The website demo shows the plan; fetching works on your own computer.

tools.name: sitemap-crawler
tools.summary: List a sitemap's pages, mark which ones robots.txt allows, and optionally crawl them.

schema.description: Explore a sitemap within robots.txt rules.

arguments.help: robots.txt URL or file (default: the site's own)
robot name to check the rules for (*)
fetch the sitemaps listed by a sitemap index (needs the network)
visit the allowed URLs (default only lists them)
seconds between page requests (a larger robots Crawl-delay wins)

sections.Purpose: Explore a website through its sitemap while following its rules. The tool reads a `sitemap.xml` (or a sitemap index), reads the site's `robots.txt`, and lists every page marked **allowed** or **BLOCKED** for your crawler name. It applies the rules the way search engines do: the most specific matching rule wins, `Allow` beats `Disallow` when equally specific, `*` and `$` work in patterns, and the group for the most specific user-agent is used. It also reports the requested `Crawl-delay` and the sitemaps declared in robots.txt. Add `--fetch` to visit the allowed pages one at a time, with a polite delay.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python sitemap_crawler.py --sitemap https://example.com/sitemap.xml [--robots URL_OR_FILE] [--agent MyBot]
                          [--limit 50] [--follow-index] [--fetch] [--delay 1]
python sitemap_crawler.py --sitemap sitemap.xml --robots robots.txt
```
The sitemap and robots.txt can be URLs or saved files, so you can check rules offline. For a URL sitemap, the site's own `/robots.txt` is read automatically. `.gz` sitemaps are unpacked. A sitemap index lists its sub-sitemaps; `--follow-index` reads them too (one request each). Pages on other hosts are skipped. With `--fetch` the delay between requests is `--delay` or the robots `Crawl-delay`, whichever is larger, and each visit shows the status, time, size and page title. Blocked pages are never requested. Only crawl sites you are allowed to crawl.
sections.Example:
```bash
python sitemap_crawler.py --sitemap sitemap-full.xml --robots robots.txt
```
```
10 URL(s) in the sitemap, robots rules for '*'
  allowed     https://example.com/
  allowed     https://example.com/products
  allowed     https://example.com/products/widget-a
  allowed     https://example.com/blog/launch
  BLOCKED     https://example.com/admin/dashboard
  BLOCKED     https://example.com/private/notes
  allowed     https://example.com/private/public/faq
  allowed     https://example.com/about
  allowed     https://example.com/contact
  BLOCKED     https://example.com/admin/users

7 allowed, 3 blocked by robots.txt.
robots.txt asks for a Crawl-delay of 5.0s; using 5s between requests.
Sitemaps declared in robots.txt: https://example.com/sitemap.xml
Use --fetch to visit the allowed pages (one at a time, politely).
```
sections.Notes:
- A missing robots.txt means "everything allowed", with a note.
- This is not a full crawler: it visits the sitemap's pages only and doesn't follow links (see `link-graph-builder`).
- Use `robots-checker` to test a single URL and `sitemap-lister` to just list a sitemap.
- The website demo checks saved files; fetching pages works on your own computer.

tools.name: link-graph-builder
tools.summary: Build a link graph of a small site (from a folder of HTML files, or by crawling a URL).

schema.description: Build a link graph of a small site.

arguments.help: folder holding the site's HTML files
start page of a live site (needs --fetch)
allow requests to the live site
write the graph as JSON (new file)

sections.Purpose: See the structure of a small website at a glance. The tool follows the links between pages and builds a graph: which pages are linked most, how many clicks each page is from the home page, which pages are **orphans** (nothing links to them, so visitors can't find them), which are **dead ends** (no links out) and which internal links are **broken**. It works on a folder of HTML files (ideal for static sites, with no network at all) or, if you allow it, on a live site. You can export the graph for Graphviz or as JSON.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install. (Graphviz is only needed if you want to draw the `.dot` file.)
sections.Usage:
```bash
python link_graph_builder.py --dir site/ [--start index.html] [--dot site.dot] [--json graph.json]
python link_graph_builder.py --url https://example.com/ --fetch [--max-pages 50] [--delay 1]
```
With `--dir`, links are resolved the way a web server would (`blog/` means `blog/index.html`, `../x.html`, `/root-relative.html`, `#anchors` ignored); images and other files count as assets, not pages. With `--url`, only pages on the same site are followed, and **nothing is requested unless you add `--fetch`**; requests are `--delay` seconds apart and capped by `--max-pages`, so only crawl sites you may crawl. `--dot` and `--json` create new files and refuse to overwrite existing ones. The exit code is 1 when broken links or orphan pages are found.
sections.Example:
```bash
python link_graph_builder.py --dir site/ --dot site.dot
```
```
7 page(s), 15 internal link(s), 1 external site(s); start: index.html

Most linked-to pages:
   4 in  index.html  Home
   2 in  about.html  About us
   2 in  blog/index.html  Blog
   2 in  blog/post-1.html  First post
   2 in  blog/post-2.html  Second post

Clicks from the start page:
  0: index.html
    1: about.html
    1: blog/index.html
    1: products.html
      2: blog/post-1.html
      2: blog/post-2.html
      2: team.html

Not reachable by clicking from the start page (orphans):
  secret.html

Broken internal links:
  products.html  ->  old-products.html

External sites linked: github.com
```
sections.Notes:
- Render the graph with `dot -Tpng site.dot -o site.png` after installing Graphviz.
- Links to other sites are listed but never followed.
- Use `broken-link-finder` for a link check of a single page and `sitemap-crawler` to explore a site through its sitemap.

tools.name: mock-server
tools.summary: Serve mock API responses from a JSON file, or preview what a request would get.

schema.description: Serve mock API responses from a JSON file.

arguments.help: the JSON file describing the routes
port to listen on (the file's, or 8080)

sections.Purpose: Pretend to be an API while you build something that depends on it. Describe the endpoints in a JSON file (method, path, status, headers, body, optional delay) and the tool serves them on a local port, with CORS headers so browser apps can call it. Paths can have parameters (`/users/{id}`), and `{id}` or `{query.name}` placeholders inside the response body or headers are filled in from the request. Unknown requests get a 404 that lists the routes you did define, which makes typos easy to spot.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python mock_server.py serve mock-api.json [--port 8080] [--host 127.0.0.1] [--no-cors] [--max-requests N]
python mock_server.py check mock-api.json
python mock_server.py simulate mock-api.json "GET /users/7?verbose=1"
```
```json
{"port": 8080,
 "routes": [
   {"method": "GET", "path": "/users/{id}", "body": {"id": "{id}", "name": "User {id}"}},
   {"method": "POST", "path": "/users", "status": 201, "headers": {"Location": "/users/3"}, "body": {"created": true}},
   {"method": "GET", "path": "/slow", "delay_ms": 1500, "body": {"ok": true}}]}
```
`method` can be `"*"` for any method; the first matching route wins. Object and list bodies are sent as JSON, strings as plain text. `check` validates the file and lists the routes; `simulate` shows the response a request would get without starting a server (handy for testing templates). The server listens on `127.0.0.1` (your computer only) unless you pass `--host`, and prints one line per request.
sections.Example:
```bash
python mock_server.py simulate mock-api.json "GET /users/7?verbose=1"
```
```
HTTP 200
Content-Type: application/json

{"id": "7", "name": "User 7"}
```
sections.Notes:
- Use `api-recorder` to capture real responses and paste them into the routes.
- A route with `delay_ms` makes timeouts and loading states easy to test.
- The website demo uses `simulate`; running the server works on your own computer.

tools.name: latency-benchmark
tools.summary: Benchmark an endpoint's latency with percentiles (p50, p90, p95, p99) or summarise timings.

schema.description: Benchmark endpoint latency with percentiles.

arguments.help: the endpoint to benchmark (your own server!)
save every measurement to this new CSV file
summarise saved timings (one number per line, or a CSV with 'ms')

sections.Purpose: Measure how fast an endpoint really responds. The tool sends a number of requests (a few at a time or in parallel), times each one and reports the **minimum, mean, median, standard deviation, maximum and the p90, p95 and p99 percentiles** (p95 = 95% of requests were faster than this), plus the throughput in requests per second, the status codes seen and a text histogram showing the shape of the distribution. Percentiles matter more than the average: a few slow requests can hide behind a good mean.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python latency_benchmark.py URL [-n 100] [-c 5] [--warmup 3] [--method GET|HEAD] [--timeout 10] [--csv raw.csv]
python latency_benchmark.py --summarise timings.txt [--slow 1000]
```
The warm-up requests aren't counted (they let connections and caches settle). `--csv` saves every measurement to a new file (never overwriting). `--summarise` analyses saved timings, either one number per line or a CSV with an `ms` column such as the one `--csv` writes. Requests are limited to 5000 and concurrency to 100. The exit code is 1 if any request failed or returned an error. **Only benchmark servers you own or have permission to test**: this tool can generate real load.
sections.Notes:
- Timings include connection setup (a fresh connection per request), so they are a bit higher than a browser reusing connections.
- Run it from a machine close to the server if you want to measure the server rather than the network.
- Use `health-check-poller` for repeated uptime checks and `api-smoke-tester` to verify responses.
- The website demo summarises saved timings; benchmarking a live endpoint works on your own computer.

tools.name: repo-health-scorer
tools.summary: Score a project folder on what makes a repo trustworthy: README, license, tests, CI...

schema.description: Score a repository folder's health.

arguments.help: also score the last commit's age

sections.Purpose: Find out how healthy a project looks to a newcomer, and what to fix first. The tool inspects a project folder and awards points for the things that make a repository trustworthy: a README (with enough detail and Install/Usage sections), a LICENSE, automated tests, CI configuration, a `.gitignore`, a dependency list, CONTRIBUTING and CHANGELOG files, a SECURITY or CODE_OF_CONDUCT file, and no committed junk such as `node_modules`, `__pycache__` or `.env` (unless your `.gitignore` already hides it). It prints a percentage, a letter grade and a checklist with advice for every missing piece.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install. `--git` also needs the `git` command.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python repo_health_scorer.py [FOLDER] [--min-score 60] [--git]
```
Without a folder it scores the current one. Test files are recognised for Python, JavaScript/TypeScript and Go; CI for GitHub Actions, GitLab, Travis, Jenkins, Azure and others. `--git` adds a "Recent activity" check (last commit within 90 days is full marks) when the folder is a git repository's own root. The exit code is 1 when the score is below `--min-score`, so it can guard a pull request or a template repo.
sections.Example:
```bash
python repo_health_scorer.py pyproj/
```
```
pyproj: 12 file(s), health 78% (grade B)

  [PASS] README                 10/10
  [MISS] README detail           0/5   Expand the README (at least ~100 words)
  [PASS] README install/usage    5/5 
  [PASS] License                10/10
  [PASS] Tests                  15/15
  [PASS] CI                     15/15
  [PASS] .gitignore              5/5 
  [PASS] Dependencies listed     5/5 
  [MISS] CONTRIBUTING            0/5   Add CONTRIBUTING.md for newcomers
  [MISS] CHANGELOG               0/5   Keep a CHANGELOG.md of notable changes
  [MISS] SECURITY / conduct      0/5   Add SECURITY.md or CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md
  [PASS] No junk committed       5/5 

70 of 90 points.
```
sections.Notes:
- The score is a conversation starter, not a verdict: a tiny script doesn't need a CHANGELOG.
- Folders like `.git`, `node_modules`, `.venv` and `build` are not scanned.
- Use `repo-readme-generator` to draft a README and `gitignore-generator` for a `.gitignore`.

tools.name: license-header-adder
tools.summary: Add a license header (copyright + SPDX id) to the source files of a project; dry run first.

schema.description: Add license headers to source files.

arguments.help: use this text as the header instead
only these extensions, e.g. py,js (default: all known)
really change the files (default is a dry run)

sections.Purpose: Put a short license notice at the top of every source file, the way many open-source projects and the REUSE standard ask for: a copyright line, one sentence naming the license, and an `SPDX-License-Identifier` tag that tools can read. The tool knows the comment style of each language (`#`, `//`, `--`, `/* */`, `<!-- -->`), keeps shebang lines, Python encoding lines and XML declarations at the top, leaves files that already have a header alone, and preserves each file's line endings.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python license_header_adder.py PATH [PATH ...] [--license mit|apache-2.0|gpl-3.0|bsd-3-clause|isc|unlicense]
                               [--holder "Your Name"] [--year 2026] [--text-file header.txt]
                               [--ext py,js] [--apply]
```
**Dry run by default:** it lists the files that would get a header and the ones that already have one (it looks for `SPDX-License-Identifier`, "copyright" or "licensed under" in the first lines). Add `--apply` to write the changes. `--text-file` uses your own header text instead (it is wrapped in the right comment style for each file). Folders like `.git`, `node_modules`, `.venv`, `build` and `dist` are skipped, and files that can't be read as UTF-8 text are reported, not touched. Commit or back up first; the tool adds a header but cannot automatically remove it.
sections.Example:
```bash
python license_header_adder.py pyproj/ --holder "Demo Author" --year 2026
```
```
would add  pyproj\.github\workflows\ci.yml
would add  pyproj\app\__init__.py
would add  pyproj\app\core.py
would add  pyproj\app\legacy.py
would add  pyproj\app\main.py
has header   pyproj\app\models.py
would add  pyproj\app\utils.py
would add  pyproj\tests\test_core.py

Would add headers to 7 file(s); 1 already had one or were skipped. Use --apply to do it.
```
sections.Notes:
- This adds a short notice, not the full license text; keep the full text in a `LICENSE` file at the project root.
- Check that the license you choose is compatible with the project's dependencies and your employer's rules.
- Use `repo-health-scorer` to see whether the project has a LICENSE at all.

tools.name: import-graph-builder
tools.summary: Map the imports between the Python modules of a project, and find import cycles.

schema.description: Map imports between Python modules.

arguments.help: write the graph as JSON (new file)

sections.Purpose: See how the modules of a Python project depend on each other. The tool reads every `.py` file (without running any code), resolves `import x`, `from x import y` and relative imports like `from . import sibling`, and builds the graph of which module imports which. The report shows each module's imports and importers, the most-imported modules, isolated modules, the third-party packages the project needs, and **import cycles** (modules that import each other in a loop, a common cause of "partially initialised module" errors).
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python import_graph_builder.py PROJECT_FOLDER [--dot imports.dot] [--json imports.json] [--fail-on-cycles]
```
The folder is the import root: `pkg/sub/mod.py` becomes the module `pkg.sub.mod`. `__pycache__`, virtual environments and `node_modules` are skipped. `--dot` writes a Graphviz file (modules in a cycle are drawn in red) and `--json` the full data; both create new files and refuse to overwrite existing ones. The exit code is 1 when a file can't be parsed, or when cycles exist and you passed `--fail-on-cycles`, so it can guard a CI pipeline.
sections.Example:
```bash
python import_graph_builder.py pyproj/
```
```
7 module(s), 6 internal import(s)

MODULE                 IMPORTS IMPORTED BY  external packages
app                          0           0  -
app.core                     2           3  -
app.legacy                   0           0  -
app.main                     2           0  requests
app.models                   0           1  -
app.utils                    1           2  -
tests.test_core              1           0  -

Most imported: app.core (3), app.utils (2), app.models (1)
Isolated (no imports in or out): app, app.legacy
Third-party packages used: requests
CYCLE: app.core <-> app.utils
```
sections.Notes:
- Imports inside functions and `if TYPE_CHECKING:` blocks count too, and standard-library modules are not listed as third-party.
- Dynamic imports (`importlib.import_module(name)`) can't be seen.
- Render the graph with `dot -Tpng imports.dot -o imports.png` after installing Graphviz.
- Use `dead-code-finder` to find functions nobody calls.

tools.name: dead-code-finder
tools.summary: Find functions, methods and classes in a Python project that nothing seems to use.

schema.description: Find unused functions in a Python project.

arguments.help: extra names that are used from outside (entry points), comma-separated
also check the test files' own functions
exit with 1 if any are found

sections.Purpose: Spot functions, methods and classes that nothing in your project appears to use, so you can delete them with confidence or wire them up. The tool parses every Python file (without running it), collects the names of all definitions, then collects every name that is *mentioned* anywhere (calls, attribute access, imports, keyword arguments, and even strings, so `getattr(obj, "name")` and `__all__` lists keep things alive). A definition that is never mentioned is reported with its file and line. Code used only by the tests is listed separately.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Nothing to install.
sections.Usage:
```bash
python dead_code_finder.py PROJECT_FOLDER [--entry name1,name2] [--include-tests] [--fail-on-found]
```
Not judged: dunder methods (`__init__`...), `main` and similar entry points (`run`, `setup`, `handler`), `test_*` functions, and anything with a framework decorator (such as `@app.route` or `@pytest.fixture`), because those are called by something outside your code; the summary says how many were skipped. Add your own entry points with `--entry`. The exit code is 1 with `--fail-on-found` when unused code exists, which makes it a code-health gate.
sections.Example:
```bash
python dead_code_finder.py pyproj/
```
```
app/core.py:11  unused function _unused_helper
app/core.py:22  unused method never_called
app/legacy.py:4  unused function legacy_import
app/legacy.py:8  unused function legacy_export
app/utils.py:11  unused function old_format
app/utils.py:15  unused function uses_core

Checked 11 definition(s): 6 look unused, 0 used only by tests; 0 decorated (framework-registered) definition(s) were not judged.
This is a name-based guess: check each hit before deleting it.
```
sections.Notes:
- The check is **name-based**, not a full program analysis: two different functions called `render` count as one name, so some dead code will be missed, and code reached only by plugins, templates or reflection can look dead when it isn't. Review each hit.
- Common libraries like `vulture` do a deeper analysis; this tool is the dependency-free quick check.
- Use `import-graph-builder` to find whole modules that nothing imports.

tools.name: git-hook-installer
tools.summary: Install ready-made git hooks (pre-commit checks, commit-message rules...) from templates.

schema.description: Install git hooks from templates.

arguments.help: which hooks: pre-commit, pre-push, commit-msg, protect-branch
checks for pre-commit/pre-push: python, node, go (none)
a check to run in pre-commit/pre-push; repeat for several
really change the hooks (default is a dry run)

sections.Purpose: Catch mistakes before they reach the repository. Git can run a script at certain moments (a "hook"); this tool installs ready-made ones in one command: **pre-commit** and **pre-push** run the checks you choose (for example `ruff check .` and your tests) and stop the commit or push if one fails, **commit-msg** requires Conventional Commit messages (`feat: add search`, `fix(api): handle nulls`), and **protect-branch** refuses commits made directly on `main` or `master`. Each hook is a small, readable shell script.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Hooks run with the `sh` that comes with Git (including Git for Windows).
sections.Usage:
```bash
python git_hook_installer.py list
python git_hook_installer.py install pre-commit commit-msg [--preset python|node|go] [--command "make lint"] [--apply]
python git_hook_installer.py uninstall commit-msg [--apply]
```
Run it inside the repository, or point to it with `--repo`. **Dry run by default:** it shows each hook's location and the first lines of its script. With `--apply` the hooks are written and made executable. A hook that someone else wrote is never overwritten: it is renamed to `NAME.bak` first. Hooks installed by this tool are marked with a comment, so reinstalling replaces them and `uninstall` removes only those. `--command` can be repeated; presets add the usual commands for Python, Node or Go. `--hooks-dir` installs into another folder.
sections.Example:
```bash
python git_hook_installer.py install commit-msg pre-commit --hooks-dir hooks-demo/ --preset python
```
```
would install  commit-msg -> hooks-demo\commit-msg  (existing hook is kept as commit-msg.bak)
    first_line=$(head -n 1 "$1")
    case "$first_line" in Merge*|Revert*|fixup!*|squash!*) exit 0 ;; esac
    if echo "$first_line" | grep -Eq '^(feat|fix|docs|style|refactor|perf|test|build|ci|chore|revert)(\([^)]+\))?!?: .+'; then exit 0; fi
    echo "commit-msg: use the form type: description, e.g. feat: add search" >&2
would install  pre-commit -> hooks-demo\pre-commit  (new)
    set -e
    echo "pre-commit: ruff check ."
    ruff check . || { echo "pre-commit: failed: ruff check ." >&2; exit 1; }
    echo "pre-commit: python -m pytest -q"

Dry run. Use --apply to do it.
```
sections.Notes:
- Hooks live in `.git/hooks`, which isn't shared by `git clone`; each developer installs them (or a team keeps this command in its setup docs).
- In an emergency, `git commit --no-verify` skips the commit hooks; CI is the real safety net.
- Use `commit-message-linter` to check messages that are already written.
- The website demo shows what would be installed; installing hooks works on your own computer.

tools.name: changed-files-finder
tools.summary: List the files changed since a git ref and which monorepo projects they belong to.

schema.description: List changed paths since a git ref.

arguments.help: read saved `git diff --name-status` output instead of running git
projects affected when a library changes, e.g. libs/shared=apps/web
also count uncommitted and new files

sections.Purpose: In a monorepo, answer the question every CI pipeline asks: **what changed, and which projects does it affect?** The tool compares your branch with a ref (default `origin/main`, using the merge base like a pull request does), lists the added, modified, deleted and renamed files, and groups them by project folder (`apps/web`, `libs/shared`...). It can also add the projects that *depend* on a changed library, and print the result as plain text, JSON, one path per line or just the project names, ready to feed a build matrix.
sections.Install: Standard library only, Python 3.11+. Needs `git` on your PATH (unless you use `--from-file`).
sections.Usage:
```bash
python changed_files_finder.py [--ref origin/main] [--projects 'apps/*' 'libs/*'] [--depends libs/shared=apps/web,apps/api]
                               [--ext py,ts] [--exclude 'docs/*'] [--include-uncommitted]
                               [--format text|json|paths|projects]
python changed_files_finder.py --from-file diff.txt --projects 'apps/*'
```
`--projects` takes folder patterns: `apps/*` makes every direct subfolder of `apps` a project. Files in no project are grouped under their top-level folder, and files in the repository root under `(root)`. `--depends LIB=USER,USER` (repeatable) lists the projects to rebuild when `LIB` changes. `--from-file` reads saved `git diff --name-status` output, which is handy when the checkout isn't available. `--include-uncommitted` also counts working-tree changes and new files. Renames count for both the old and the new project.
sections.Example:
```bash
python changed_files_finder.py --from-file diff-names.txt --projects 'apps/*' 'libs/*' 'services/*' --depends libs/shared=apps/web,apps/mobile
```
```
10 changed file(s) in saved diff diff-names.txt

(root)  (1)
  modified     README.md
.github  (1)
  added        .github/workflows/ci.yml
apps/api  (2)
  added        apps/api/handlers/users.py
  deleted      apps/api/handlers/legacy.py
apps/web  (2)
  modified     apps/web/src/app.tsx
  modified     apps/web/package.json
docs  (1)
  modified     docs/guide.md
libs/shared  (1)
  renamed      libs/shared/new_name.py (from libs/shared/old_name.py)
libs/ui  (1)
  modified     libs/ui/button.tsx
services/billing  (1)
  modified     services/billing/main.go

Also affected through dependencies:
  apps/mobile  (depends on libs/shared)

2 added, 1 deleted, 6 modified, 1 renamed.
```
sections.Notes:
- The three-dot comparison (`ref...HEAD`) shows only what *your* branch changed, not what the main branch gained since you branched.
- In CI, make sure the base ref is fetched (for example `fetch-depth: 0` on GitHub Actions).
- Use `git-log-summarizer` and `changelog-generator` to describe the changes in words.

tools.name: bulk-repo-cloner
tools.summary: Clone many repositories from a list file, a GitHub user or organisation, or saved API output.

schema.description: Clone many repositories at once.

arguments.help: text file: owner/repo or git URL per line
saved GitHub API output (a JSON list of repositories)
use SSH URLs for API repositories
really clone (default only shows the plan)

sections.Purpose:
Clone many repositories in one go, from a text list, a GitHub user or organisation, or saved
GitHub API output. Forks and archived repositories are skipped unless you ask for them.
sections.Install: No dependencies beyond Python 3.11+ and `git`.
sections.Usage:
```
python bulk_repo_cloner.py --list repos.txt --dest ~/code
python bulk_repo_cloner.py --user octocat --language Python --apply
python bulk_repo_cloner.py --org my-team --pattern "api-*" --depth 1 --jobs 8 --apply
python bulk_repo_cloner.py --from-json gh-repos.json --dest repos
```

- The list file takes one `owner/repo` or git URL per line, plus an optional folder name.
  Lines starting with `#` are ignored.
- `--update` runs `git pull --ff-only` in repositories that already exist.
- Set `GITHUB_TOKEN` (or `GH_TOKEN`) for private repositories and higher rate limits. The token is
  only sent to the GitHub API host and never goes into clone URLs or output.
- Nothing is cloned until you pass `--apply`. Existing folders are never overwritten.

`--from-json gh-repos.json --dest repos`

```
4 repositories -> repos/

  web-app                  will clone        https://github.com/octo-demo/web-app.git [TypeScript]
  data-tools               will clone        https://github.com/octo-demo/data-tools.git [Python]
  dotfiles                 will clone        https://github.com/octo-demo/dotfiles.git [Shell]

Dry run: 4 action(s). Use --apply to start (4 at once).

- `--ssh` switches API repositories to their SSH URLs.

tools.name: git-large-file-finder
tools.summary: Find the biggest files in a repository's whole git history, including ones deleted long ago.

schema.description: Find the largest files in git history.

arguments.help: saved `type sha size path` lines instead of running git
branch or tag to scan, or 'all' for every branch and tag (all)
only files that are no longer in the latest commit
exit 1 if a file in the latest commit is bigger

sections.Purpose:
Find the biggest files across a repository's entire history, including files that were deleted
long ago but still make every clone heavy. Marks which ones are gone from the latest commit.
sections.Install: No dependencies beyond Python 3.11+ and `git`.
sections.Usage:
```
python git_large_file_finder.py                        # this repo, files of 1M or more
python git_large_file_finder.py --min-size 500k --top 50
python git_large_file_finder.py --only-removed         # history-only bloat
python git_large_file_finder.py --fail-over 5M         # CI guard for the latest commit
python git_large_file_finder.py --format json
python git_large_file_finder.py --from-file objects.txt
```

`objects.txt` can be made with:
`git rev-list --objects --all | git cat-file --batch-check='%(objecttype) %(objectname) %(objectsize) %(rest)'`

It only reads the repository and never changes it. For removals it prints a
`git filter-repo` command for you to run yourself, since that rewrites history.
sections.Example:
`--from-file git-objects.txt --min-size 1M`

```
4 file(s) at or above 1.0 MB, biggest first:

    46.0 MB  data/export-2025.csv  (2 versions)
    12.0 MB  assets/demo-video.mp4
     5.0 MB  build/app.zip
     1.2 MB  docs/manual.pdf
```
sections.Notes:
- A file stored under several names is counted once.
- Exit code 1 means `--fail-over` found a file in the latest commit above the limit, or git failed.
- Without git (like the browser demo) the "removed" marker isn't available.

tools.name: history-secret-scanner
tools.summary: Scan a repository's git history for secrets, including ones that were deleted afterwards.

schema.description: Find secrets anywhere in git history.

arguments.help: a saved `git log -p` output instead of running git
only commits after this, e.g. '6 months ago'
also report values that look like examples or placeholders

sections.Purpose:
Scan every commit on every branch for leaked secrets (cloud keys, tokens, private keys,
hard-coded passwords). Deleting a secret from the latest version doesn't remove it from history,
so this shows which commit added it and whether a later commit took it out.
sections.Install: No dependencies beyond Python 3.11+ and `git`.
sections.Usage:
```
python history_secret_scanner.py
python history_secret_scanner.py --repo ~/code/app --since "6 months ago"
python history_secret_scanner.py --max-count 200 --format json
python history_secret_scanner.py --from-file history.patch --include-placeholders
```

`history.patch` can be made with `git log -p --all -U0 > history.patch`.

It only reads the repository. Secrets are always shown masked (first and last three characters).
Exit code is 1 when anything is found, which suits a CI check; add `--exit-zero` to just report.
sections.Example:
`--from-file git-history.patch --include-placeholders`

```
4 possible secret(s) in the history:

  AWS access key: AKI**********PLE
    deploy/config.env  commit 9f3a1c2d by Dev One <dev1@example.com>
    Mon Nov 3 10:12:00 2026 +0000  (removed in 5e4d3c2b, still in history)
  Hard-coded credential: cor**********ple
    deploy/config.env  commit 9f3a1c2d by Dev One <dev1@example.com>
    Mon Nov 3 10:12:00 2026 +0000  (removed in 5e4d3c2b, still in history)
  Hard-coded credential: not**********890
    notes/todo.md  commit 7a6b5c4d by Dev One <dev1@example.com>
    Wed Nov 5 09:05:00 2026 +0000  (no later removal found)
  Private key block: ---**********---
    keys/id_deploy  commit 7a6b5c4d by Dev One <dev1@example.com>
    Wed Nov 5 09:05:00 2026 +0000  (no later removal found)

A secret that was ever committed must be treated as leaked: rotate it first, then clean the history if you need to.
```
sections.Notes:
- Only added lines are scanned. A removed line is used to mark an earlier finding as "removed".
- Values that look like examples or placeholders are skipped unless you pass
  `--include-placeholders`.
- This is a pattern check, so expect some false positives and some misses. Treat every real hit
  as leaked: rotate the secret before cleaning history.
