tools.name: markdown-report-builder
tools.summary: Assemble one markdown report from a folder (or list) of section files.

schema.description: Build a markdown report from section files.

arguments.help: date shown under the title, YYYY-MM-DD (today)
skip file names matching this, e.g. 'draft*' (repeatable)
write this new file instead of printing

sections.Purpose:
Combine a folder of section files into one markdown report, with a title, byline and optional
table of contents. Keep each section in its own file and rebuild the report whenever one changes.
sections.Install: No dependencies beyond Python 3.11+.
sections.Usage:
```
python markdown_report_builder.py sections/ --toc
python markdown_report_builder.py sections/ --title "Q4 review" --author "Ada" --output q4.md
python markdown_report_builder.py intro.md results.md --exclude "draft*"

`report-sections/ --exclude "draft*" --toc --date 2026-11-23`

```

tools.name: html-dashboard-builder
tools.summary: Turn a JSON file of metrics, chart series and tables into one self-contained HTML dashboard.

schema.description: Build a static HTML dashboard from JSON.

arguments.help: JSON with metrics, charts and tables
write this new file instead of printing

sections.Purpose:
Turn a small JSON file into a single, self-contained HTML dashboard: metric cards with up/down
changes, line and bar charts (inline SVG) and tables. No JavaScript, no internet needed, and it
follows the reader's light or dark mode.
sections.Install: No dependencies beyond Python 3.11+.
sections.Usage:
```
python html_dashboard_builder.py data.json --output dashboard.html
python html_dashboard_builder.py data.json > dashboard.html
```

The JSON can contain any of:
```
{"title": "...", "subtitle": "...",
 "metrics": [{"label": "Revenue", "value": 48210, "unit": "$", "change": 3.1,
              "lower_is_better": false}],
 "charts":  [{"title": "Signups", "type": "line" or "bar", "labels": [...], "values": [...]}],
 "tables":  [{"title": "Top pages", "columns": [...], "rows": [[...], ...]}]}
```
`change` is a percentage. Set `lower_is_better` for things like churn or open bugs, so a drop is
shown in green. `--output` refuses to overwrite a file unless you add `--force`.
sections.Example:
`dashboard-data.json --output dashboard.html`

```
Wrote dashboard.html (5,959 bytes). It needs no internet connection.
```
sections.Notes:
- All text from the JSON is HTML-escaped.
- Charts have tooltips and text labels for screen readers; tables use real header cells.
- Chart values should be numbers; the y axis starts at zero.

tools.name: chart-generator
tools.summary: Plot one or more CSV columns as a line or bar chart (SVG file or terminal text).

schema.description: Plot CSV columns as a chart.

arguments.help: the CSV file (with a header row)
numeric column to plot (repeat for several)
column for the x axis labels (default: row number)
write this new file instead of printing

sections.Purpose:
Plot one or more numeric CSV columns as a line or bar chart. It writes a clean SVG (colour-blind
safe palette, tooltips, a title and a legend) or prints a quick bar chart in the terminal.
sections.Install: No dependencies beyond Python 3.11+. The SVG is built by hand, so there is no plotting library.
sections.Usage:
```
python chart_generator.py sales.csv --x month --y revenue --output revenue.svg
python chart_generator.py sales.csv --x month --y revenue --y costs --type bar --title "2026"
python chart_generator.py sales.csv --x month --y revenue --format text
```

- `--y` can be repeated to plot several columns together.
- `--x` names the label column; without it the rows are numbered.
- Rows where a plotted column isn't a number are skipped and counted. Thousands separators
  such as `1,200` are understood.
- `--output` refuses to overwrite a file unless you add `--force`.
sections.Notes:
- The y axis always includes zero and uses round tick values.
- With many points only about a dozen x labels are drawn, so they stay readable.

tools.name: sparkline-printer
tools.summary: Print compact sparklines (tiny inline charts) from numbers, a text file or CSV columns.

schema.description: Print sparklines from numbers.

arguments.help: text file of numbers separated by spaces, commas or lines
CSV file to read columns from
CSV column to draw (repeat for several)
shrink longer series to this width
add min, max, last and change

sections.Purpose:
Print compact sparklines, tiny one-line charts, for a list of numbers, a text file or CSV columns.
Handy in terminal dashboards, logs, commit messages and reports.
sections.Install: No dependencies beyond Python 3.11+.
sections.Usage:
```
python sparkline_printer.py 3 7 4 9 12 8 15
python sparkline_printer.py --from-file latencies.txt --stats
python sparkline_printer.py --csv sales.csv --column revenue --column costs --stats
python sparkline_printer.py --from-file big.txt --width 40 --min 0 --max 100
```

- Each series is scaled between its own lowest and highest value. `--min` and `--max` fix the scale
  so several lines can be compared fairly.
- `--width` averages long series down to that many characters.
- `--stats` adds the min, max, last value and the percentage change from the first value.
- `--style auto` uses block characters when the terminal can show them and plain ASCII otherwise.
sections.Example:
`--csv sales-monthly.csv --column revenue --column costs --stats --style unicode`

```
revenue  ▁▂▃▄▅▆▆▆▅▆▇█  min 8,928  max 14,171  last 14,171 (+58.7%)
costs    ▂▁▃▃▆██▆▄██▇  min 5,317  max 8,911  last 8,576 (+49.2%)
```
sections.Notes:
- A flat series is drawn at mid height.
- In CSV columns, blank or non-numeric cells are skipped. Thousands separators are understood.

tools.name: time-tracking-report
tools.summary: Summarise hours by project, task, day or week from a CSV time log.

schema.description: Hours by project from a CSV time log.

arguments.help: CSV with date, project, [task], hours or start,end
round every entry up to a multiple of this, e.g. 15
hourly rate, overall or per project (repeatable)

sections.Purpose:
Turn a simple CSV time log into a report of hours by project, task, day or week, with each
group's share of the total and, if you give hourly rates, the amount to bill.
sections.Install: No dependencies beyond Python 3.11+.
sections.Usage:
```
python time_tracking_report.py log.csv
python time_tracking_report.py log.csv --group-by week --from 2026-11-01 --to 2026-11-30
python time_tracking_report.py log.csv --round 15 --rate 50 --rate website=80
python time_tracking_report.py log.csv --project website --format markdown
```

The log needs the columns `date` and `project`, plus either `hours` (like `1.5`) or `start` and
`end` (like `09:00` and `10:30`). A `task` column is optional. An end time earlier than the start
counts as working past midnight.

- `--round 15` rounds every entry up to the next 15 minutes.
- `--rate 50` is the default hourly rate; `--rate website=80` sets one project's rate.
- Bad rows are skipped with a note on stderr, and the rest of the report still runs.
- Formats: `text` (default), `markdown`, `json`, `csv`.
sections.Example:
`time-log.csv --rate 60 --rate website=85`

```
hours  share      amount
website       18.50    39%    1,572.50  ########
mobile-app    17.75    38%    1,065.00  ########
admin         11.00    23%      660.00  #####
Total         47.25           3,297.50

30 entries over 10 day(s), about 4.72 h per active day.
```
sections.Notes:
- Weeks are ISO weeks (Monday to Sunday), shown as `2026-W47`.
- Projects are sorted by hours; days and weeks are sorted by date.

tools.name: invoice-generator
tools.summary: Generate a print-ready HTML invoice (or a text summary) from a JSON file.

schema.description: Generate an HTML invoice from JSON.

arguments.help: write this new file instead of printing

sections.Purpose:
Turn a small JSON file into a clean, print-ready HTML invoice with exact totals, tax and
discount. Open it in a browser and use "Print to PDF" to get a PDF.
sections.Install: No dependencies beyond Python 3.11+.
sections.Usage:
```
python invoice_generator.py invoice.json --output invoice-2026-014.html
python invoice_generator.py invoice.json --format text
```

The JSON looks like this:
```
{"number": "2026-014", "date": "2026-11-20", "due_date": "2026-12-20", "currency": "USD",
 "from": {"name": "Ada Studio", "address": ["12 Analytical Way"], "email": "billing@example.com"},
 "to": {"name": "Northwind", "address": ["500 Harbour Road"]},
 "items": [{"description": "Website redesign", "quantity": 1, "unit_price": 2400}],
 "tax_rate": 8.5, "discount": 100, "notes": "Payment within 30 days."}
```
`number`, `from`, `to` and at least one item are required. `tax_rate` is a percentage and
`discount` is an amount taken off before tax. `--output` refuses to overwrite a file unless you add
`--force`.
sections.Example:
`invoice.json --format text`

```
Invoice 2026-014 for Northwind Traders
  Website redesign                      1 x  $2,400.00 =   $2,400.00
  Extra revision rounds                 3 x    $150.00 =     $450.00
  Hosting setup (hours)               4.5 x     $80.00 =     $360.00
  Subtotal                                                $3,210.00
  Discount                                                 -$100.00
  Tax 8.5%                                                  $264.35
  TOTAL DUE                                               $3,374.35
```
sections.Notes:
- Money uses exact decimal arithmetic, rounded half-up to cents per line and for the tax.
- Known currencies get a symbol (USD, EUR, GBP, INR, JPY); others show the code after the amount.
- All text is HTML-escaped. The page follows light/dark mode on screen and prints black on white.

tools.name: expense-summary
tools.summary: Monthly expense summary from a CSV: category breakdown, comparison, budgets and top items.

schema.description: Monthly expense summary from a CSV.

arguments.help: CSV with date, amount, category and optional note
YYYY-MM to summarise (default: the latest month)

sections.Purpose:
Summarise one month of spending from a CSV: totals by category with each category's share,
the change since the month before, the biggest single expenses, a daily average and budget checks.
sections.Install: No dependencies beyond Python 3.11+.
sections.Usage:
```
python expense_summary.py expenses.csv
python expense_summary.py expenses.csv --month 2026-10 --top 5
python expense_summary.py expenses.csv --budget groceries=400 --budget "eating out=120"
python expense_summary.py expenses.csv --format markdown
```

The CSV needs `date` (YYYY-MM-DD), `amount` and `category` columns; `note` is optional. It is the
same layout `expense-logger` writes. Without `--month` the latest month in the file is used.

- Amounts use exact decimal arithmetic, and `1,020.10` style numbers are understood.
- Rows that can't be read are skipped and listed on stderr, so one typo doesn't stop the report.
- Rows with no category are grouped as `uncategorised`.
- Formats: `text` (default), `markdown`, `json`.
sections.Example:
`expenses-2026.csv --budget groceries=400 --budget dining=150`

```
Expenses for 2026-11 (27 entries)

Category       Amount  Share  vs 2026-10
rent           900.00    46%       +0.00
utilities      501.26    25%     +389.43
dining         186.71     9%      +29.27
transport      129.68     7%      -62.08
fun            113.46     6%       -7.23
groceries       92.65     5%      -61.55
coffee          26.87     1%       +3.05
health          26.02     1%     -182.00
Total        1,976.65            +108.89

Daily average: 65.89
Biggest expenses:
  2026-11-01     900.00  rent - monthly rent
  2026-11-19     110.94  utilities - utilities spend
  2026-11-28     102.68  utilities - utilities spend
Budgets:
  groceries: 92.65 of 400.00 (307.35 left)
  dining: 186.71 of 150.00 (OVER by 36.71)
```
sections.Notes:
- The change column compares with the previous calendar month, if the file has it.
- The daily average divides by the number of days in the month.

tools.name: habit-streak-report
tools.summary: Report habit streaks and consistency from a habit-tracker JSON file.

schema.description: Habit streaks and consistency report.

sections.Purpose:
Report on your habits from a `habit-tracker` file: current and best streaks, how consistent you
were over the last few weeks, a 14-day strip for each habit and which streaks are at risk today.
sections.Install: No dependencies beyond Python 3.11+.
sections.Usage:
```
python habit_streak_report.py ~/.habits.json
python habit_streak_report.py ~/.habits.json --window 60 --habit read --habit exercise
python habit_streak_report.py ~/.habits.json --format markdown
python habit_streak_report.py habits.json --today 2026-01-08
```

The file looks like `{"habits": {"read": ["2026-01-01", "2026-01-02"], "exercise": [...]}}`, which
is what `habit-tracker` writes. Duplicate dates are counted once.

- A streak is a run of consecutive days. It stays alive until the end of today, so a habit you did
  yesterday still counts, and is flagged "at risk" until you do it.
- `--window` sets how many days the consistency percentage covers (default 30).
- Habits are ordered by current streak, then consistency.
- Formats: `text` (default), `markdown`, `json`.
sections.Example:
`habits.json --today 2026-01-08 --window 7`

```
Habit streaks as of 2026-01-08

          streak  best  last 7d  last 14 days  note
read           3     3     71%     ------###-###-  do it today to keep the streak
meditate       1     1     14%     ------------#-  do it today to keep the streak
exercise       0     5     71%     -------#####--  broken 2 day(s) ago

Overall: 11 check-ins of 21 possible (52%) in the last 7 days.
Longest running streak: read (3 day(s)).
```
sections.Notes:
- In the 14-day strip `#` is a day you did it and `-` is a day you didn't; the last character is today.
- Dates after `--today` are ignored.

tools.name: email-report-sender
tools.summary: Email a report (text or HTML, with attachments) over SMTP. Previews first; --send sends.

schema.description: Email a report over SMTP (preview by default).

arguments.help: optional HTML version of the body
environment variable holding the SMTP password (SMTP_PASSWORD)

sections.Purpose:
Email a report, as plain text with an optional HTML version and attachments, over SMTP. It shows
a preview of exactly what would go out and only sends when you add `--send`.
sections.Install: No dependencies beyond Python 3.11+.
sections.Usage:
```
python email_report_sender.py --to team@example.com --from me@example.com \
    --subject "Weekly report" --body-file report.txt --attach report.pdf
python email_report_sender.py ... --send
python email_report_sender.py ... --html-file report.html --cc boss@example.com --send
```

SMTP settings come from the environment, so no secret goes on the command line or into a file:

| Variable | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `SMTP_HOST` | the SMTP server (or pass `--smtp-host`) |
| `SMTP_PORT` | port; defaults to 587 (starttls), 465 (ssl) or 25 (none) |
| `SMTP_USER` | login name, also used as the sender if `--from` is missing |
| `SMTP_PASSWORD` | password; use `--password-env NAME` to read another variable |
| `REPORT_FROM` | default sender |

`--security` picks `starttls` (default), `ssl` or `none`. `--bcc` recipients get the mail but are
never written into the message headers. Attachments are limited to 10 MB in total. The password
is never printed.
sections.Example:
`--to team@example.com --from reports@example.com --subject "Weekly report" --body-file report-body.txt --attach report-sections/02-results.md`

```
Preview (nothing sent):

From:    reports@example.com
To:      team@example.com
Subject: Weekly report
Sending to: 1 recipient(s)
Attachments:
  02-results.md  (138 bytes)

--- message ---
Hello team,

Here is this week's summary.

- 2 releases shipped
- Open bugs down to 9
- P95 latency 280 ms

Full details are in the attached report.

Thanks,
Platform team

Add --send to deliver it.
```
sections.Notes:
- Addresses are checked, and subjects or addresses containing line breaks are refused, so a
  report title can't be used to inject extra headers.
- The browser demo only shows the preview. Sending needs a real SMTP server.
- Tested against a local fake SMTP server, not against a real mail provider.

tools.name: process-monitor
tools.summary: Watch the CPU and memory use of chosen processes, grouped by name.

schema.description: Watch CPU and memory of chosen processes.

arguments.help: process names or patterns (all if none)
alert above this CPU %% (100 = one core)
alert above this memory in MB

sections.Purpose:
Watch the CPU and memory use of the processes you care about. Processes are grouped by name, so
twelve `chrome` helpers show up as one line with a count, a total memory figure and a CPU %.
sections.Install: No dependencies beyond Python 3.11+. It uses `ps` on Linux and macOS and PowerShell on Windows.
sections.Usage:
```
python process_monitor.py                       # everything, sorted by CPU
python process_monitor.py chrome python         # names match as substrings, or use patterns
python process_monitor.py "nginx*" --interval 5 --count 12
python process_monitor.py postgres --cpu-over 80 --mem-over 2000
python process_monitor.py --format csv > snapshot.csv
```

- `CPU %` is measured between two samples `--interval` seconds apart; 100 means one full core.
- `--cpu-over` and `--mem-over` (MB) print `ALERT` lines and make the exit code 1, which is handy
  in a cron job or a script.
- `--from-file` reads a saved `ps -axo pid=,etime=,cputime=,rss=,comm=` listing. That is a single
  snapshot, so it shows total CPU time and memory instead of CPU %.
sections.Example:
`--from-file ps-snapshot.txt chrome nginx python node`

```
process  count   memory MB   CPU time
python       1      1806.6    1:55:00
chrome       3       996.1    2:39:21
node         2       502.9    0:16:14
nginx        4       156.2    0:36:57
```
sections.Notes:
- Names are the program name only (no path or arguments).
- On Windows the memory figure is the working set; on Linux and macOS it is resident memory.
- Short-lived processes that start and end between two samples are not counted.

tools.name: service-status-checker
tools.summary: Check whether named services are running (systemd, Windows services or launchd).

schema.description: Check whether services are running.

arguments.help: service names (or part of the display name)
saved `systemctl list-units`, `sc query` or `launchctl list` output
the state that counts as OK (running)

sections.Purpose:
Check whether named services are running. It works with systemd on Linux, Windows services and
launchd on macOS, and exits with 1 if any service isn't in the state you expect, so it is easy to
use from a script, a cron job or a health check.
sections.Install:
No dependencies beyond Python 3.11+. It uses `systemctl`, `sc` or `launchctl`, whichever your
system has.
sections.Usage:
```
python service_status_checker.py nginx postgresql
python service_status_checker.py "print spooler" w32time       # Windows display names work too
python service_status_checker.py docker --expect stopped
python service_status_checker.py --list                       # everything found
python service_status_checker.py nginx --format json
python service_status_checker.py nginx --from-file services.txt
```

- A name matches exactly first (with or without `.service`), then the display name, then as part of
  either.
- States are `running`, `stopped`, `failed`, or the system's own word (for example
  `start pending`). Services that are not found count as a failure.
- `--from-file` reads saved `systemctl list-units --type=service --all --no-legend --plain`,
  `sc query state= all` or `launchctl list` output.
sections.Example:
`--from-file services-systemctl.txt nginx redis docker cron --list`

```
OK   nginx: running (active/running)
FAIL redis-server: failed (failed/failed)
FAIL docker: stopped (inactive/dead)
OK   cron: running (active/running)
  redis-server  failed    Advanced key-value store
  cron          running   Regular background program processing
  nginx         running   A high performance web server
  postgresql    running   PostgreSQL database server
  ssh           running   OpenBSD Secure Shell server
  docker        stopped   Docker Application Container Engine

2 of 4 as expected (running).
```
sections.Notes:
- It only reads service state. It never starts or stops anything.
- Windows `sc query` can take a few seconds on a busy machine.

tools.name: resource-logger
tools.summary: Log CPU, memory and disk use to a CSV file at a fixed interval.

schema.description: Log CPU, memory and disk use to CSV.

arguments.help: CSV file to write (a new file)
repeatable fake readings instead of the real machine (for demos)

sections.Purpose:
Record CPU, memory and disk use to a CSV file at a fixed interval, so you can see what a machine
was doing overnight or while a job ran. Open the CSV in a spreadsheet, or chart it with
`chart-generator`.
sections.Install:
No dependencies beyond Python 3.11+. On Windows it asks PowerShell for CPU and memory, on macOS it
reads `top` and `vm_stat`, and on Linux it reads `/proc`.
sections.Usage:
```
python resource_logger.py --interval 5 --count 12
python resource_logger.py --output usage.csv --interval 60 --count 1440     # one day, per minute
python resource_logger.py --output usage.csv --append --interval 60 --count 60
python resource_logger.py --disk D:\ --quiet --output usage.csv
```

- `--output` creates a new CSV with a header row. An existing file is never overwritten; add
  `--append` to keep adding rows to it (the header is written only once).
- Each row is flushed to disk as it is written, so you lose nothing if you stop it with Ctrl+C.
- A min/avg/max summary is printed at the end.
- `--simulate` produces repeatable fake readings (use `--start` for the first timestamp). It's for
  demos and for trying out charts without a real machine.
sections.Notes:
- CPU % is the whole machine's busy time between samples. On Linux the first reading waits a
  quarter of a second to get a baseline.
- Memory used excludes cache that can be freed (Linux `MemAvailable`).
- CSV columns: `time`, `cpu_percent`, `memory_percent`, `memory_used_mb`, `disk_percent`,
  `disk_free_gb`.

tools.name: speed-tester
tools.summary: Measure download speed by fetching a test file, or summarise saved timings.

schema.description: Measure download speed.

arguments.help: file to download (a 25 MB test file)
stop each run after this many bytes
stop each run after this many seconds (30)
exit 1 if the average is below this
append each run to this CSV file
summarise saved 'bytes seconds' lines instead of downloading

sections.Purpose:
Measure your download speed by fetching a test file and timing it. It shows each run, the time to
the first byte, and the average, median, best and worst speed. It can append every run to a CSV so
you can watch how your connection changes through the day.
sections.Install: No dependencies beyond Python 3.11+.
sections.Usage:
```
python speed_tester.py                                  # 3 runs against a 25 MB test file
python speed_tester.py --runs 5 --max-seconds 10
python speed_tester.py --url https://example.com/100MB.bin --max-bytes 50000000
python speed_tester.py --log speed.csv --min-mbps 50     # exit 1 if the average is below 50
python speed_tester.py --from-file speed-runs.txt
```

- The default file is a public 25 MB test file from Cloudflare. Use `--url` for your own server.
  Only `http://` and `https://` addresses are accepted.
- `--max-bytes` and `--max-seconds` stop a run early, so slow links don't download for ages.
- `--log` appends rows (`time,url,bytes,seconds,mbps`) to a CSV and writes the header once.
- `--from-file` summarises saved `bytes seconds` lines without any network access.
sections.Example:
`--from-file speed-runs.txt`

```
1.   25.0 MB in  2.31 s =    86.6 Mbit/s   10.8 MB/s
  2.   25.0 MB in  2.05 s =    97.6 Mbit/s   12.2 MB/s
  3.   25.0 MB in  3.40 s =    58.8 Mbit/s    7.4 MB/s
  4.   25.0 MB in  2.18 s =    91.7 Mbit/s   11.5 MB/s

4 run(s): average 83.7 Mbit/s, median 89.2, best 97.6, worst 58.8
```
sections.Notes:
- Speeds are in megabits per second (1 Mbit/s = 125,000 bytes per second), the way providers
  quote them. The MB/s column is megabytes per second.
- This measures one connection to one server, so results vary with the server and the time of day.
- The browser demo can only summarise saved timings; it can't download.

tools.name: wifi-info-reporter
tools.summary: Report the current Wi-Fi network, signal strength and speed (Windows, macOS and Linux).

schema.description: Report the current Wi-Fi connection.

arguments.help: saved `netsh wlan show interfaces`, airport -I or nmcli output
exit 1 if the signal is below this %%

sections.Purpose:
Report which Wi-Fi network you are on and how good the connection is: signal percentage and dBm,
band, channel, security type and link speed. Handy for diagnosing a flaky connection or logging
Wi-Fi quality from a script.
sections.Install:
No dependencies beyond Python 3.11+. It uses `netsh` on Windows, `nmcli` on Linux and the
`airport` tool on macOS.
sections.Usage:
```
python wifi_info_reporter.py
python wifi_info_reporter.py --nearby                 # also list other networks (Linux)
python wifi_info_reporter.py --min-signal 40          # exit 1 if the signal is weaker than 40%
python wifi_info_reporter.py --format json
python wifi_info_reporter.py --from-file wifi.txt
```

- Signal is shown as a percentage with a word (`excellent` from 75%, `good` from 50%, `fair` from
  30%, otherwise `weak`). Where the system only gives a percentage the dBm value is estimated.
- The exit code is 1 when you are not connected or the signal is below `--min-signal`.
- `--from-file` reads saved `netsh wlan show interfaces`, `airport -I` or `nmcli -t` output.
sections.Example:
`--from-file netsh-wlan.txt`

```
Network:   HomeNet-5G
Signal:    82% excellent (-59 dBm)
Band:      5 GHz
Channel:   44
Security:  WPA2-Personal
Speed:     866.7 Mbit/s
Radio:     802.11ax
BSSID:     aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff
```
sections.Notes:
- macOS 14.4 and later removed the `airport` command, so live macOS reports aren't available
  there; use a saved report with `--from-file`.
- It only reads connection details. It never connects, disconnects or changes any setting.
- The SSID and BSSID identify your network, so think before posting the output publicly.

tools.name: task-scheduler-helper
tools.summary: Generate cron, Task Scheduler, launchd or systemd entries to run a command on a schedule.

schema.description: Generate scheduler entries for a command.

arguments.help: the command to run, e.g. 'python backup.py'
time of day, HH:MM (09:00); hourly uses only the minute
append the command's output to this file
which scheduler to write for (auto = this system's)

sections.Purpose:
Turn "run this command every weekday at 08:30" into ready-to-paste entries for the system's
scheduler: a crontab line, a Windows Task Scheduler (`schtasks`) command, a macOS launchd plist, or
systemd service and timer files. You don't need to remember each system's syntax.
sections.Install: No dependencies beyond Python 3.11+.
sections.Usage:
```
python task_scheduler_helper.py --command "python backup.py" --every daily --at 02:30
python task_scheduler_helper.py --command "python sync.py" --every 15m --target cron
python task_scheduler_helper.py --command "python report.py" --every weekly --days mon,fri --at 08:00
python task_scheduler_helper.py --command "python report.py" --every monthly --day-of-month 1 --target all
python task_scheduler_helper.py --command "python backup.py" --log ~/backup.log --name nightly-backup
```

- `--every` takes `15m`, `2h`, `hourly`, `daily`, `weekly` or `monthly`. Use `--at HH:MM` for the
  time of day, `--days mon,wed,fri` for weekly and `--day-of-month 1-28` for monthly.
- `--target` picks `cron`, `schtasks`, `launchd` or `systemd`; the default is the right one for this
  system and `all` prints all four.
- `--log FILE` appends the command's output to that file.
- It only prints text. Nothing is installed, so you can read it first and then paste or save it.
sections.Example:
`--command "python C:/scripts/backup.py --apply" --name nightly-backup --every weekly --days mon,wed,fri --at 02:30 --target all`

```
Schedule: every Mon, Wed, Fri at 02:30
Nothing has been installed; copy what you need.

============ cron ============
# Add with: crontab -e   (list with: crontab -l)
30 2 * * MON,WED,FRI python C:/scripts/backup.py --apply

============ schtasks ============
REM Run in a Command Prompt. Remove later with: schtasks /Delete /TN "nightly-backup"
schtasks /Create /TN "nightly-backup" /TR "python C:/scripts/backup.py --apply" /SC WEEKLY /D MON,WED,FRI /ST 02:30 /F

============ launchd ============
# Save as ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.user.nightly-backup.plist, then: launchctl load ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.user.nightly-backup.plist
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<plist version="1.0">
<dict>
  <key>Label</key>
  <string>com.user.nightly-backup</string>
  <key>ProgramArguments</key>
  <array>
    <string>python</string>
    <string>C:/scripts/backup.py</string>
    <string>--apply</string>
  </array>
  <key>StartCalendarInterval</key>
  <array>
    <dict><key>Hour</key><integer>2</integer><key>Minute</key><integer>30</integer><key>Weekday</key><integer>1</integer></dict>
    <dict><key>Hour</key><integer>2</integer><key>Minute</key><integer>30</integer><key>Weekday</key><integer>3</integer></dict>
    <dict><key>Hour</key><integer>2</integer><key>Minute</key><integer>30</integer><key>Weekday</key><integer>5</integer></dict>
  </array>
</dict>
</plist>

============ systemd ============
# Save as ~/.config/systemd/user/nightly-backup.service
[Unit]
Description=nightly-backup

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=python C:/scripts/backup.py --apply

# Save as ~/.config/systemd/user/nightly-backup.timer
[Unit]
Description=Run nightly-backup

[Timer]
OnCalendar=Mon,Wed,Fri *-*-* 02:30:00
Persistent=true

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target

# Then: systemctl --user daemon-reload && systemctl --user enable --now nightly-backup.timer
```
sections.Notes:
- Monthly days are limited to 1-28 so the task runs in every month, including February.
- Use full paths in commands: schedulers don't start in your usual folder or with your usual PATH.
- launchd calls Sunday 0 and Monday 1; the generated plist already takes care of that.

tools.name: startup-lister
tools.summary: List the programs that start automatically with the OS (Windows, macOS and Linux).

schema.description: List programs that start with the OS.

arguments.help: scan this folder like a home folder (.config/autostart, Library/LaunchAgents, Startup) instead of the real system

sections.Purpose:
List every program that starts automatically with your OS, so you can see what slows down your
login or runs without you knowing. It flags disabled entries and ones that run from a temp or
downloads folder, which is unusual for something legitimate.
sections.Install: No dependencies beyond Python 3.11+.
sections.Usage:
```
python startup_lister.py
python startup_lister.py --only-enabled
python startup_lister.py --format csv > startup.csv
python startup_lister.py --root ~/backup-of-home        # scan a copy of a home folder
```

What it looks at:

| System | Places |
|---|---|
| Windows | the `Run` and `RunOnce` registry keys (user and machine) and the Startup folders |
| macOS | `~/Library/LaunchAgents`, `/Library/LaunchAgents` and `/Library/LaunchDaemons` |
| Linux | `~/.config/autostart` and `/etc/xdg/autostart` |

It only reads; it never disables or removes anything. To turn an entry off, use your system's own
tool (Task Manager's Startup tab, `launchctl unload`, or your desktop's Startup Applications).
sections.Example:
`--root startup-demo`

```
autostart (desktop) (3)
  Dropbox: dropbox start -i
  Old Tool: /opt/old/tool  [disabled]
  Slack: /usr/bin/slack --startup

launchd agent (2)
  com.example.manual: /usr/local/bin/manual  [disabled]
  com.example.sync: /usr/local/bin/sync --daemon

startup folder (1)
  OneDrive: startup-demo\Startup\OneDrive.cmd

6 item(s), 4 enabled, 2 disabled.
```
sections.Notes:
- A launchd entry only counts as enabled if it has `RunAtLoad` or `KeepAlive`.
- Linux autostart entries with `Hidden=true` or `X-GNOME-Autostart-enabled=false` show as
  disabled.
- Windows services and scheduled tasks that start at boot are not covered; use
  `service-status-checker` for services.

tools.name: event-log-exporter
tools.summary: Export recent system events (journald, Windows Event Log or macOS log) to a file.

schema.description: Export recent system events to a file.

arguments.help: write to this new file (else print)
only the last N hours (24 when reading live)
only events whose source contains this text
saved journalctl -o json, Get-WinEvent JSON or `log show` ndjson

sections.Purpose:
Export recent system events, with errors and warnings by default, to a CSV, JSON or text file you
can attach to a bug report, search, or keep as a record. It reads journald on Linux, the Windows
Event Log (System and Application) and the unified log on macOS, and gives every event the same
columns: `time`, `level`, `source`, `id`, `message`.
sections.Install:
No dependencies beyond Python 3.11+. It uses `journalctl`, PowerShell or `log` depending on the
system.
sections.Usage:
```
python event_log_exporter.py --output events.csv                  # last 24 hours, warnings and errors
python event_log_exporter.py --hours 6 --level error --format json --output errors.json
python event_log_exporter.py --source nginx --contains timeout --format text
python event_log_exporter.py --level info --limit 5000 --format jsonl --output all.jsonl
python event_log_exporter.py --from-file saved-journal.jsonl
```

- `--level` is the lowest level to include: `info`, `warning` (default) or `error`.
- `--output` writes a new file and refuses to overwrite one unless you add `--force`.
- Messages are tidied onto one line. A one-line summary (counts per level and the busiest sources)
  is printed after the export.
- `--from-file` reads saved `journalctl -o json`, `Get-WinEvent | ConvertTo-Json` or
  `log show --style ndjson` output, so you can filter an export that someone sent you.
sections.Example:
`--from-file journal-events.jsonl --level error --format text`

```
2026-11-24T03:07:00Z  ERROR   cron.service: I/O error, dev sda, sector 4096
2026-11-24T03:28:00Z  ERROR   sshd.service: I/O error, dev sda, sector 4096
2026-11-24T03:44:00Z  ERROR   cron.service: I/O error, dev sda, sector 4096
2026-11-24T04:32:00Z  ERROR   nginx.service: I/O error, dev sda, sector 4096
2026-11-24T05:36:00Z  ERROR   systemd: Failed to start Redis service
2026-11-24T06:49:00Z  ERROR   sshd.service: I/O error, dev sda, sector 4096
2026-11-24T08:11:00Z  ERROR   cron.service: Failed to start Redis service
2026-11-24T09:52:00Z  ERROR   cron.service: Failed to start Redis service
2026-11-24T10:14:00Z  ERROR   cron.service: Failed to start Redis service
2026-11-24T11:00:00Z  ERROR   sshd.service: Failed to start Redis service

10 event(s): 10 error; top sources: cron.service (5), sshd.service (3), nginx.service (1)
```
sections.Notes:
- Reading the Windows Security log or some journal entries may need administrator or `sudo`
  rights; this tool only asks for System and Application events.
- System logs can contain usernames, hostnames and IP addresses, so check an export before sharing.
- On Windows, events with no text message are exported with an empty message.

tools.name: battery-reporter
tools.summary: Report battery charge and health, and keep a simple charge history in a CSV.

schema.description: Report battery charge and health.

arguments.help: append this reading to a history CSV
exit 1 if health is below this %%

sections.Purpose:
Report your battery's charge, status and health (how much capacity it has left compared with when
it was new), plus cycle count and an estimate of the time left. It can also log readings to a CSV
and summarise that history, so you can see how fast the battery is wearing out.
sections.Install:
No dependencies beyond Python 3.11+. It reads `/sys/class/power_supply` on Linux, `ioreg` on macOS
and PowerShell plus `powercfg` on Windows.
sections.Usage:
```
python battery_reporter.py
python battery_reporter.py --format json
python battery_reporter.py --log battery.csv           # run it daily from a scheduler
python battery_reporter.py --history battery.csv       # summarise the log
python battery_reporter.py --min-health 70             # exit 1 if the battery is worn out
python battery_reporter.py --sysfs ./power_supply      # read a saved Linux folder
```

- Health is the full-charge capacity as a percentage of the design capacity: 80% or more is good,
  60-80% is fair, below that is worn.
- The time left is only estimated while discharging, from the current draw.
- `--log` appends `time,percent,status,health` to a CSV (the header is written once). Use
  `task-scheduler-helper` to run it every day, then `--history` shows the trend.
- No battery, such as on a desktop, exits with 1 and a message.
sections.Example:
`--sysfs battery-demo`

```
Charge:    74% (Discharging)
Health:    82.4% of design capacity (good)
Capacity:  41,200 now vs 50,000 when new (mWh or mAh)
Cycles:    312
Type:      Li-ion
Model:     SMP DELL 7XFMD
Draw:      8.4 W
Time left: 3.6 h
```
sections.Notes:
- Windows builds a temporary battery report with `powercfg` to read the capacities; nothing is
  kept. If it isn't available you still get the charge and status.
- Numbers come from the battery's own firmware, so different laptops differ a little.
- The capacity unit (mWh or mAh) depends on the system; the ratio is what matters.

tools.name: process-cleaner
tools.summary: Stop duplicate or runaway processes by name. Dry-run by default; --apply stops them.

schema.description: Stop duplicate or runaway processes by name.

arguments.help: process names or patterns, e.g. node 'python*'
stop extra copies, keeping the oldest --keep of each name
stop processes averaging more than this CPU %% since they started
stop processes using more than this MB
ignore processes younger than this many seconds (60)
seconds to wait after asking a process to quit (5)
kill what ignores the polite request
really stop processes (default only shows the plan)

sections.Purpose:
Stop processes that pile up or run away: extra copies of the same program (for example five
stray `node` dev servers) and processes that use too much memory or have been hogging CPU. It
shows exactly what it would stop first, and only acts when you add `--apply`.
sections.Install:
No dependencies beyond Python 3.11+. It uses `ps` on Linux and macOS, and PowerShell and
`taskkill` on Windows.
sections.Usage:
```
python process_cleaner.py node --duplicates                  # show the plan (nothing is stopped)
python process_cleaner.py node --duplicates --apply          # keep the oldest, stop the rest
python process_cleaner.py "python*" --mem-over 2000 --apply  # anything over 2 GB
python process_cleaner.py ffmpeg --cpu-over 90 --min-age 300 --apply
python process_cleaner.py chrome --duplicates --keep 5 --force --apply
python process_cleaner.py nginx --duplicates --from-file ps.txt
```

Safety rules built in:
- You must name the programs (exact names or patterns like `python*`) and say what to look for
  (`--duplicates`, `--cpu-over` or `--mem-over`). It never acts on "everything".
- System processes (`systemd`, `explorer`, `svchost`, `sshd`, `launchd` and similar), the first few
  process ids, and this tool and its parent are always skipped.
- Processes younger than `--min-age` seconds (60) are ignored for the runaway checks.
- `--apply` first asks each process to quit and waits `--grace` seconds (5). Only with `--force`
  does it kill one that ignores the request. Some Windows console programs refuse the polite
  request, so they need `--force`.
- `--cpu-over` is the average CPU use over the process's whole life, since a one-off sample is
  noisy. `--duplicates` keeps the oldest `--keep` copies.
sections.Example:
`nginx systemd --duplicates --min-age 0 --from-file ps-snapshot.txt`

```
skip        1  systemd  (protected system process)
would stop    1051  nginx                   51 MB  duplicate: instance 2 of 4 (keeping the oldest 1)
would stop    1052  nginx                   50 MB  duplicate: instance 3 of 4 (keeping the oldest 1)
would stop    1053  nginx                   48 MB  duplicate: instance 4 of 4 (keeping the oldest 1)

Dry run: 3 process(es) would be stopped. Add --apply to do it.
```
sections.Notes:
- Be careful with programs that legitimately run many copies (browsers, `svchost`, build workers).
  Read the dry-run output before using `--apply`.
- Stopping a process loses any unsaved work in it.
- `--from-file` only prints a plan; `--apply` needs the live system.
